EconNexus Study Guide. A Level and Introductory University Economics. Diagram Mastery Series

106 Complex Economics Diagrams You Actually Need to Master

Indirect taxes, externalities, monopoly, price discrimination, monopsony labour markets, the full AD/AS ecosystem including self correction and stagflation, the Phillips curve, real wage unemployment, economic growth, the foreign exchange market, the circular flow of income, the Keynesian multiplier, money and loanable funds markets, oligopoly, contestable markets, the Laffer curve, the Lorenz curve, and the balance of payments, joined by a full run of market structure, consumer theory, and producer theory diagrams, and now extended into advanced macroeconomic modelling: the IS-LM model, crowding out, the Solow-Swan and AK growth models, and the business cycle wave. Every diagram is built stage by stage, twenty four of them respond to a slider in real time so you can set your own numbers, and every diagram ends with a short self test.

EconNexus Deep Dive Levels: A Level (Edexcel, AQA, CIE 9708/9609), IB Economics, IGCSE Economics, AP Micro and Macro, first year university economics Reading and interaction time: around 220 minutes 75 interactive diagrams, twenty four fully customisable in real time, each checked algebraically for consistent gradients and intersections Diagram scope guided by the topics flagged as highest complexity in major examiner reports and mark schemes, and the full market structure, consumer/producer theory, and advanced macroeconomics syllabus, including the parts most guides skip

Most students do not lose marks in economics because they misunderstand the theory in words. They lose marks because, under exam pressure, they draw a diagram slightly wrong: the wrong curve shifts, a shaded area sits in the wrong place, or they forget which of three prices on the same graph is the one the question actually wants. This guide takes seventy five diagrams that examiners' reports repeatedly flag as the ones students get wrong, and rebuilds each one stage by stage so you can watch the shift actually happen instead of only seeing the finished picture. Diagrams one through eight cover microeconomics: markets, market failure and market structure. Nine through fourteen cover the AD/AS macroeconomic model as one connected story. Fifteen covers the foreign exchange market. The ten diagrams from sixteen through twenty five extend the set into the circular flow of income, the Keynesian multiplier, money and loanable funds markets, oligopoly, contestable markets, tax policy, income inequality, and the balance of payments. Diagrams twenty six through thirty return to core microeconomics with market equilibrium, price elasticity, price controls, consumer and producer surplus, and short-run cost curves. Thirty one through forty five fill in the market structure, consumer theory and producer theory diagrams that most study guides skip entirely: monopolistic competition, the long run average cost curve, game theory, dominant firm pricing, perfect price discrimination, natural monopoly regulation, indifference curves, income and substitution effects, utility theory, isoquants and isocosts, the backward bending labour supply curve, public goods, the Edgeworth box, and bilateral monopoly. Forty six through fifty five complete the intermediate set with income and cross elasticity, the elasticity of supply over time, buffer stock schemes, comparative advantage, tariffs and quotas, the law of diminishing returns, Keynesian versus classical aggregate supply, the marginal revenue product theory of labour demand, and the money multiplier. Fifty six through fifty nine round out market failure and market structure with demerit goods, a positive externality of production, cartels and collusive oligopoly, and merit goods and information failure. Sixty through seventy cover a run of macro policy and advanced oligopoly diagrams: the investment decision, exchange rate systems, the quantity theory of money, the business cycle, purchasing power parity, the monetary transmission mechanism, Cournot and Bertrand competition, Stackelberg leadership, repeated games, and peak-load pricing. Seventy one through seventy five bring the whole guide up to the level of a first year university macroeconomics course: the IS-LM model, the crowding-out effect, the Solow-Swan growth model, the AK endogenous growth model, and the output gap as a continuous business cycle wave. Seventy six through ninety five add a further run of university-level macro, unemployment and behavioural economics diagrams: the Mundell-Fleming model, the impossible trinity, Okun's law, the Fisher equation, quantitative easing, the Kuznets curve, the tragedy of the commons, Ricardian equivalence, the market for lemons, two-part tariffs, network externalities, prospect theory, the Taylor rule, the liquidity trap, hysteresis in the NAIRU, the twin deficits hypothesis, and debt dynamics. The final five, ninety six through one hundred, were chosen by researching which diagrams students actually get wrong most often across every level from A-Level and IB through first year university, and fill in five genuine gaps: open economy crowding out linking the loanable funds and foreign exchange markets, the paradox of thrift, efficiency wages, general equilibrium gains from trade, and deriving the AD curve itself from the Keynesian cross. Twenty four diagrams across the whole set hand you the controls directly through a slider. Diagrams one hundred and thirty one through one hundred and forty two are a different kind of exercise: each is rebuilt from a numerical table in the OpenStax textbook Principles of Microeconomics 3e, so every point, intersection, surplus and profit rectangle can be checked against the source table printed beneath it, and every one has been verified against the official OpenStax figures.

For teachers: every diagram below has a row of stage buttons. Click through them on a projector and pause on any stage to question the class before revealing the next one. Many diagrams also have a toggle row above the stage buttons, letting you run a second scenario without redrawing anything. Diagrams marked with a customisable badge hand students a slider so they can set the tax rate, the money supply, the point on a production possibility frontier, the degree of income inequality, a firm's scale, the degree of price discrimination, a consumer's income, the quantity consumed, a producer's budget, or a wage rate, and watch the curve respond immediately, which research on learning consistently finds builds stronger intuition than watching a fixed animation alone. Every diagram also ends with a short two question self check. Students should try to answer before checking, since the act of attempting a retrieval, even incorrectly, strengthens memory more than passively rereading an explanation. The Replay button resets a diagram to stage one, and every shaded region can be hovered or tapped for a short explanation of what it represents.

1. Indirect taxes and elasticity: who really pays

An indirect tax such as VAT, fuel duty, or a duty on cigarettes is collected from the seller, but that does not mean the seller bears the cost of it. A specific tax shifts the supply curve vertically upward by exactly the amount of the tax per unit, because the firm now needs a higher price at every quantity just to keep receiving what it did before. The genuinely examinable insight is that who actually pays, meaning the split between consumers and producers, depends almost entirely on the price elasticity of demand rather than on who writes the cheque to the tax authority.

Toggle elasticity, then step through the tax. Hover the shaded areas on stage four
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Straight line demand and supply, drawn to scale so both toggled scenarios share the same free market price and quantity but diverge once the tax is applied.
Analysis. A specific, per unit tax shifts supply vertically by the tax amount. The new price consumers pay, Pc, and the lower price producers keep, Pp, diverge by exactly the tax per unit. Government revenue equals the tax per unit multiplied by the new, lower quantity traded, Qt. It is not the tax multiplied by the original quantity, which is a common exam slip.
Evaluation. The rule that the less elastic side of the market pays more tax is genuinely two sided in real markets. Cigarette duty relies on inelastic demand to raise steady revenue with limited output loss, which is precisely why governments tax addictive goods rather than easily substituted ones. Real elasticities also change over time. Demand for cigarettes has become more elastic as vaping has spread as a substitute, so a diagram accurate for 2010 may already understate the deadweight loss today. Always state the time period and the availability of substitutes that your elasticity assumption relies on.

2. Subsidies: the mirror image of a tax

A subsidy is a tax running in reverse. Government pays producers an amount per unit, so supply shifts vertically downward by the subsidy per unit. Governments subsidise goods with positive spillovers, such as public transport, renewable energy, or apprenticeships, to push output above the free market level and closer to the socially optimal one. That is the same underlying logic used in diagram four for merit goods, but applied directly to price rather than routed through an externality diagram.

Four stage build
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Compare directly against diagram one. Identical curves, opposite direction of shift.
Analysis. Consumers pay a lower price, Pc, producers effectively receive a higher price, Pp, equal to Pc plus the subsidy, and quantity rises above Q0. The gap between Pc and Pp equals the subsidy per unit, and total government spending is the shaded rectangle, the subsidy multiplied by Q1.
Evaluation. Subsidies are only as good as the government's ability to target and fund them. Opportunity cost matters, since money spent subsidising bus fares is money not spent elsewhere. Subsidies can also be captured by producers rather than passed on to consumers if supply is relatively inelastic, following the same elasticity logic as diagram one, just running in reverse.

3. Negative externalities of production

This is arguably the single most tested market failure diagram at A Level. A firm's private costs, MPC, which also serve as its supply curve, understate the true cost to society once the external cost imposed on third parties is added in, whether that is pollution, noise, or congestion. The socially optimal output is lower than the free market output, and the gap between them is where welfare is lost.

Toggle the Pigouvian tax on stage four to see the welfare loss close up
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Switch to Pigouvian tax added on stage two to see how a correctly sized tax simply relabels MPC as MSC, removing the welfare loss triangle entirely.
Analysis. The welfare loss triangle sits strictly between Qopt and Qm, bounded above by MSC and below by the demand curve. A common error is shading the whole area under MSC up to Qm. Only the triangle beyond Qopt is a genuine loss, since everything up to Qopt is still efficient production.
Evaluation. A Pigouvian tax is the textbook fix, but setting it correctly requires knowing the monetary value of the external cost, which regulators rarely know precisely. Get it wrong and you either under correct, leaving some welfare loss, or over correct, pushing output below the true optimum. Real world alternatives such as tradeable permits, regulation, or direct provision each carry their own information and enforcement costs, which is why simply taxing it is a necessary but not sufficient exam answer.

4. Positive externalities of consumption (merit goods)

Merit goods such as education and vaccination are under consumed in a free market because individuals judge only their own private benefit, MPB, and ignore the wider social benefit, MSB. A vaccinated person also protects everyone around them. This diagram is the mirror image of diagram three. The market under produces relative to the social optimum instead of over producing.

Toggle the subsidy on stage two to see MPB pulled up to meet MSB
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Notice the triangle points the opposite way to diagram three. The loss here comes from too little output rather than too much.
Analysis. The socially optimal quantity Qopt sits to the right of the market quantity Qm, the reverse of the negative externality case, because ignoring a positive spillover means the market stops too early. The price at the optimum is read off wherever MSC and MSB actually intersect. It is the quantity that moves, not necessarily a higher or lower price.
Evaluation. Subsidies raise take up but cost the treasury money that has an opportunity cost elsewhere in the health or education budget, and demand for some merit goods, such as childhood vaccination in high income countries, is already close to saturation, so the subsidy may buy little extra quantity. Free provision, information campaigns, or compulsion such as school attendance laws are policy alternatives worth setting against a subsidy in a full evaluation.

5. Monopoly versus perfect competition welfare loss

A monopolist does not set price directly the way a price taking firm does. It chooses the profit maximising quantity where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, then reads the price consumers are willing to pay off the demand curve at that quantity. Because marginal revenue falls twice as steeply as demand under a single uniform price, the monopoly quantity always sits below, and the monopoly price always sits above, the competitive outcome.

Four stage build. Hover the deadweight loss triangle on stage four
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
MR is drawn with the same price intercept as demand but twice the slope, a rule worth memorising for freehand exam sketches.
Analysis. Find Qm where MC crosses MR, then move vertically up to the demand curve, not to MC, to read off Pm. The price charged always sits above marginal cost at that quantity, which is the source of the allocative inefficiency, since P exceeds MC even before you consider any supernormal profit rectangle.
Evaluation. Static welfare loss triangles miss dynamic effects. Schumpeter argued that monopoly profits fund the research and development that produces genuinely new products, and network industries such as search engines or operating systems may be natural monopolies where a single large firm has lower unit costs than several small rivals would. Whether the static loss or the dynamic gain dominates is exactly the kind of judgement A Level essays are marked on.

6. Price discrimination between markets

Third degree price discrimination happens when a firm with market power splits customers into separate groups by elasticity, such as peak versus off peak rail fares, business versus leisure flights, or student discounts, and charges each group a different price for an identical product. The rule is simple: the group with the more inelastic demand pays the higher price.

Same firm, same marginal cost, two different prices
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
A simplified two market sketch, with each price sitting directly on that segment's demand curve. A fully rigorous diagram derives each price by equating marginal revenue in each market to a single shared marginal cost, useful to mention for top marks but rarely required to draw in full under exam time pressure.
Analysis. Three conditions must hold for this to work. The firm needs price setting power, it must be able to identify and separate the two groups, and resale between groups must be prevented, since you cannot let a leisure traveller buy a ticket and resell it to a business traveller. Remove any one condition and price discrimination collapses back to a single uniform price.
Evaluation. Price discrimination is often framed as unfair, but it can expand overall output beyond what a single uniform monopoly price would produce, since the firm can now profitably serve price sensitive customers it would otherwise price out. Some economists argue this raises total welfare even as it redistributes it from the inelastic group toward the firm. Whether that trade off is acceptable is a value judgement rather than a testable fact.

7. Perfect competition: short run to long run

The long run adjustment story turns perfect competition from a static picture into a mechanism. Supernormal profit in the short run attracts new entrants, since free entry is one of the defining assumptions of the model, industry supply grows, price falls, and the process only stops once every firm is back down to normal profit, meaning zero economic profit, just enough to keep it in the industry.

Two linked panels, one firm on the left, the whole industry on the right. Both panels share the same price axis
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Watch price P1 in the firm panel fall to P2, exactly matching the drop shown in the industry panel on the right. Both panels share the same price scale, so P1 and P2 line up horizontally across the whole diagram.
Analysis. The long run equilibrium price P2 is where the AR equals MR line becomes tangent to the bottom of the AC curve, meaning it just touches AC at its single minimum point rather than merely sitting lower than before. At that point, price equals MC equals the minimum of AC, satisfying both productive and allocative efficiency at once, which is the textbook justification for using perfect competition as the efficiency benchmark against which other market structures are judged.
Evaluation. Real markets rarely have the frictionless entry this model assumes. Licensing, capital requirements, brand loyalty, and economies of scale all slow the adjustment, sometimes for years. The model remains useful precisely because it identifies which frictions matter. The slower entry actually is in a real market, the longer supernormal profits persist, which is a genuinely testable prediction rather than an abstract assumption.

8. Monopsony labour markets and the minimum wage

This diagram flips the standard minimum wage causes unemployment story on its head, and examiners love testing whether students actually understand why. Where one employer dominates a local labour market, such as a hospital trust or a mining town's only major employer, it faces an upward sloping labour supply curve and must raise wages for everyone already employed in order to hire one more worker, which makes its marginal cost of labour rise faster than the wage itself.

Use the toggle above on stage four to see wage and jobs both rise together
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The minimum wage line is flat up to where it meets the original supply curve, called the kink, and beyond that point the firm's effective marginal cost jumps back onto the original MCL curve.
Analysis. The monopsonist maximises profit where MCL equals MRP, finding Qm, then pays the lowest wage that will attract that many workers, read off ACL rather than MCL, at Qm. This is why Wm sits below the MCL equals MRP intersection point rather than on it. A minimum wage set anywhere between Wm and the competitive wage Wc becomes the firm's new flat MCL up to the point it rejoins the original supply curve, which is why it can raise employment instead of destroying jobs, as long as it is not set above Wc.
Evaluation. This result depends entirely on genuine monopsony power existing. In a competitive labour market with many employers and workers who can easily switch jobs, the standard result reasserts itself and a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage does cause unemployment, as shown directly in diagram thirteen. UK Low Pay Commission research is frequently cited as evidence that modest, phased minimum wage rises have not produced the job losses simple competitive models predict, which many economists read as evidence of at least partial monopsony power in low wage UK labour markets. This remains a genuinely live empirical debate rather than a settled one.

9. AD/AS: demand pull inflation in the short run

This is the first of six macroeconomics diagrams, and they are all built around the same imagined economy so that a change made in one diagram carries through logically to the next. Aggregate demand, AD, shows total planned spending in the economy at each price level. Short run aggregate supply, SRAS, shows how much output firms are willing to produce at each price level given their current wage and input costs. Long run aggregate supply, LRAS, is drawn vertically at the economy's potential output, since in the long run output is determined by the quantity and productivity of an economy's resources rather than by the price level. When AD rises because of stronger consumer confidence, higher government spending, or rising exports, the economy moves along the existing SRAS curve, and both the price level and real output rise together. This is demand pull inflation.

This exact starting position is reused in diagrams ten, eleven and fourteen
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Output can move past Yfe temporarily because firms can respond to higher demand in the short run by paying overtime, running machinery harder, or drawing down inventories, even though this cannot be sustained forever. What happens next is the subject of the following diagram.
Analysis. In the short run, demand pull inflation raises both the price level and real output together, since the economy simply moves along the existing SRAS curve. The new output level, Y2, can sit above the long run potential level, Yfe, creating a positive or inflationary output gap. This is only possible in the short run, because it relies on input costs, especially wages, staying temporarily fixed while the price of output rises.
Evaluation. Whether demand pull inflation is a policy success or a policy risk depends entirely on how much spare capacity existed before the shock. If the economy started well below Yfe, the same rightward AD shift mostly raises output with only a small rise in prices. If the economy started at or above Yfe, as shown here, the same shift is mostly inflationary. This is exactly why the position of the starting equilibrium relative to potential output matters so much in real world macroeconomic policy debates, and it is the reason diagram fourteen distinguishes actual growth from potential growth.

10. The self correcting mechanism: inflationary and recessionary gaps

What happens after the short run shock in diagram nine. Classical and monetarist economists argue that wages and prices eventually adjust to close any output gap automatically, without any need for government intervention, though they usually accept this can take months or years rather than happening instantly. Keynesian economists accept the same long run destination but argue that wages are sticky, especially downward, so the adjustment can be slow and painful, which is their case for using demand management policy to speed it up rather than waiting.

Toggle between the two gaps to see the self correcting mechanism run in both directions
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both scenarios begin from the identical starting equilibrium used in diagram nine, so you can see the two possible directions an economy can move in from the same starting point.
Analysis. In both scenarios, real output ends up back at Yfe once the labour market fully adjusts, because LRAS is fixed by an economy's underlying resources and productivity rather than by the price level. What differs permanently is the price level: an inflationary gap leaves prices permanently higher than where they started, and a recessionary gap leaves them permanently lower. The output gap is always temporary in this model. The change in the price level is always permanent.
Evaluation. The entire disagreement between classical and Keynesian economists sits inside stage three of this diagram, in how quickly and how reliably SRAS actually shifts back. Falling wages are especially slow in practice, because of minimum wage laws, trade union contracts, and simple resistance from workers to accepting a pay cut, which is usually called downward wage rigidity. This is precisely why the recessionary gap side of this diagram is the more contested half in real policy debates: a classical economist expects it to close on its own within a reasonable time, while a Keynesian economist expects it to persist for years without active government or central bank intervention such as the fiscal and monetary stimulus used after the 2008 financial crisis.

11. Supply side shocks and stagflation

Not every shock to an economy comes from the demand side. A supply side or cost push shock changes firms' costs of production directly, most famously a sharp rise in oil prices, and shifts SRAS itself rather than AD. The key exam distinction from diagram nine is the direction of movement: a demand shock pushes price level and output in the same direction, while a supply shock pushes them in opposite directions. A rise in the price level combined with a fall in output is called stagflation, and it is one of the hardest situations for policymakers to respond to, because the usual tools for fighting inflation make unemployment worse, and the usual tools for fighting unemployment make inflation worse.

Same starting point as diagrams nine and ten. Only the direction of the supply shift changes with the toggle
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Toggle between the two scenarios to see how identical shaped shifts in SRAS, one left and one right, produce opposite effects on both price level and output.
Analysis. A cost push shock reduces the quantity firms are willing to supply at every price level, shifting SRAS left, so the new equilibrium has both a higher price level and lower output than before, the definition of stagflation. A favourable supply shock does the reverse, shifting SRAS right, and lowers the price level while raising output, which is the most desirable outcome an economy can experience since it involves no policy trade off at all.
Evaluation. The 1970s oil price shocks are the standard historical example of cost push stagflation, and they are usually credited with breaking the simple Keynesian consensus of the time, since a straightforward AD only model could not explain rising unemployment and rising inflation occurring together. Favourable supply shocks are rarer and slower to arrive in practice, since they usually depend on structural change such as productivity growth, deregulation, cheaper energy, or an expansion of the workforce, rather than a single policy decision, which is exactly the subject of diagram fourteen.

12. The Phillips curve: short run versus long run

The Phillips curve describes the relationship between unemployment and inflation. In the short run there does appear to be a trade off: governments can push unemployment temporarily below its natural rate by boosting aggregate demand, at the cost of higher inflation. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that this trade off disappears once workers adjust their inflation expectations, leaving a vertical long run Phillips curve at the natural rate of unemployment, often written as NAIRU, the non accelerating inflation rate of unemployment.

Toggle to run the story in either direction
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The vertical long run curve is the Phillips curve equivalent of the vertical LRAS used in diagrams nine, ten and eleven: both express the idea that real variables such as output and unemployment cannot be permanently changed by demand side policy alone.
Analysis. Along a single short run Phillips curve, inflation expectations are held constant, so a government can trade unemployment for inflation in the short run. Once workers revise their expectations to match the new, higher actual inflation rate, they bargain for higher wages, firms' costs rise, and unemployment drifts back toward the natural rate, but now on a new, higher short run curve. Repeat this process and you get the accelerationist conclusion: any attempt to hold unemployment permanently below its natural rate requires accelerating inflation, not just a one off rise.
Evaluation. The natural rate itself is not a fixed number. It depends on labour market flexibility, the generosity and design of unemployment benefits, the extent of trade union bargaining power, and the speed at which workers can retrain and relocate to new jobs, so it can shift over time even without any demand side policy at all. Critics also point out that the 1990s and 2000s saw many economies enjoy both low unemployment and low, stable inflation simultaneously, which some economists attribute to a genuine fall in NAIRU during that period rather than to the short run Phillips curve breaking down entirely.

13. Real wage unemployment in a competitive labour market

Diagram eight showed a monopsony employer paying below the competitive wage, where a minimum wage could raise both pay and jobs. This diagram deliberately shows the opposite case: an otherwise competitive labour market, with many employers and no single firm holding market power, where a real wage is pushed above the level that would clear the market. This is the classical explanation of unemployment, sometimes just called real wage unemployment or real wage inflexibility.

Hover the shaded gap on stage four
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Compare directly with diagram eight. The curves and the gap are drawn with the same geometry in both diagrams, but here the labour market is competitive to begin with, which changes the conclusion completely.
Analysis. At any wage above We, the quantity of labour supplied, Qs, exceeds the quantity demanded, Qd, and the horizontal distance between the demand and supply curves at that wage is the resulting unemployment. This is a straightforward excess supply diagram, the labour market equivalent of a price floor set above the equilibrium price in a goods market. The result only holds because the market was competitive before the wage floor was introduced. If a single dominant employer already held monopsony power, as in diagram eight, the very same wage floor can raise employment instead.
Evaluation. This is exactly why economists disagree sharply about the real world employment effects of the minimum wage. The outcome predicted by theory depends entirely on how competitive the labour market actually is, which is an empirical question, not a theoretical one, and it can vary by sector, region, and skill level within the same economy at the same time. Trade unions raise a similar issue: bargaining power that pushes wages above the market clearing level can protect existing workers' pay, sometimes called insiders, while potentially pricing some job seekers, sometimes called outsiders, out of employment altogether.

14. Economic growth: actual growth versus potential growth

A Level specifications draw a sharp line between two different kinds of economic growth. Actual growth is a rise in real output achieved by using existing spare capacity more fully, shown as a movement of AD along an unchanged SRAS toward an unchanged LRAS. Potential growth is a rise in an economy's productive capacity itself, shown as an outward shift of LRAS, driven by more or better factors of production such as investment, technological progress, education, or net migration of workers. Confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes examiners report in growth essays.

Toggle to compare using spare capacity against expanding it
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
This diagram deliberately reuses the exact SRAS, LRAS1 and initial equilibrium from diagrams nine, ten and eleven, so it reads as the same economy considered from a growth perspective rather than a separate example.
Analysis. Actual growth and potential growth are not substitutes for each other and can move independently. An economy can experience actual growth with no change in potential output at all, simply by using idle factories and unemployed workers more fully. It can also experience potential growth with no immediate rise in actual output, if the new capacity created by investment or immigration is not yet matched by higher demand, which is exactly what stage four shows under the potential growth toggle: the frontier moves out, but the output gap does not close by itself.
Evaluation. Sustainable long run improvements in living standards ultimately require potential growth, since actual growth alone runs out once spare capacity is fully used and starts generating demand pull inflation instead, as shown back in diagram nine. Potential growth itself is not automatically good news for everyone: investment led growth can take years to arrive and often requires short run sacrifice in the form of lower consumption today, and growth driven mainly by population increase raises total GDP without necessarily raising GDP per person, which is normally the more meaningful measure of a rising standard of living.

15. The foreign exchange market

Exchange rates are just another price, set by the demand for and supply of a currency, and they are tested constantly because they connect trade, monetary policy, and inflation within one diagram. A rise in a country's interest rate attracts foreign investors chasing a better return, raising demand for the currency and causing it to appreciate. A rate cut does the reverse.

Try all three scenarios on stage three
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Try both scenarios in turn to see the equilibrium marker move in opposite directions from the same starting point.
Analysis. Depreciation makes UK exports cheaper in foreign currency terms and imports more expensive in sterling terms, the intended trade balance effect. The Marshall Lerner condition states that this only improves the trade balance if the combined price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceed one. If demand is inelastic, which is common in the short run because many contracts and consumer habits are sticky, the trade balance can initially worsen before improving, an effect known as the J curve.
Evaluation. Interest rates are only one driver among several. Relative inflation rates, speculation, political stability, and the current account balance all shift currency demand and supply too, often simultaneously and in conflicting directions, which is exactly why exchange rate forecasting is notoriously unreliable even for professional economists.

16. Production possibility frontier and opportunity cost

A production possibility frontier, or PPF, shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its existing resources and technology, assuming everything available is fully and efficiently employed. It bows outward from the origin because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods, so as an economy produces more and more of one good, it must give up increasing amounts of the other. That increasing sacrifice is opportunity cost, and it is the reason the curve curves at all rather than being a straight line.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider on stage two to move along the frontier in real time
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
balanced mix
The curve is a mathematically exact bow, not a freehand sketch, so the slider always lands the marker precisely on the frontier itself.
Analysis. Every point on the curve itself is productively efficient, using all available resources. Moving the slider from more capital goods toward more consumer goods traces the real opportunity cost: because resources are imperfectly substitutable between the two goods, each extra unit of consumer goods costs a little more in forgone capital goods than the last, which is exactly why the curve gets steeper as you slide toward the consumer goods end.
Evaluation. A point inside the frontier is not necessarily a policy failure. It can reflect a deliberate choice, such as holding spare capacity for a future demand shock, rather than pure waste. Whether an economy should prioritise moving toward the frontier, point C toward point A, or pushing the whole frontier outward, stage four, depends on whether the immediate problem is underused resources or a genuine limit on productive capacity.
Quick check: if a government builds a new port that raises the economy's capacity to trade, which point on this diagram best describes the result?

17. The circular flow of income, injections and leakages

The circular flow of income is the foundation diagram underneath the entire AD/AS model used earlier in this guide. It shows money moving in a continuous loop between households and firms, and it explains why an economy can be pushed off its steady path in two ways at once: leakages pulling money out of the loop, and injections putting new money back in.

Four stage build
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The inner loop, stage one, never stops on its own. Whether the whole economy grows, shrinks, or stays the same size depends entirely on the balance between the two side flows added in stages two and three.
Analysis. This is a real, national income accounting identity, not just a loose metaphor. Every leakage has a matching destination, savings flow through the financial sector, taxes flow to government, and spending on imports flows abroad, and every injection has a matching source, investment funded by the financial sector, government spending funded by tax and borrowing, and exports funded by foreign demand.
Evaluation. Governments can influence this balance directly, cutting interest rates to discourage saving and encourage investment, or raising government spending, but they cannot fully control it, since export demand depends on conditions in other countries and consumer saving behaviour can shift quickly during periods of uncertainty, regardless of what policy intends.
Quick check: if households suddenly decide to save a larger share of their income and nothing else changes, what happens to national income?

18. The Keynesian income expenditure model and the multiplier

This diagram answers a question the circular flow only gestures at: exactly where does national income settle, and what happens when one extra pound, dollar, or rupee of spending enters the economy. The forty five degree line marks every point where planned expenditure equals national income. Equilibrium is where the actual aggregate expenditure line crosses it.

Watch how far income moves compared to the size of the injection
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The AE line's slope is the marginal propensity to consume out of national income. A flatter AE line means more of each extra pound of income leaks into saving, tax, or imports instead of being spent again, which shrinks the multiplier.
Analysis. The multiplier exists because one person's spending is another person's income. A construction firm's new spending becomes wages for its workers, who then spend part of that on other goods, generating further rounds of income. The formula, the multiplier equals one divided by the marginal propensity to withdraw, follows directly from the flatter slope of the AE line relative to the forty five degree line: the flatter the AE line, the larger the eventual horizontal shift in income for the same vertical shift in spending.
Evaluation. A larger multiplier sounds unambiguously good, but it also means the economy is more exposed to shocks in the opposite direction, a fall in investment or export demand shrinks income by more than the size of the original fall too. Governments trying to use fiscal stimulus effectively need a reasonably accurate estimate of the multiplier, and in practice estimates vary considerably depending on how open the economy is to trade and how much spare capacity exists at the time.
Quick check: an economy with a very flat AE line, close to horizontal, would have a multiplier that is:

19. The money market and interest rate determination

Just like any other market, money has a price, the rate of interest, determined by demand and supply. The demand for money, sometimes called liquidity preference, slopes downward because a higher interest rate raises the opportunity cost of holding cash rather than an interest bearing asset. The supply of money is normally drawn as a vertical line, since a central bank sets the money supply directly rather than letting it respond automatically to the interest rate.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider to change the money supply in real time
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
medium
Drag left to shrink the money supply and watch the interest rate rise along the fixed demand curve. Drag right to expand it and watch the rate fall.
Analysis. Because the demand curve never moves in this diagram, every possible interest rate the economy could face is already sitting on it. The central bank's only real lever, in this simplified model, is choosing where to place the vertical supply line. A leftward shift, tightening, always raises the rate. A rightward shift, easing, always lowers it, and the slider lets you confirm that relationship holds at every point along the curve, not only near the middle.
Evaluation. Real central banks, including the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve, more often set an interest rate target directly and let the money supply adjust to meet it, rather than fixing the money supply and letting the rate float, which is why this vertical supply curve is best understood as a simplified teaching model rather than a literal description of modern monetary policy operations.
Quick check: if the central bank wants to fight inflation by raising interest rates, which way should the slider move?

20. The loanable funds market and government borrowing

The loanable funds market brings savers and borrowers together at a market clearing interest rate. Households and firms who save supply funds. Households, firms and, crucially, governments who borrow demand them. When a government runs a large budget deficit, it enters this market as an extra borrower, and the consequences for private investment are one of the most frequently examined ideas in macroeconomics.

Four stage build
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every coordinate above was solved algebraically from the two original lines and a 110 pixel rightward shift, so Q1, Q2, r1, r2 and the crowding out gap are all mutually consistent rather than placed by eye.
Analysis. Government borrowing shifts total demand for loanable funds to the right, from D1 to D2. The interest rate rises from r1 to r2. Reading up from the new higher rate to the original D1 curve, rather than the new D2 curve, shows what private investment alone falls to. The gap between that reduced private investment and the new higher total quantity borrowed, Q2, is the government's own borrowing. This is the standard crowding out result: government borrowing raises rates and displaces some private investment.
Evaluation. Crowding out is weaker, or can even reverse into crowding in, when the economy has spare capacity and the extra government spending itself raises incomes and therefore private saving, or when the borrowed money is spent on productive infrastructure that raises the future return on private investment. The size of the effect shown here depends heavily on how steep the supply of savings curve is assumed to be, which varies significantly between countries with different saving habits and different access to foreign capital.
Quick check: after the government borrows more, which curve should you read from to find the new level of private investment alone?

21. Oligopoly and the kinked demand curve

Oligopoly markets, dominated by a handful of large firms, behave strangely in one specific way: prices tend to stay remarkably stable even when costs change. The kinked demand curve model, developed by Paul Sweezy, explains this through an asymmetric assumption about how rivals react. If one firm raises its price, rivals do not follow, so it loses a lot of customers. If one firm cuts its price, rivals match the cut immediately to avoid losing market share, so it gains very few new customers.

Try both cost scenarios on stage three
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The marginal revenue curve has a genuine vertical break directly below the kink, which is the entire mechanism behind price rigidity in this model.
Analysis. Profit maximisation always occurs where marginal cost equals marginal revenue. Because MR is discontinuous at Q0, a whole range of possible marginal cost curves can cross it at exactly the same quantity, which means the profit maximising price stays fixed at P0 even after a moderate cost change. Only a large enough cost shock, one that pushes MC entirely above or below the gap, will actually change the price.
Evaluation. The kinked demand curve model explains price stability well, but it has a well known gap of its own: it assumes the current price and quantity exist without ever explaining how firms arrived there in the first place. Critics also point out that real oligopoly pricing evidence is mixed, some industries show exactly this kind of stickiness, such as supermarket pricing on staple goods, while others, particularly ones with frequent price wars such as budget airlines, show far more volatile pricing behaviour than the model predicts.
Quick check: according to this model, why does a firm avoid cutting its price below P0?

22. Contestable markets and natural monopoly

Some industries, water supply, rail infrastructure, and increasingly the largest AI data centres, have such enormous fixed costs relative to the size of the market that average cost keeps falling across almost the entire range of realistic output. Economists call this a natural monopoly, and it raises an awkward question: if only one firm can operate efficiently, does that firm automatically get to charge whatever it likes?

Compare both scenarios on stage three
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both scenarios use the same LRAC and demand curves. Only the assumption about whether new entrants can threaten the incumbent changes.
Analysis. Baumol's contestable markets theory argues that market structure, the actual number of firms, matters less than whether entry and exit are genuinely free and low cost. Even a single firm will behave close to a competitive one if a rival could enter quickly, undercut it, and exit again before the incumbent can retaliate, a strategy called hit and run entry.
Evaluation. True contestability requires low sunk costs, the ability to exit without losing money already spent, which is precisely what many natural monopolies lack. A rail operator cannot easily remove track it has already laid, so the threat of entry is often weaker in practice than the theory assumes, which is exactly why most real natural monopolies, from water utilities to national grids, are regulated directly rather than left to contestability alone.
Quick check: what condition does contestable markets theory rely on most heavily?

23. The Laffer curve: tax rates and tax revenue

The Laffer curve makes a deceptively simple point: a tax rate of zero raises no revenue, and, less obviously, a tax rate of one hundred percent also tends to raise very little, since almost nobody keeps working, investing, or reporting income once the state takes all of it. Somewhere between those two extremes sits a revenue maximising rate. The genuinely difficult, and genuinely contested, question is where that point actually is.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag to set any tax rate from 0 to 100 percent, in real time
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
50% rate
This curve is generated from the exact formula revenue equals rate multiplied by one hundred minus rate, so the slider always sits precisely on the mathematical peak at fifty percent for this illustrative version.
Analysis. Try dragging past the peak. Revenue at an 85% rate is lower than revenue at a 60% rate here, purely because the tax base itself shrinks faster than the rate rises, through avoidance, reduced hours worked, and capital moving elsewhere. This is the entire logic of the curve in one interaction: past the peak, cutting the rate can raise revenue, and raising the rate can lose it.
Evaluation. This specific curve is a deliberately simple, symmetric illustration peaking at fifty percent, chosen for clarity, not a claim about any real tax system. Empirical estimates of where real economies actually sit vary enormously by country, by which tax is being studied, and by how mobile the tax base is, and most peer reviewed estimates for labour income taxes put the genuine revenue maximising rate considerably higher than fifty percent, often in a sixty to eighty percent range, with substantial uncertainty even then. Treat the existence of the curve as solid economics. Treat any specific claimed peak, including this diagram's, as a modelling assumption to be checked, not a fact.
Quick check: if a country is currently taxing at 90% and revenue is falling, what does the Laffer curve suggest a rate cut might do?

24. The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient

The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of total income earned against the cumulative share of the population, ranked from poorest to richest. A perfectly equal society, everyone earning exactly the same, produces a straight forty five degree diagonal. Every real economy bows below that line by some amount, and the size of that bow is what the Gini coefficient measures.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag to change inequality and watch the Gini coefficient recalculate live
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Gini ≈ 0.20
The shaded area is generated from the real Lorenz curve equation for a power function, and the displayed Gini coefficient is calculated from the same underlying curvature parameter the slider controls, not estimated by eye.
Analysis. The Gini coefficient is defined geometrically as the shaded area between the diagonal and the Lorenz curve, divided by the entire triangular area beneath the diagonal. It always falls between 0, perfect equality, and 1, one person holding all the income. For the family of curves used in this slider, the Gini coefficient can be calculated exactly rather than only estimated visually, which is why the number updates precisely as you drag rather than only approximately.
Evaluation. A single Gini number can hide very different underlying distributions, two countries can share an identical Gini coefficient while one has a small extremely wealthy elite and the other has a broad, moderately unequal middle, so economists studying inequality in depth usually pair the Gini coefficient with additional measures, such as the income share held by the top one percent specifically, rather than relying on it alone.
Quick check: as the slider moves further from perfect equality, what happens to the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient?

25. Balance of payments adjustment and the J curve effect

When a currency devalues or depreciates, the immediate effect on a country's trade balance is often the opposite of what people expect. Rather than improving straight away, the trade balance frequently gets worse for a period first, then improves beyond its original level. Plotted over time, this produces a shape that gives the effect its name.

Four stage build
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The dip and the recovery are not two separate effects, they are the same devaluation, observed at two different points in time as contracts and habits catch up with the new price.
Analysis. Immediately after a devaluation, the volume of imports and exports barely changes, because existing contracts, shipping schedules, and consumer habits are sticky in the short run. Since imports now cost more in domestic currency even at the same quantity, the trade balance mechanically worsens first, a valuation effect. Only once quantities have time to adjust, consumers switching away from now expensive imports, foreign buyers switching toward now cheap exports, does the balance improve, a volume effect, and it only improves beyond the starting point if the Marshall Lerner condition introduced in diagram fifteen is satisfied.
Evaluation. The J curve is well documented empirically but its exact timing varies hugely by country and by how the specific goods involved are priced and contracted, from a matter of months for consumer goods to several years for capital equipment and commodities locked into long term supply agreements, which is exactly why governments relying on a devaluation to fix a trade deficit need to be honest about a likely uncomfortable period where things look worse before they look better.
Quick check: in the first few months after a devaluation, why does the trade balance typically get worse rather than better?

26. Market equilibrium, shortages and surpluses

Every diagram from here on builds on this one, so it earns its place first even though it is the simplest idea in the whole guide. A market is in equilibrium when the price has no tendency to change, because the quantity buyers want to buy exactly matches the quantity sellers want to sell. Push the price away from that point in either direction and the market itself generates pressure to move back.

Customisable, drag the slider
Predict first: if demand rises, will price and quantity both rise, both fall, or move in opposite directions? Then drag the slider on stage four to check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
original demand
Drag left of centre to shrink demand, right of centre to grow it. Watch price and quantity move together in the same direction when demand shifts, which is the single most tested prediction in this whole topic.
Analysis. At equilibrium there is no shortage and no surplus, so there is no incentive for price to move: this is why it is called a market clearing price. Move away from it in either direction and a gap opens between the quantity buyers want and the quantity sellers offer, and that gap is exactly what pushes price back. A shortage pushes price up, which rations demand and encourages more supply. A surplus pushes price down, which encourages more demand and less supply, until the gap closes.
Evaluation. Real markets rarely sit exactly on this point for long, because PIRATES and PINTSWC factors are constantly shifting both curves at once. The diagram is a snapshot logic, not a claim that prices are always at rest. It is also worth flagging that this model assumes a competitive market with many buyers and sellers and no price controls, assumptions that the next two diagrams in this guide deliberately relax.
Quick check: demand for a good falls while supply is unchanged. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?

27. Price elasticity of demand: the live elasticity lab

Price elasticity of demand measures how sharply quantity demanded reacts to a price change, and along a single straight-line demand curve it is not constant: the same curve is elastic near the price axis and inelastic near the quantity axis, turning unit elastic exactly halfway between them. This single fact explains a huge share of exam questions on total revenue, since a firm's price cut only raises revenue where demand is elastic. Drag the slider below to move a single point down the entire length of one demand curve and watch elasticity, and total revenue, change continuously in real time.

Customisable, drag the slider
Predict first: does total revenue rise or fall as you drag right, from the elastic zone into the inelastic zone? Then drag and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
E ≈ -1.00, unit elastic
The little bar on the right is total revenue, price multiplied by quantity, redrawn live at every position. It rises while you are in the elastic zone, peaks exactly at the midpoint, then falls through the inelastic zone, which is the entire logic behind the total revenue test for elasticity.
Analysis. On any straight-line demand curve the algebra is exact: elasticity equals minus the quantity axis intercept distance divided by the point's own quantity, so it runs from negative infinity at the price axis to zero at the quantity axis, passing through minus one at the exact midpoint. Because marginal revenue is positive whenever demand is elastic and negative whenever it is inelastic, total revenue must be rising in the elastic zone and falling in the inelastic zone, with its single maximum sitting exactly where elasticity equals minus one.
Evaluation. A firm that only ever reads its own past sales data can misjudge this: cutting price when already deep in the inelastic zone will shrink revenue further, not grow it, even though the demand curve itself has not changed shape. Real demand curves are also rarely perfectly straight, so the numerical elasticity value at any point is model specific, though the underlying pattern, elastic near the top and inelastic near the bottom of any downward sloping demand curve, still holds for curved demand curves too.
Quick check: a firm is currently in the inelastic zone of its demand curve. What happens to total revenue if it raises its price?

28. Price ceilings and price floors

Governments sometimes reject the market clearing price entirely and impose a legal maximum, a price ceiling such as rent control, or a legal minimum, a price floor such as a minimum wage or an agricultural support price. Both interventions are only interesting when they are binding, meaning set away from the free market equilibrium, and both create a gap between quantity supplied and quantity demanded rather than closing one. Toggle between the two policies below, then drag the slider to make the control bind more tightly and watch the gap grow.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider to move the control further from equilibrium
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
not binding, set at the equilibrium price
A ceiling only bites when set below the equilibrium price, and a floor only bites when set above it. A ceiling above equilibrium, or a floor below it, would simply be ignored by the market, since it is not binding on anyone's behaviour.
Analysis. A binding price ceiling creates a shortage, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, because it stops price from rising to ration the good, which is why ceilings are typically followed by queues, waiting lists, or a black market. A binding price floor creates a surplus, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, because it stops price from falling to clear excess stock, which is why floors are typically followed by government buying up the surplus, unsold inventory, or unemployment in the specific case of a minimum wage floor in a labour market.
Evaluation. The size of the gap in both cases depends on the price elasticities of supply and demand: steeper, more inelastic curves produce a smaller quantity gap for the same price gap, while flatter, more elastic curves produce a much larger one. Governments sometimes accept the resulting shortage or surplus deliberately, valuing the equity goal, such as affordable housing or a living wage, above the efficiency cost shown here.
Quick check: a legal minimum wage is set above the free market equilibrium wage. What does this diagram predict for the labour market?

29. Consumer and producer surplus, with and without a tax

Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers were willing to pay and what they actually pay, and producer surplus is the gap between what sellers actually receive and the lowest price they would have accepted. Their sum is total welfare, and it is maximised exactly at the free market equilibrium. An indirect tax breaks that outcome apart: it raises the price consumers pay, lowers the price producers keep, shrinks the quantity traded, and the surplus that used to belong to consumers and producers does not all reappear as tax revenue. Some of it simply vanishes, the deadweight loss. Drag the slider to set the size of the tax and watch all four areas move together.

Customisable, drag the slider
Predict first: as the tax grows, does the deadweight loss triangle grow faster, slower, or at the same rate as the tax itself? Then drag and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
no tax imposed
Teal is consumer surplus, navy is producer surplus, amber is tax revenue, and grey is the deadweight loss that belongs to no one. At zero tax the grey triangle disappears completely, and the teal and navy areas together equal the full amber-plus-grey region combined.
Analysis. Before the tax, consumer surplus and producer surplus together equal the whole triangle between the two curves, with nothing wasted. The tax drives a wedge between Pc and Pp and shrinks quantity to Qt. Part of the lost consumer and producer surplus is captured by the government as tax revenue, the amber rectangle, but the rest, the grey triangle, is deadweight loss: mutually beneficial trades between Qt and the original equilibrium quantity that simply no longer happen.
Evaluation. The deadweight loss grows faster than the tax itself, roughly with the square of the tax rate, which is exactly why very high tax rates raise revenue far less efficiently than moderate ones, the same underlying logic that drives the Laffer curve in diagram twenty three. Governments often deliberately accept a larger deadweight loss anyway when taxing a good with negative externalities, such as tobacco, because part of that lost quantity is exactly the over-consumption they are trying to reduce.
Quick check: which single area on this diagram represents value that is lost completely, captured by neither consumers, producers, nor the government?

30. Short-run cost curves: AC, AVC, AFC and MC

Every firm's short-run cost structure can be summarised in four curves. Average fixed cost, AFC, falls continuously as fixed costs are spread over more output. Average variable cost, AVC, is U-shaped, falling as specialisation improves then rising as diminishing returns set in. Marginal cost, MC, is also U-shaped but always crosses both AVC and average total cost, ATC, at their exact minimum points, a calculus result worth simply memorising for exams. Drag the slider to set the market price and watch the firm's profit-maximising output, and its profit or loss, respond in real time.

Customisable, drag the slider
Predict first: as price falls from a profit-making level toward the shutdown point, does profit-maximising output rise, fall, or stay fixed? Then drag and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
supernormal profit
The firm always produces where price equals marginal cost, on the rising part of MC. The coloured block shows profit, teal, or loss, red, as the gap between price and average total cost at that output. Once price falls below the minimum of AVC, the shutdown point, producing anything at all loses more than closing down entirely, so output drops to zero.
Analysis. Marginal cost is the firm's short-run supply curve above the shutdown point, since profit maximisation always requires price equals marginal cost. Whether that output is actually profitable depends on comparing price with average total cost, not marginal cost: price above ATC means supernormal profit, price between AVC and ATC means a loss that is still worth producing through in the short run because it still covers all variable costs and part of the fixed costs, and price below AVC means every unit produced loses money on its variable cost alone, so the firm shuts down.
Evaluation. This entire model assumes the firm is a passive price taker, which fits perfect competition well but breaks down for a monopoly or an oligopolist, who instead choose their own price and output jointly using marginal revenue rather than simply reading a given price off the vertical axis. Fixed costs are also only truly fixed in the short run: given long enough, a firm making losses even after covering AVC will eventually exit the industry entirely once it can renegotiate or walk away from those fixed commitments.
Quick check: price sits between the minimum of AVC and the minimum of ATC. What should the firm do in the short run?

31. Monopolistic competition: short run profit to long run normal profit

Monopolistic competition sits between perfect competition and monopoly: many firms sell differentiated products, so each firm faces its own slightly downward sloping demand curve rather than being a pure price taker. That small amount of market power is exactly what makes this the market structure examiners most often mix up with monopoly, so watch closely for what does and does not carry over.

Watch AR rotate down and flatten as rivals enter, exactly like diagram 7, but this time it never becomes perfectly flat.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Compare this with diagram 7. Perfect competition drives AR all the way down until it is flat, tangent to the very bottom of AC. Monopolistic competition stops rotating while AR is still downward sloping, so the tangency happens on the falling part of AC, left of its true minimum.
Analysis. The defining long run result is that AR2 is tangent to AC, not that price falls to the AC minimum. Because AR2 still slopes down, the tangency point sits to the left of Qeff, the quantity that minimises average cost. That gap is called excess capacity: each firm produces less, at a higher unit cost, than it would under perfect competition.
Evaluation. Excess capacity sounds like a criticism, but consumers are also gaining product variety, which the perfect competition model assumes away entirely. Whether the welfare loss from higher unit costs outweighs the welfare gain from variety and choice is a judgement call, and it depends heavily on how much consumers actually value the differentiation on offer, from coffee shops to hairdressers.
Quick check: in the long run under monopolistic competition, what happens to supernormal profit?

32. A perfectly competitive firm's three possible outcomes

A price-taking firm in perfect competition always produces where MC equals the given market price, but that same rule can land the firm in three very different situations depending on where the market price happens to sit relative to its AC and AVC curves. Examiners like to test whether you can tell these three apart on sight, since only one of them ends with the firm actually leaving the market.

Switch the toggle above to move the price line through all three cases in real time.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The shutdown rule is about AVC, not AC. A firm covering its variable costs but not all of its fixed costs is still better off producing in the short run than shutting down, since fixed costs are sunk either way.
Analysis. There are exactly three zones. Price above minimum AC gives supernormal profit. Price between minimum AVC and minimum AC gives a loss, but the firm still produces, because it is covering all of its variable costs plus a contribution towards its fixed costs, which it would have to pay anyway even at zero output. Only once price falls below minimum AVC does producing anything actually make the loss bigger than producing nothing, which is the shutdown rule.
Evaluation. This is a short run rule only. In the long run, a firm earning below normal profit will exit even if price is still above AVC, since fixed costs are no longer sunk once contracts, leases and licences can be renewed or not. The distinction between short run and long run shutdown decisions is a common source of dropped marks in extended answers.
Quick check: price sits between minimum AVC and minimum AC. What should the firm do in the short run?

33. The long run average cost curve: economies and diseconomies of scale

Every short run average cost curve, SRAC, describes one fixed plant size. The long run average cost curve, LRAC, is the outer envelope of every possible SRAC a firm could build, since in the long run all inputs, including the size of the factory itself, are variable. Drag the slider to move a growing firm along its own LRAC and watch which SRAC curve is actually relevant at each scale.

Customisable, drag the slider
The dot always sits on the LRAC curve. Watch which of the three SRAC curves lights up as you drag.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
small scale plant: economies of scale still being exploited
Internal economies of scale, such as bulk buying, specialisation and spreading fixed costs, pull LRAC down on the left. Internal diseconomies, such as coordination and communication problems in a very large organisation, push it back up on the right.
Analysis. LRAC is an envelope, not a single U-shaped curve of its own: at every point it is equal to whichever SRAC is lowest at that particular output, and it is only tangent to that SRAC, touching it at a single point, everywhere except at the very bottom, the minimum efficient scale, where LRAC is tangent to the minimum point of the relevant SRAC.
Evaluation. How long the falling section lasts, and how sharply diseconomies bite afterwards, differs enormously by industry. Capital intensive industries such as car manufacturing or utilities often have a long falling section and a flat bottom, which is part of why they tend towards a small number of very large firms, while industries with limited economies of scale, such as hairdressing, support many small firms instead.
Quick check: at the very bottom of the LRAC curve, what is true of the relevant SRAC?

34. Game theory: the prisoner's dilemma and why cartels break down

Oligopoly is defined by interdependence: each firm has to think about how its rivals will react. Game theory formalises that with a payoff matrix. This is the single most useful tool for explaining why collusive agreements between oligopolists tend to be unstable even when both firms would be better off cooperating.

Predict first: if both firms could trust each other completely, which cell would they choose? Then look at stage four.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every cell shows Firm A’s payoff then Firm B’s payoff. The Nash equilibrium is the cell neither firm can unilaterally improve on given the other’s choice, which is exactly the mutual-cheat cell here, even though it makes both firms worse off than mutual collusion would.
Analysis. A dominant strategy is one that is best for a player regardless of what the other player does. Both firms have cheat as a dominant strategy here, so both cheat, landing on the Nash equilibrium in the bottom right. That outcome is Pareto inferior to mutual collusion, which is exactly what makes this a genuine dilemma rather than just a simple best-response problem.
Evaluation. Real cartels sometimes sustain collusion for years, which this one-shot game does not explain. Repeated interaction changes the incentives: firms that expect to play the game again and again can credibly threaten to punish cheating in future rounds, which is why real world cartels rely heavily on retaliation strategies, price leadership, and monitoring mechanisms to make collusion self-enforcing.
Quick check: why does the cartel in this game break down even though both firms know collusion pays more in total?

35. Dominant firm price leadership and the competitive fringe

Not every oligopoly relies on explicit collusion. In many real markets, one large firm sets the price and a group of smaller firms, the competitive fringe, simply accept it and supply whatever they can profitably sell at that price. The dominant firm serves whatever demand is left over, called residual demand, after the fringe has sold its share.

The dominant firm never faces the whole market demand curve. It only ever faces what is left after the fringe has supplied its share.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
All firms, dominant and fringe, end up charging the same price P* purely because the fringe are price takers who will simply sell nothing if they try to charge more than the leader.
Analysis. Build the residual demand curve by taking, at every price, the total quantity demanded and subtracting whatever the fringe would supply at that price. The dominant firm then treats this residual demand exactly like a monopolist would treat ordinary demand: find MR from it, set MC equal to MR, and read the profit maximising price off the residual demand curve at that quantity.
Evaluation. This model explains real world patterns such as OPEC’s role in oil markets or a large supermarket chain’s effect on independent grocers, but it assumes the fringe firms passively accept the price rather than trying to undercut it, and it assumes the dominant firm can actually identify its residual demand accurately, which is informationally demanding in practice.
Quick check: what does the dominant firm’s residual demand curve represent?

36. Perfect price discrimination: capturing the entire consumer surplus

Third degree price discrimination, covered in diagram 6, splits the market into a few groups charged different prices. First degree, or perfect, price discrimination is the extreme case: the firm somehow charges every single consumer exactly the maximum price they are willing to pay for every unit. Drag the slider to move continuously from an ordinary single-price monopoly to this extreme case.

Customisable, drag the slider
Watch the deadweight loss triangle shrink to nothing as the shaded area grows to fill the entire space under demand and above MC.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
no discrimination: a single uniform price
At full discrimination the firm produces the same quantity as a competitive market would, Qc, because it now captures the value of every extra unit right up to the point where that value falls to MC. There is no deadweight loss left, but there is no consumer surplus left either.
Analysis. A single price monopolist restricts output to Qm to avoid discounting every unit just to sell one more. A perfectly discriminating monopolist has no reason to hold back, since selling one more unit at a slightly lower price never forces it to lower the price on any other unit. Output rises all the way to the allocatively efficient quantity, Qc, but every scrap of consumer surplus is transferred to the firm as producer surplus instead.
Evaluation. Perfect discrimination is rarely fully achievable, since it requires knowing each consumer’s exact maximum willingness to pay and preventing resale between them, but modern data collection, personalised online pricing, and haggling in markets such as car dealerships all move markets some way in this direction, which is why regulators increasingly scrutinise algorithmic personalised pricing.
Quick check: compared with a single price monopoly, what happens to output under perfect price discrimination?

37. Natural monopoly: marginal cost pricing versus average cost pricing

Some industries, such as water pipes, rail track, or electricity grids, have such enormous fixed costs relative to demand that average cost keeps falling right across the whole range of realistic output. A single large firm can always produce more cheaply per unit than two smaller ones could, which is why it is called a natural monopoly, and why simply breaking it up is not an obvious solution.

Switch the toggle to compare the unregulated outcome with the two classic regulatory rules.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Notice the ordering of the three quantities: the unregulated monopoly restricts output the most, average cost pricing produces more, and marginal cost pricing produces the most of all, exactly matching the allocatively efficient level.
Analysis. Because AC is still falling at every output level shown, MC always sits below AC, so setting price equal to MC, the allocatively efficient rule, necessarily prices below AC and makes a loss that only a government subsidy can cover. Average cost pricing avoids the subsidy and lets the firm break even, but it only partially solves the problem, since price still exceeds MC, leaving some allocative inefficiency in place.
Evaluation. Marginal cost pricing is the textbook efficiency answer, but funding the subsidy has its own opportunity cost and its own deadweight loss from the taxation needed to raise it. Many real regulators, including UK utility regulators such as Ofwat and Ofgem, use a form of average cost pricing or rate-of-return regulation instead, precisely to avoid relying on taxpayer subsidy, accepting some residual inefficiency as the price of financial sustainability.
Quick check: why does marginal cost pricing require a government subsidy for a natural monopoly?

38. Indifference curves and the budget line: how consumers choose

An indifference curve joins every combination of two goods that gives a consumer exactly the same total satisfaction, or utility. The budget line shows every combination they can actually afford. Consumer theory says a rational consumer picks the point where the budget line is tangent to the highest indifference curve it can reach, since that is the best affordable bundle available.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider to change income and watch the budget line shift outward while the chosen bundle slides up the income consumption curve.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
lower income
Because only income is changing here, not either price, the budget line shifts outward in a parallel line, keeping the same slope, which is fixed by the ratio of the two prices.
Analysis. The tangency condition, where the slope of the budget line, the price ratio, equals the slope of the indifference curve, the marginal rate of substitution, is the mathematical heart of consumer theory. Off that point, the consumer could reallocate spending between the two goods and reach a higher indifference curve without spending any more money.
Evaluation. The model assumes consumers have full information, consistent preferences, and can rank every bundle, none of which behavioural economics finds fully realistic. It remains useful as a benchmark precisely because it identifies exactly which assumption is being relaxed when real behaviour, such as reference dependence or bounded rationality, departs from it.
Quick check: what condition defines the consumer’s optimal bundle in this model?

39. Income and substitution effects: normal, inferior and Giffen goods

When the price of a good falls, two separate forces are at work. The substitution effect always pushes consumption of the now relatively cheaper good up. The income effect reflects the fact that the consumer is now effectively richer, and can push consumption either up or down depending on whether the good is normal or inferior. Splitting the two apart explains one of the strangest results in microeconomics: a good whose demand curve slopes the wrong way.

The substitution effect, A to B, never changes. Only the income effect, B to C, differs between the three cases.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Only the toggle changes where C ends up. Everything else on this diagram, A, B, and both budget lines, is identical across all three cases, since the substitution effect never depends on whether the good is normal or inferior.
