Analysis. The Hicksian decomposition splits the total price effect, A to C, into a pure substitution effect, A to B, isolated using a hypothetical budget line with the new price ratio but just enough income to stay on the original indifference curve, and an income effect, B to C, which is whatever is left over once the hypothetical budget line is replaced with the real one.
Evaluation. Genuinely Giffen goods are extremely rare in practice, since it requires a good that is both strongly inferior and takes up a very large share of the consumer’s budget, historically associated with staple foods such as bread or rice among very poor households. It remains a favourite exam question precisely because it is the one case where the basic law of demand appears to break down, and testing whether students can explain why, rather than just describe it, is a strong discriminator of real understanding.
Quick check: what makes a Giffen good different from an ordinary inferior good?

40. Total utility and marginal utility: why demand curves slope down

Total utility is the whole satisfaction a consumer gets from a good. Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from just the next unit. The law of diminishing marginal utility, that each additional unit adds less satisfaction than the one before, is the underlying reason consumers are only willing to pay progressively less for extra units, which is exactly why demand curves slope downward.

Customisable, drag the slider
Both dots always sit at the same quantity. Watch total utility keep rising while marginal utility falls, then watch what happens once marginal utility turns negative.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
each extra unit still adds to total satisfaction, but by a smaller amount than the one before
The quantity where MU crosses zero is exactly the quantity where TU reaches its peak. Past that point, consuming more genuinely makes the consumer worse off, which almost never happens in practice simply because rational consumers stop before they get there.
Analysis. Marginal utility is the slope, the rate of change, of total utility. TU rises for as long as MU is positive, even while MU itself is falling, because adding a positive number, however small, still increases the total. TU only starts falling once MU turns negative.
Evaluation. Utility itself is not directly measurable or comparable between people, which is why modern microeconomics mostly relies on ordinal tools such as indifference curves rather than cardinal utility numbers. The diminishing marginal utility story remains useful as an intuitive first explanation for downward sloping demand, even though the more rigorous justification comes from the substitution effect covered in diagram 39.
Quick check: at the quantity where total utility is at its maximum, what is marginal utility equal to?

41. Isoquants and isocost lines: the firm’s least cost combination

An isoquant joins every combination of labour and capital that produces the same level of output. An isocost line shows every combination of labour and capital a firm can afford for a given total spending. Producer theory is the mirror image of consumer theory: the firm minimises the cost of producing a given output by finding the isocost line tangent to that isoquant.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider to change the firm’s total budget for inputs and watch the least cost combination slide along the expansion path.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
smaller budget
This is structurally the same diagram as diagram 38, with the axes relabelled: isoquants replace indifference curves, and the isocost line replaces the budget line. The economics of tangency works identically in both.
Analysis. At the tangency point, the slope of the isocost line, the ratio of input prices, equals the slope of the isoquant, the marginal rate of technical substitution between labour and capital. Off that point, the firm could produce the same output more cheaply by substituting between labour and capital.
Evaluation. The shape of the isoquant map reflects how easily a firm can substitute capital for labour. Highly automatable production, such as a bottling plant, has isoquants closer to straight lines, while production that genuinely needs both inputs in fixed proportions, such as a taxi needing both a driver and a car, has sharply kinked, right angled isoquants instead.
Quick check: what does the point of tangency between an isocost line and an isoquant represent?

42. The backward bending individual labour supply curve

A market labour supply curve usually slopes up, but a single individual’s own labour supply curve can bend backward at high wages. As the wage rises, the substitution effect makes leisure more expensive relative to work, encouraging more hours. But the income effect of a higher wage can eventually dominate, as a richer worker chooses to buy back some leisure time instead of working ever more hours.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider up through the wage rate and watch the dot travel forward, then bend back to the left, along the curve.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
low wage: substitution effect dominates, hours rise with the wage
This is an individual’s supply curve, not the whole market’s. A market labour supply curve can still slope upward throughout even if every single worker in it has their own backward bending curve, since new workers keep entering the market as the wage rises.
Analysis. At low to moderate wages, the substitution effect, work becomes more rewarding relative to leisure, tends to dominate, so hours supplied rise with the wage. Past some critical wage, the income effect, the worker can now afford more leisure while maintaining or improving their standard of living, can dominate instead, bending the curve backward.
Evaluation. This helps explain why some highly paid professionals choose to work fewer hours as their pay rises, and is relevant to debates about taxation, since a sufficiently high marginal tax rate on additional earnings can push a worker’s effective net wage back down the curve, changing the predicted effect on labour supply depending on which side of the bend the worker sits.
Quick check: what causes the labour supply curve to bend backward at high wages?

43. Public goods: vertical summation and the free rider problem

A pure public good, such as a lighthouse or national defence, is non-excludable, you cannot stop anyone from consuming it, and non-rival, one person consuming it does not reduce how much is left for anyone else. That changes how you build the market demand curve entirely: instead of adding quantities side by side, as with a private good, you add the price each person is willing to pay for the same unit, stacking the individual demand curves vertically.

Compare this with any ordinary market diagram in this guide, where two demand curves would instead be added side to side, horizontally, not stacked vertically.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
This vertical summation logic is the textbook justification for governments providing pure public goods directly and funding them out of general taxation rather than relying on individual purchase decisions.
Analysis. For a private good, two people can consume different quantities, so you add quantities at a given price, horizontal summation, which is why diagram 43 works completely differently from every ordinary demand and supply diagram in this guide. For a public good, everyone necessarily consumes the same quantity, since it cannot be divided between them, so you add the prices, or values, each would be willing to pay for that same quantity, hence vertical summation.
Evaluation. Real government provision does not require perfectly measuring MSB(A+B), which is informationally very demanding, only a judgement that some provision is better than the free market’s under provision. Not every good with public good characteristics is provided directly by the state: many, such as broadcasting or open-access research, rely instead on subsidy, advertising funding, or voluntary contribution to work around the free rider problem.
Quick check: why is the market demand curve for a public good found by adding curves vertically rather than horizontally?

44. The Edgeworth box: efficiency in exchange and the contract curve

An Edgeworth box packs two consumers and a fixed total stock of two goods into one diagram. Person 1’s origin is the bottom left corner, Person 2’s origin is the top right, rotated a hundred and eighty degrees. Any point in the box is a way of splitting the fixed total endowment between the two people, and the contract curve marks out every split that is Pareto efficient, meaning nobody can be made better off without making the other person worse off.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider to move along the contract curve itself, from allocations that favour Person 1 to allocations that favour Person 2.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
near Person 1’s origin: favours Person 2 almost entirely
Every point on the contract curve is efficient, but efficiency alone says nothing about fairness: the leftmost end gives almost everything to Person 2 while still technically being efficient, and the same is true in reverse at the other end.
Analysis. Point E sits inside the lens shape formed by the two indifference curves through it, meaning both people could trade their way to a point that makes at least one of them better off without harming the other, a Pareto improvement. Once an allocation sits on the contract curve itself, any further trade that helps one person necessarily harms the other, so no further Pareto improvement is possible.
Evaluation. The first welfare theorem states that a competitive market equilibrium is always somewhere on this contract curve, but it says nothing about which point, so a highly unequal endowment can lead to a perfectly efficient but very unequal outcome. This is the formal basis for the standard economics distinction between efficiency and equity being two separate questions requiring two separate kinds of policy answer.
Quick check: what is true of every point that lies exactly on the contract curve?

45. Bilateral monopoly: a strong union facing a monopsony employer

Diagram 8 showed a monopsony employer holding the wage down below the competitive rate. Now add a single, powerful trade union on the other side of the same market, acting as the sole seller of labour. With one buyer and one seller both able to influence price, standard supply and demand analysis breaks down, and the resulting wage becomes genuinely indeterminate within a range, decided by relative bargaining strength rather than a market clearing mechanism.

Notice that a union can raise both the wage and employment here at the same time, unlike in the ordinary competitive labour market shown in diagram 13.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Compare this with the ordinary minimum wage story in diagram 13. There, a wage floor above the competitive rate always reduces employment. Here, because the starting point is a monopsony, a wage floor imposed between Wm and Wc actually raises employment as well as the wage.
Analysis. A monopsonist alone sets employment where MCL equals MRP, then pays the lowest wage, Wm, that the supply curve will accept for that many workers. A union strong enough to impose a wage floor effectively flattens the employer’s marginal cost of labour up to the new wage, which is exactly how the minimum wage diagram in diagram 8 works, so any union wage between Wm and Wc raises both the wage and the level of employment simultaneously.
Evaluation. Outside this range, results reverse: a union pushing the wage above Wc starts to reduce employment again, just as an ordinary wage floor above a competitive equilibrium would. Bilateral monopoly is genuinely indeterminate in theory, real outcomes depend on strike costs, legal frameworks, public opinion and the relative patience of both sides, which is why it is often assessed through real world case studies rather than a single predicted number.
Quick check: within the bargaining range between Wm and Wc, what happens if the union pushes the wage up?

46. Income elasticity of demand: normal and inferior goods

Income elasticity of demand, YED, measures how quantity demanded responds to a change in consumer income, holding price constant. Its sign, not just its size, does the real classifying work: a positive YED marks a normal good, a negative YED marks an inferior good, and among normal goods, a value below one marks a necessity while a value above one marks a luxury. Toggle between three real spending patterns below, then drag the slider through the income range to watch YED update live.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider through the income range and watch the dot, and the YED reading, respond
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
YED ≈ 0.40, a necessity
Every curve here is a normal good's Engel curve except the inferior one, which turns down beyond a certain income: at low income, instant noodles behave like a normal good, but past a threshold, rising income lets consumers switch to better alternatives, so quantity demanded falls even as income keeps rising.
Analysis. YED is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income. Necessities sit between 0 and 1 because spending on them grows more slowly than income. Luxuries exceed 1 because spending on them grows faster than income, which is exactly why luxury goods industries are so sensitive to the economic cycle. Inferior goods carry a negative sign entirely because of the direction of the effect, not its size.
Evaluation. Whether a good is classed as normal or inferior is not fixed forever: it depends on the income level and the reference group being studied, and it can differ hugely between countries at different stages of development. A good that is a luxury in a low income country, such as a private car, may be treated as an everyday necessity in a high income one.
Quick check: a good has a YED of minus 0.3. What kind of good is it?

47. Cross elasticity of demand: substitutes and complements

Cross elasticity of demand, XED, measures how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of a different good. The sign again carries the meaning: a positive XED means the two goods are substitutes, since a price rise in one pushes buyers toward the other, and a negative XED means they are complements, since a price rise in one drags down demand for the other too, because they are consumed together.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider to raise or lower the price of the other good and watch this good's demand curve shift
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
unchanged, at the starting price
A rise in the price of tea makes coffee relatively more attractive, shifting the whole demand curve for coffee right, so more coffee is bought at every price of coffee. A rise in the price of sugar makes a cup of coffee more expensive to prepare exactly the way a customer wants it, shifting demand for coffee left instead.
Analysis. XED is the percentage change in quantity demanded of good A divided by the percentage change in the price of good B. The further from zero the value, the stronger the relationship: two very close substitutes, such as two brands of the same soft drink, carry a high positive XED, while two goods with only a loose complementary relationship carry an XED close to zero in either direction.
Evaluation. Firms use cross elasticity for real pricing decisions, such as predicting how a rival's price cut will hit their own sales, and competition regulators use it to help define the boundaries of a market: goods with a high positive cross elasticity are usually judged to be in the same market for merger and monopoly investigations, since they constrain each other's pricing power.
Quick check: the price of butter rises and the quantity of bread demanded falls at every price. What does this tell you about butter and bread?

48. Price elasticity of supply and the time period

Supply becomes more price elastic the longer a producer has to respond. In the momentary period there is simply no time to change output at all, so supply is perfectly inelastic. In the short run a firm can vary some inputs, such as overtime or existing machinery, giving some flexibility. In the long run every input, including entirely new factories, can be adjusted, making supply far more responsive to price. Toggle the time period, then drag the slider to shock demand and see how differently each supply curve reacts.

Same demand shock, three very different price and quantity responses depending on how much time producers have
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
no shock yet, starting equilibrium
Watch the same rightward demand shift produce almost pure price change under the momentary curve, a mix of price and quantity change under the short run curve, and mostly quantity change under the long run curve.
Analysis. All three supply curves cross the same starting equilibrium, so the difference you see is entirely down to elasticity, not a different starting point. Perishable goods, such as fresh fish at a morning market, sit close to the momentary case, since that day's catch is fixed. Manufactured goods with spare factory capacity sit closer to the short run case, and commodities like housing sit closer to the long run case once enough time passes for new building.
Evaluation. Real markets rarely sit neatly in one category forever: an oil market can behave almost like the momentary case during a sudden supply disruption, then become far more elastic over several years as new wells are drilled or alternatives are developed, which is exactly why short run and long run price forecasts for the same market can look so different.
Quick check: following an identical rise in demand, which time period sees the largest rise in price?

49. Buffer stock schemes: stabilising volatile commodity prices

Agricultural commodities such as cocoa or wheat see wildly swinging supply from one harvest to the next, even though demand stays fairly stable. A buffer stock scheme sets a target price band, a minimum and a maximum, and a manager who buys up the surplus during a bumper harvest to stop price collapsing below the minimum, then releases stock during a poor harvest to stop price spiking above the maximum. Drag the slider to move from a poor harvest through to a bumper one and watch the scheme respond.

Customisable, drag the slider
Predict first: during a bumper harvest, does the buffer stock manager buy or sell? Then drag right and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
an average harvest, price sits inside the target band, no intervention needed
The grey dot marks where price would freely settle this year, and the black dot marks where price actually ends up once the scheme steps in. When they coincide, the band was never tested.
Analysis. A bumper harvest shifts supply right, and without help price would fall below the minimum. Buying up the surplus at the minimum price is exactly what keeps farmer incomes from collapsing in a good year. A poor harvest shifts supply left, and releasing stock at the maximum price stops consumers facing a price spike. In theory the scheme can be self-financing, since stock bought cheaply in good years is sold at a higher price in bad ones.
Evaluation. In practice, many buffer stock schemes have collapsed, including well known cases in tin and cocoa. Setting the minimum price too high encourages chronic overproduction, since farmers know any surplus will be bought regardless, leaving the scheme permanently buying and running out of storage or funds. Perishable commodities cannot be stored at all, and running the scheme requires large upfront capital that many commodity producing countries struggle to fund.
Quick check: after a poor harvest, what does the buffer stock manager do?

50. Comparative advantage and the gains from trade

Comparative advantage does not require being the best at everything, only having the lowest opportunity cost of producing one particular good. Country A gives up less wine per unit of cloth than Country B does, or equivalently Country B gives up less cloth per unit of wine, so each country specialises in whichever good it sacrifices least to produce, trades at a price between their two opportunity costs, and both end up consuming outside their own production possibility frontier.

Four stage build. Watch stage four: both consumption points end up outside their own country's frontier
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Country A gives up 0.75 units of wine per unit of cloth, Country B gives up only 0.4, so B has the comparative advantage in cloth and A has it in wine, even without knowing which country is more productive overall.
Analysis. The trading price sits between the two countries' domestic opportunity costs, here roughly 0.55 units of wine per unit of cloth, strictly between A's 0.75 and B's 0.4. Any price in that range makes trade worthwhile for both sides, since each country gets a better deal trading than it could get producing the other good domestically. The gap between each country's autarky point and its post-trade consumption point is the gain from trade.
Evaluation. This model assumes constant opportunity costs, giving straight line frontiers, free and costless trade, and full employment of resources in both countries, none of which hold exactly in reality. It also says nothing about how the gains are shared between the two countries or between workers and firms within each one, which is exactly why the case for free trade is more contested in practice than the clean theory above suggests.
Quick check: Country B has a lower opportunity cost of producing cloth than Country A. What does the theory of comparative advantage say Country B should do?

51. Tariffs and quotas: the case for and against protectionism

A tariff is a tax on imports, and a quota is a limit on the physical quantity that may be imported. Both raise the domestic price above the world price and both reduce imports, but they differ in one crucial way: a tariff's revenue goes to the government, while an equivalent quota's rents typically go to whoever holds the import licences, often the foreign exporters themselves. Toggle between the two and drag the slider to set how restrictive the policy is.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider and watch both deadweight loss triangles grow as trade is restricted further
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
imports fall from 252 to 151 units
Grey triangles are the two deadweight losses: the left one from domestic firms producing units more cheaply available abroad, the right one from domestic consumers priced out of units they valued above the world price. The amber rectangle is government tariff revenue, or under a quota, licence holders' rents instead.
Analysis. Domestic producers gain from a higher protected price, and domestic consumers lose, but the consumer loss is strictly larger than the producer gain plus the government's revenue, and that gap is the deadweight loss. A large enough tariff, one at least as big as the original gap between the world price and the closed economy price, eliminates trade entirely and returns the country to its pre-trade equilibrium.
Evaluation. Governments still use both tools, often citing infant industry protection, national security in sectors like steel or semiconductors, or simple domestic job protection, but the efficiency loss shown here means these are almost always redistributive choices, favouring producers and government revenue or licence holders over the wider pool of consumers, rather than a free efficiency gain.
Quick check: under an import quota rather than a tariff, who typically captures the amber revenue rectangle?

52. The law of diminishing returns: total, average and marginal product

Add more and more of one variable input, such as labour, to a fixed input, such as land or machinery, and output eventually grows more slowly, then may even fall. Marginal product, the extra output from one more worker, always turns down first. Average product follows once marginal product drops below it. Total product keeps rising as long as marginal product is positive, and peaks exactly when marginal product hits zero. Drag the slider to add workers one at a time and watch all three curves respond together.

Customisable, drag the slider
Watch the three dots move together: MC crosses AC exactly where AC peaks is the same rule you saw in diagram thirty, just relabelled for production
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
increasing marginal returns: each new worker adds more than the last
Notice the order the three landmarks appear in as you drag right: marginal product peaks first, average product peaks second exactly where MP crosses it, and total product peaks last exactly where MP hits zero. That ordering is not a coincidence, it falls straight out of the calculus relationship between the three curves.
Analysis. Marginal product is the slope of total product at every point, which is why TP is still rising, just more slowly, throughout the diminishing returns region: MP only needs to be positive, not rising, for TP to keep climbing. Average product only starts falling once MP drops below it, since AP is pulled up by any MP above it and pulled down by any MP below it, the same logic linking marginal cost to average cost in diagram thirty.
Evaluation. This law only bites in the short run, since it assumes at least one input is fixed. Given enough time to also vary the fixed input, for instance building a second factory rather than just hiring more workers into the first one, a firm can escape diminishing returns entirely, which is exactly the distinction that separates this diagram from the long run economies of scale story in diagram thirty three.
Quick check: total product is at its absolute maximum. What must be true of marginal product at that exact point?

53. Keynesian versus classical long run aggregate supply

This is the long run aggregate supply curve, LRAS, and economists split into two camps over its shape. Classical economists model it as vertical at full employment output, Yf, since they assume wages and prices are flexible enough to keep the economy at full employment in the long run regardless of the price level, so any rise in aggregate demand can only raise prices, never real output. Keynesian economists instead draw a curve that is flat while there is spare capacity, since firms can expand output without raising prices, then curves increasingly steeply as the economy approaches full employment, where output can no longer respond and only price does. Toggle the assumption, then step through three rising levels of aggregate demand.

Same three demand increases, compare how differently price and output respond under each view
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The classical view treats the whole AS curve as if the economy always sat at, or instantly returned to, full employment. The Keynesian view allows genuine spare capacity in a recession, which is exactly why it implies demand-side policy can raise real output, not just prices, when the economy has room to grow into.
Analysis. Under the classical view, expansionary demand-side policy is powerless to raise output even briefly and only causes inflation, which is why classical economists favour supply-side policy to shift the vertical line itself rightward. Under the Keynesian view, the correct policy response depends entirely on where the economy currently sits on the curve: demand-side stimulus is far more effective, and far less inflationary, deep in the flat section than it is near full employment.
Evaluation. Most modern macroeconomists treat this less as a straight either-or choice and more as a description of the same economy at different points in the business cycle: closer to Keynesian behaviour during a deep recession with genuine spare capacity, and closer to classical behaviour once the economy is already close to full employment, which is exactly the shape the Keynesian curve itself is built to capture.
Quick check: in the Keynesian view, why does the same rise in aggregate demand raise output with almost no inflation on the flat section, but mostly raise price near the vertical section?

54. The competitive labour market: marginal revenue product and wage determination

A profit maximising firm hires workers up to the point where the extra revenue from one more worker, the marginal revenue product, MRP, just equals the wage. Since MRP falls as more workers are added, due to diminishing marginal product, the labour demand curve slopes down. Market labour supply slopes up as higher wages draw in more workers. Where the two meet sets both the market wage and the level of employment. Drag the slider to raise the price of the firm's output and watch labour demand shift.

Customisable, drag the slider
A higher output price raises MRP at every level of employment, since MRP = marginal physical product × price. Watch labour demand shift right as you drag.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
starting output price
This is the same shifting-curve mechanic as diagram twenty six, relabelled: instead of a shift in demand for a good, a rise in output price shifts demand for the labour that makes it, raising both the equilibrium wage and the level of employment together.
Analysis. MRP is the product of marginal physical product, how much extra output one more worker produces, and the price that output sells for. A rise in either raises MRP and shifts labour demand right, raising the wage. This is the theoretical foundation underneath the monopsony diagram in eight and the bilateral monopoly diagram in forty five, both of which modify this simple competitive base case by giving one side of the market power over the wage.
Evaluation. This model assumes both output and labour markets are perfectly competitive, so the firm is a wage taker with no power to influence pay. Real labour markets frequently deviate from this, through monopsony power, trade unions, minimum wage laws, or search frictions that make it costly for workers to move between employers, all of which can push the actual wage away from the simple MRP-equals-wage prediction shown here.
Quick check: the price of a firm's output rises. What happens to its labour demand curve, and to the equilibrium wage?

55. The money multiplier and credit creation

When a bank receives a new deposit, it keeps only a fraction back as reserves and lends the rest out. That loan gets spent and redeposited somewhere else in the banking system, which again lends most of it back out, and so on. The size of the reserve ratio alone determines how much brand new money the banking system can ultimately create from one original deposit, following the money multiplier formula, one divided by the reserve ratio.

Customisable, drag the slider
Predict first: does a lower reserve ratio make the bars shrink faster or slower across each lending round? Then drag and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
5% reserve ratio
Each bar is one round of lending, always a fixed share of the round before it. A low reserve ratio means banks keep back very little, so each round barely shrinks and the eventual total, the sum of every round including rounds far too small to see here, is enormous. A high reserve ratio makes each round shrink fast, choking off the process much sooner.
Analysis. If the reserve ratio is r, an initial deposit D generates further rounds of D(1-r), D(1-r) squared, and so on, an infinite geometric series that sums to exactly D divided by r. Total new money created, excluding the original deposit itself, is therefore D divided by r minus D, or equivalently D multiplied by (1-r) divided by r.
Evaluation. This simple textbook multiplier assumes every single loan is fully redeposited in the banking system and that banks are always willing to lend up to their legal limit, neither of which holds exactly in reality: some money leaks out as cash holdings outside banks, and during a financial crisis banks often hold reserves well above the legal minimum, causing actual credit creation to fall well short of the theoretical maximum shown here.
Quick check: the reserve ratio falls from 20% to 10%. What happens to the money multiplier?

56. Negative externality of consumption: demerit goods

Some goods harm people other than the buyer when they are consumed: secondhand smoke from a cigarette, the risk a drink driver poses to other road users, antibiotic resistance from overused medication. The buyer's own private benefit, MPB, sits above the true social benefit, MSB, because the buyer never weighs the harm to everyone else. Left alone, the market consumes more of the good than is socially desirable.

Toggle the tax on stage four to see it close the welfare loss triangle
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Compare this with diagram 3. There the wedge sat between MPC and MSC on the supply side; here it sits between MPB and MSB on the demand side, but the welfare loss logic is identical.
Analysis. The welfare loss triangle sits strictly between Qopt and Qm, bounded above by the supply curve, MSC, and below by MSB. A tax that exactly matches the external cost per unit shifts the effective demand curve consumers act on down to MSB, restoring the socially optimal output without banning the good outright.
Evaluation. Setting the tax correctly requires putting a monetary value on harm to others, which is genuinely difficult for goods like alcohol where the harm varies hugely between a moderate drinker and an addict. A single flat tax rate cannot price discriminate between the two, which is why some economists favour minimum unit pricing or outright bans for the most harmful demerit goods instead.
Quick check: for a demerit good, how does the socially optimal quantity compare with the free market quantity?

57. Positive externality of production

Some production processes benefit third parties beyond the firm doing the producing: a beekeeper's hives pollinate a neighbouring farmer's orchard for free, or a firm's staff training raises the skills of workers who later move to other employers. The true social cost, MSC, sits below the firm's own private cost, MPC, because the firm is never paid for the spillover benefit it creates. Left alone, the market underproduces the good.

Toggle the subsidy on stage four to see it close the welfare loss triangle
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
This is the mirror image of diagram 3: instead of a welfare loss from overproduction, this is a welfare loss from underproduction, since the firm has no financial reward for the spillover benefit it creates.
Analysis. The welfare loss triangle sits strictly between Qm and Qopt, bounded above by demand (MSB) and below by MSC: at every unit in that range the social benefit read off the demand curve exceeds the true social cost read off MSC, so the gap is widest at Qm (where it equals the external benefit) and closes to zero at Qopt. A subsidy equal to the external benefit per unit lowers the firm's effective cost to MSC, pushing output up to the social optimum. Notice the triangle here represents missed benefit, not wasted cost, the opposite of diagram 3's triangle.
Evaluation. Governments do subsidise activities like vocational training and vaccination for exactly this reason, but subsidies must be funded from taxation somewhere else in the economy, which carries its own distortionary cost. Measuring the external benefit accurately is just as hard as measuring an external cost, so subsidies are frequently set too high or too low in practice.
Quick check: a positive production externality exists. What does the free market do relative to the social optimum?

58. Cartels and collusive oligopoly

Instead of competing, oligopolists can collude to act as a single joint monopolist, restricting industry output and raising price above the competitive level. But every cartel carries the seeds of its own destruction: once the price is fixed above cost, each individual member has a private incentive to secretly produce more than its agreed quota, since it can sell extra units at the high cartel price while only paying its own low marginal cost.

Watch how far output falls, and price rises, once the cartel starts behaving like a single monopolist
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
If every member cheats a little, industry output drifts back toward Qc and price collapses back toward Pc, which is exactly why cartels tend to be unstable without a credible way to detect and punish cheating.
Analysis. A profit maximising cartel sets industry MC equal to industry MR, restricting output to Qcartel and raising price to Pcartel, precisely the monopoly rule applied to a group of firms acting together. The competitive benchmark, where MC equals demand directly, sits at a lower price and higher quantity, so the welfare loss from collusion is identical in shape to the welfare loss from a single monopoly in diagram five.
Evaluation. The cheating incentive shown here is a textbook illustration of the prisoner's dilemma from diagram thirty four applied to a real market: every member is individually better off cheating regardless of what rivals do, yet all members are worse off if everybody cheats. Cartels that survive tend to have a credible enforcement mechanism, transparent prices that make cheating easy to detect, or a dominant firm willing to punish deviators, which is exactly why most competition law treats cartels as illegal rather than relying on them to collapse naturally.
Quick check: why does an individual cartel member have an incentive to secretly produce beyond its agreed quota?

59. Merit goods and information failure

A merit good, such as education or a vaccination, is under-consumed for a different reason than an externality: people simply underestimate the private benefit to themselves, because they lack the information to value it correctly. The good's perceived demand curve sits below its true demand curve, even before anyone else in society is affected at all.

Note there is no third party here at all, unlike diagram 57: the whole gap is inside one person's own head
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
This diagram looks almost identical to diagram 57, and that is the point: under-provision looks the same on a graph whether it comes from a spillover benefit to third parties or from a gap inside one buyer's own information, but the correct government response is different, a subsidy or regulation for the externality, and better information or advertising for information failure.
Analysis. Because there is no third party here, MSB and MPB are actually equal, both sit on the true demand curve; what differs is that the buyer perceives a lower benefit than the true one and acts on that mistaken perception instead. Correcting the information failure, rather than taxing or subsidising a genuine external cost, is therefore the economically precise policy response, even though the resulting shift in the diagram looks the same as diagram 57.
Evaluation. Government information campaigns, compulsory schooling, and health warning labels are all attempts to close this gap directly. They are often cheaper than a permanent subsidy, but they can fail if people distrust the source of the information, or if the underestimate is driven by something other than a simple lack of facts, such as present bias about long delayed benefits like a pension.
Quick check: what is the key difference between a merit good's information failure and a positive production externality?

60. The firm's investment decision: the marginal efficiency of capital

A firm ranks every possible investment project by its expected rate of return, then invests in any project whose return exceeds the cost of borrowing, the interest rate. Because the best projects get taken first, the marginal efficiency of capital curve slopes down: as more is invested, only lower and lower return projects remain. A change in the interest rate moves the firm along this curve, while a change in business confidence or technology shifts the whole curve.

Compare stage two and stage three carefully: one is a movement along the curve, the other is a shift of it
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every project between the axis and the curve, at any given interest rate, has an expected return above that rate and gets funded; every project beyond the curve does not clear the hurdle and is shelved.
Analysis. This diagram is the theoretical foundation underneath the investment component of aggregate demand: it explains why cutting interest rates is meant to boost investment spending, and why investment is widely considered the most volatile component of AD, since business confidence, the position of the whole curve, can swing sharply with expectations about the future in a way the interest rate alone cannot.
Evaluation. In deep recessions, central banks sometimes find that interest rate cuts barely move investment at all, popularly described as pushing on a string. This diagram explains why: if pessimism has shifted the entire MEC curve far enough left, even a rate cut down to zero along the new, lower curve may still leave planned investment disappointingly low, which is exactly the case some economists made for large scale fiscal stimulus, or quantitative easing, during and after the 2008 financial crisis.
Quick check: a sudden wave of business pessimism about the future hits the economy. What happens to the MEC curve, as opposed to a simple interest rate cut?

61. Fixed versus floating exchange rate systems

Diagram 15 showed a floating exchange rate finding its own level in the market. Under a fixed exchange rate, the central bank instead commits to holding the rate at a specific peg, buying or selling its own reserves of foreign currency to soak up any gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied whenever market conditions shift. Toggle between the two regimes, then drag the slider to shock demand for the currency and see how differently each system responds.

Customisable, drag the slider
Under the peg, watch the central bank's intervention gap open up instead of the price simply moving
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
starting position, no shock
Under floating, a shock simply moves the price to a new equilibrium. Under fixed, the price cannot move at all: any shock instead opens a gap that only the central bank's reserves can close, night after night if the pressure does not let up.
Analysis. If demand for the currency rises under a fixed regime, the central bank must sell its own reserves of foreign currency, buying up the domestic currency to soak up the excess demand and stop it appreciating past the peg. If demand falls, the central bank must do the reverse, buying its own currency using reserves to stop it depreciating below the peg. A floating rate needs no reserves at all, since the price itself does all the adjusting.
Evaluation. A fixed rate gives businesses valuable certainty for trade and investment, but only for as long as the central bank's reserves hold out. A government facing persistent one directional pressure, such as a currency under constant speculative attack, can be forced into a sudden and often chaotic devaluation once reserves run low, exactly what happened to the UK on Black Wednesday in 1992 and to several Asian economies during the 1997 crisis.
Quick check: under a fixed exchange rate, demand for the currency falls sharply. What must the central bank do to defend the peg?

62. The quantity theory of money

The quantity theory of money starts from an identity that must always hold true: the money supply multiplied by how often it changes hands, velocity, equals the price level multiplied by real output, MV equals PY. Classical economists add two assumptions on top of that identity: velocity is roughly stable, and the economy sits at full employment output in the long run, fixed regardless of the money supply. Put those together and the conclusion is stark: any change in the money supply feeds through entirely into prices, not output at all.

Customisable, drag the slider
Drag the slider and watch output stay pinned at Yf while the price level absorbs the entire change
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
starting money supply
Doubling the money supply, holding V and Y fixed, must exactly double the price level, since the identity MV = PY has to hold. Money is neutral here: it changes the price level one for one but leaves real output completely untouched.
Analysis. The identity MV = PY is true by definition, since velocity is itself defined as nominal spending divided by the money supply. It only turns into the strong classical prediction, that money is neutral, once you add the extra assumptions that V is stable and Y sits fixed at potential output. Change either assumption and the strict proportionality between money and prices breaks down.
Evaluation. Keynesian economists reject the assumption that the economy always sits at full employment, pointing back to diagram fifty three's flat Keynesian AS curve: with genuine spare capacity, a rise in the money supply can raise real output, not just prices. Velocity is also empirically far from stable, particularly during a financial crisis when it can collapse sharply as households and banks suddenly hoard cash, which is exactly why quantitative easing after 2008 did not translate into the large rise in prices simple quantity theory would have predicted.
Quick check: under the strict classical quantity theory assumptions, what happens to real output when the money supply rises?

63. The economic cycle: boom, downturn, recession and recovery

Real GDP does not grow in a smooth straight line. It follows a long run upward trend, driven by growth in resources, capital and technology, but actual output oscillates around that trend in a repeating cycle: a boom where output runs above trend, a downturn as growth slows, a recession where output falls below trend, and a recovery as growth resumes. Step through the four phases below.

Watch the marker travel one full lap of the cycle as you step through the four stages
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The gap between the actual GDP curve and the trend line at any moment is the output gap: positive during a boom, negative during a recession, and exactly the same idea being tracked over time here that diagram fourteen compares at a single point in time.
Analysis. The trend line represents the economy's long run productive potential, growing steadily as the labour force, capital stock and technology improve. The actual GDP line swings around it because aggregate demand itself is volatile, driven by swings in consumer and business confidence, credit conditions and, from diagram sixty, especially investment. No two real cycles are identical in length or severity, but the same four phase pattern recurs.
Evaluation. Governments use countercyclical fiscal and monetary policy specifically to smooth this cycle, cutting rates and raising spending during a downturn, then doing the reverse in a boom. Critics argue that policy often acts with a lag long enough to arrive after the economy has already turned the corner on its own, potentially amplifying the very swings it was meant to dampen, an argument closely associated with monetarist economists sceptical of discretionary fine tuning.
Quick check: during a recession, how does actual real GDP compare with the long run trend?

64. Purchasing power parity and the Big Mac Index

Purchasing power parity says that in the long run, exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same amount everywhere once converted into a common currency. The Economist's Big Mac Index is a light-hearted but genuinely used shorthand test of this idea: since a Big Mac is a near-identical product almost everywhere, comparing its price across countries, converted at the actual market exchange rate, gives a rough and ready signal of whether a currency is over or undervalued.

Bars taller than the US price suggest an overvalued currency; bars shorter suggest an undervalued one
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
These bars are illustrative, meant to show the pattern rather than today's exact published figures, which The Economist updates and which move with exchange rates. The consistent real world finding is that a Big Mac tends to be cheaper in lower income countries, suggesting their currencies trade below what strict purchasing power parity would predict.
Analysis. If a Big Mac costs more in Switzerland than in the United States once converted at the market exchange rate, the index reads the Swiss franc as overvalued relative to the dollar on a PPP basis. If it costs less, as it typically does in countries like India or Egypt, the local currency reads as undervalued. Genuine purchasing power parity would predict the bars should all reach exactly the same height.
Evaluation. The index is deliberately a simplification and economists do not treat it as a precise forecasting tool. Big Mac prices reflect local rent, labour costs and taxes as much as the exchange rate itself, non-traded inputs that pure currency theory ignores, and burgers are not actually traded across borders to arbitrage the price gap away the way the theory assumes for tradable goods. Even so, the broad pattern it captures, that price levels are systematically lower in poorer countries, is a real and well documented economic finding, sometimes called the Balassa-Samuelson effect.
Quick check: a Big Mac costs far less in Egypt than in the United States once converted at the market exchange rate. What does the Big Mac Index suggest about the Egyptian pound?

65. The monetary policy transmission mechanism

A central bank does not control inflation directly. It changes one thing, the base interest rate, and relies on a chain of knock-on effects working through the wider economy to eventually influence aggregate demand and, with a long and variable lag, inflation itself. Step through the chain below to see how one small decision in a central bank meeting room eventually reaches ordinary households and firms.

Four stage build, following one interest rate cut all the way through the economy
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Central banks routinely describe this whole chain as operating with a lag of twelve to eighteen months before the full effect on inflation is felt, which is exactly why interest rate decisions are forward looking, based on where the bank expects the economy to be over that horizon, not on where it is right now.
Analysis. Notice there are three separate channels running in parallel from stage two: the interest rate channel working through borrowing and saving directly, the asset price or wealth channel, and the exchange rate channel working through net exports. All three eventually feed into the same aggregate demand shift, which is exactly the AD curve moving in diagrams nine through eleven.
Evaluation. The strength of every channel varies with the structure of the economy: a country with a lot of variable rate mortgage debt, like the UK, sees the interest rate channel bite quickly, while a country with mostly long fixed rate mortgages, like the US, transmits policy more slowly through that particular channel. The exchange rate channel can also work in reverse of intentions during a global crisis, if a rate cut triggers capital flight rather than the textbook depreciation shown here.
Quick check: a central bank cuts interest rates. Through the exchange rate channel, what should happen to net exports?

66. Cournot duopoly: reaction functions and Nash equilibrium

Two firms sell an identical product and simultaneously choose how much to produce, each treating the other's output as fixed. Every firm's best output depends on what it expects its rival to make, which is exactly what a reaction function plots. Where the two reaction functions cross is the Cournot Nash equilibrium: the only pair of outputs where neither firm wants to change its own output given the other's.

Market: P = 100 − Q, constant marginal cost = 10 for both firms, so each firm's reaction function is q = 45 − 0.5(rival's output).
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both reaction functions have a slope of -0.5, not -1, because each firm only accounts for half the effect of its rival's output on the price it receives. That is exactly why the Cournot outcome (60 total) sits between the collusive outcome (45 total) and the perfectly competitive outcome (90 total).
Analysis. Firm 1's profit is q1(100−q1−q2−10). Maximising with respect to q1 gives the reaction function q1 = 45 − 0.5q2, and by symmetry q2 = 45 − 0.5q1. Solving the two simultaneously gives q1* = q2* = 30, total output 60, and price P = 100−60 = 40. Neither firm can raise its profit by unilaterally changing output given what the other is doing, which is exactly the definition of a Nash equilibrium.
Evaluation. Cournot output (60) sits strictly between the collusive, joint-profit-maximising output (45) and the perfectly competitive output (90), and price sits strictly between the monopoly price and the competitive price the same way. As more identical firms are added to the Cournot model, the equilibrium converges towards the competitive outcome, which is one way examiners like to link oligopoly theory back to the market structure spectrum.
Quick check: why is the Cournot equilibrium output higher than the collusive (cartel) output?

67. Bertrand price competition and the Bertrand paradox

Cournot duopolists compete by choosing quantities. Bertrand duopolists compete by choosing prices instead, selling an identical, homogeneous product. Whichever firm sets the lower price captures the whole market, so each firm has a constant incentive to undercut the other, right down to the point where price equals marginal cost. With just two firms and a homogeneous product, that single change in strategic variable is enough to produce the fully competitive outcome, a result famous enough to have its own name: the Bertrand paradox.

Same market as diagram 66: P = 100 − Q, constant marginal cost = 10. Watch what a change from quantity competition to price competition does to the outcome.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Compare this final equilibrium quantity, 90, with diagram 66's Cournot quantity, 60, and diagram 68's Stackelberg quantity, 67.5, on exactly the same demand and cost conditions. The only thing that changed across the three diagrams is the strategic variable, quantity versus price, and whether one firm moves first.
Analysis. With a homogeneous product and constant marginal cost, any price above MC leaves the higher-priced firm with zero customers, so both firms are always tempted to undercut. The only price neither firm wants to undercut further is price equal to marginal cost, since undercutting below MC would mean selling at a loss. At P = MC = 10, both firms earn zero economic profit, matching the perfectly competitive benchmark, even though there are only two firms in the market.
Evaluation. The Bertrand paradox is sensitive to its assumptions. With differentiated products, each firm retains some loyal customers even at a higher price, so equilibrium price settles above marginal cost. With capacity constraints, a firm cannot always serve the entire market even at the lowest price, which is exactly the setup used in diagram 70 on peak-load pricing. Repeated interaction, covered in diagram 69, can also let firms sustain prices above marginal cost by threatening future punishment for undercutting.
Quick check: under classic Bertrand competition with a homogeneous product and constant marginal cost, what stops price falling below marginal cost?

68. Stackelberg leadership: the first-mover advantage

Cournot duopolists choose output simultaneously. A Stackelberg duopoly changes only one thing: one firm, the leader, commits to its output first and publicly, and the follower then chooses its own best response having observed the leader's choice. That timing change alone shifts the outcome away from the symmetric Cournot equilibrium, and it rewards the leader for exactly the reason you would expect: committing first changes what the rival can credibly threaten to do.

Same market again: P = 100 − Q, marginal cost = 10. Firm 1 is now the leader and moves first.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Notice the follower's point still sits exactly on R2, its own reaction curve, since it is genuinely best-responding to whatever the leader has already committed to. The leader's point does not sit on R1, because the leader is not simply reacting to a fixed rival, it is choosing the point on R2 that maximises its own profit, which is a different optimisation problem entirely.
Analysis. The leader anticipates the follower's reaction function, q2 = 45 − 0.5q1, and substitutes it directly into its own profit function before choosing q1, rather than treating q2 as fixed the way Cournot firms do. That gives the leader's profit as q1(45 − 0.5q1), maximised at q1 = 45, which is exactly the same as the monopoly output in diagram 67. The follower then plays its best response to that, q2 = 22.5.
Evaluation. This is the first-mover advantage in its cleanest form: the leader earns strictly more profit than either firm earns under Cournot, and the follower earns strictly less, purely because of the order of moves, not because of any cost or product advantage. In practice, being a credible first mover requires the commitment to actually be irreversible and visible to the rival, for instance a large, publicly announced factory investment, otherwise the follower has no reason to believe the leader will not quietly revise its output back down.
Quick check: why does the Stackelberg leader produce more than its Cournot output of 30?

69. Repeated games and trigger strategies: why real cartels sometimes hold

Diagram 34 showed that in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, cheating is a dominant strategy and collusion always collapses. Real cartels do not play the game just once, though: they play it period after period, and that changes the incentives completely. If firms can credibly punish a rival for cheating in the future, cooperation can be sustained even though cheating still looks tempting in any single period. This diagram uses the same payoff matrix as diagram 34 and follows it over several periods under two different punishment rules.

Switch the toggle above to compare two punishment rules once you reach stage four.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Under Grim Trigger, one deviation destroys cooperation permanently, which is the harshest possible punishment and therefore the strongest deterrent, but it is also unforgiving of a single mistake or misread signal. Under Tit-for-Tat, punishment is proportionate, exactly one round, which recovers cooperation faster but is a weaker deterrent against a rival calculating whether cheating once is still worth it.
Analysis. A firm considering whether to cheat in a repeated game weighs the one-off temptation payoff, 70 instead of 50, against the discounted stream of lower payoffs the punishment triggers afterwards. Collusion is sustainable as a subgame perfect equilibrium only if the future losses from punishment outweigh the immediate gain from cheating, which depends on how patient the firms are, formally their discount factor, and on how severe and how certain the punishment is.
Evaluation. Grim Trigger is the theoretical maximum deterrent precisely because it is maximally harsh, but real firms rarely use anything that punishing, since it cannot recover from a single accidental price cut caused by, say, an unexpected demand shock rather than deliberate cheating. Tit-for-Tat is famous for performing well in repeated tournaments partly because it is forgiving, clear, and immediately retaliatory, all three of which make it easy for a rival to learn and therefore easy to cooperate with.
Quick check: what is the main real-world weakness of a Grim Trigger strategy compared with Tit-for-Tat?

70. Peak-load pricing: charging more when capacity binds

Some goods, electricity, rail travel, hotel rooms, cannot be stored, and the capacity to supply them is fixed in the short run. Demand for the same service is not constant, though: it is much higher at some times, the morning commute, a Friday evening, than others. Charging a single price around the clock either wastes spare capacity off-peak or fails to ration scarce capacity at peak. Peak-load pricing solves both problems by charging a low, cost-reflective price off-peak and a higher price at peak that reflects the true scarcity of capacity.

Same short run marginal cost serves both periods; only demand differs by time of day.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The off-peak price is read straight off the flat short run marginal cost curve, since there is spare capacity to meet that demand. The peak price is read off demand at the vertical capacity constraint instead, because output literally cannot rise past K no matter how high demand goes, so price has to do the rationing that quantity cannot.
Analysis. Off-peak, capacity is not the binding constraint, so the efficient price is simply marginal cost, P = SRMC = 20, giving quantity 40, comfortably below capacity of 70. At peak, marginal cost alone cannot ration demand, since 133 units would be demanded at that price against only 70 available, so the efficient price is instead read off the demand curve at Q = K, giving P = 58. The gap between the two prices, 38, is the scarcity or capacity charge, and in a competitive market it is exactly the revenue needed to justify further investment in capacity.
Evaluation. Peak-load pricing is allocatively efficient, since it makes each period's price reflect that period's true marginal cost, including the opportunity cost of scarce capacity at peak. The main objection is distributional and practical: peak users, who are often price-inelastic commuters rather than discretionary travellers, end up paying the most, and metering or monitoring usage finely enough to actually apply two different prices can itself be costly, which is why simpler flat-rate pricing persists in some markets despite the inefficiency.
Quick check: why is off-peak price set equal to marginal cost, while peak price is set higher, at the level demand reaches when quantity equals capacity?

71. The IS-LM model: goods and money market equilibrium together

The IS-LM model, developed by John Hicks, puts the goods market and the money market on the same diagram so that a single interest rate and a single level of national income are determined simultaneously, rather than looking at either market in isolation. The IS curve plots every combination of the interest rate and income at which planned spending equals output, the goods market clearing condition. The LM curve plots every combination at which money demand equals the fixed money supply, the money market clearing condition. Only where they cross is the whole economy in equilibrium at once.

Toggle the shock
Use the toggle above on stage three to compare a fiscal expansion against a monetary expansion
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both shifted curves were built from the same 70 pixel parallel shift and solved algebraically against the untouched curve, which is why the two new equilibria sit at exactly the same income level, Y2, even though one raises the interest rate and the other lowers it.
Analysis. IS slopes downward because a lower interest rate lowers the cost of borrowing, raising planned investment, which raises equilibrium income through the multiplier. LM slopes upward because a higher income raises transactions demand for money, and with a fixed money supply that extra demand can only be rationed by a higher interest rate. A rightward shift of either curve alone raises Y, but only a rightward IS shift raises r at the same time; a rightward LM shift lowers it, because a monetary expansion pushes the interest rate down along the unchanged IS curve.
Evaluation. This model assumes the price level is fixed, which is a reasonable short run simplification but breaks down once AD/AS effects and inflation are allowed to operate, which is exactly why diagrams nine through twelve are needed to complete the macroeconomic picture. It also assumes a fairly interest sensitive investment demand; if investment barely responds to the interest rate, IS becomes close to vertical and monetary policy loses most of its power to change Y, a case Keynes himself associated with a liquidity trap and deep recession.
Quick check: which policy raises national income while also raising the interest rate?

72. The crowding-out effect: loanable funds and AD/AS side by side

Crowding out is the idea that when a government borrows more to finance extra spending, the resulting rise in the interest rate discourages some private investment, so the final increase in aggregate demand is smaller than the government spending increase alone would suggest. The two panels below show exactly why: the left panel finds the new, higher interest rate in the loanable funds market, and the right panel carries that higher rate across into the AD/AS model to show its dampening effect on the final outcome.

Two linked panels, loanable funds on the left, AD/AS on the right
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Left panel: government borrowing shifts D right by 40 pixels; the resulting rate rise cuts private investment by exactly that much read off the ORIGINAL D1 curve, not the new one. Right panel: AD(net) uses only a 30 pixel shift, smaller than the naive 55 pixel AD(gross) shift, exactly reflecting that lost private investment.
Analysis. The correct method, examiners specifically check for this, is to read private investment off the original D1 curve at the new, higher interest rate r2, not off the new D2 curve, since D2 already includes the government's own borrowing. The gap between D1's reading and Q2 is the government's borrowing; on the right, that lost private investment is exactly why AD only shifts out to AD(net) rather than the full AD(gross) that a naive spending multiplier calculation, ignoring the interest rate, would predict.
Evaluation. Crowding out is strongest when the economy is already near full capacity, so LRAS is a binding constraint and the central bank is unlikely to accommodate the extra borrowing. It is weaker, or can reverse into crowding in, during a recession with spare capacity and very low interest rates, since extra government spending can raise incomes, saving, and business confidence by more than it raises the interest rate, an argument frequently made about fiscal stimulus during and after the 2008 and 2020 downturns.
Quick check: to find how far private investment actually falls, which curve should you read from at the new interest rate r2?

73. The Solow-Swan neoclassical growth model

The Solow-Swan model explains long run growth through capital accumulation. Output per worker, f(k), rises with capital per worker, k, but at a diminishing rate, since each extra unit of capital has less labour to work with than the last. A constant fraction, s, of that output is saved and invested each period, sf(k). Some of that investment is needed just to replace depreciating capital and equip new workers as the population grows, the break-even line (n+d)k. Where actual investment meets the break-even line, capital per worker stops changing: the steady state, k*.

Toggle the savings rate
Use the toggle above on stage four to shift sf(k) and find the new steady state
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The break-even line is a straight line solved exactly; sf(k) is a curve constructed to pass through the steady state sitting exactly on that line, so k1*, k2* and every dashed guide are mutually consistent rather than placed by eye.
Analysis. The steady state is stable: displace k below k*, and sf(k) exceeds break-even investment, so capital per worker rises back towards k*; displace it above k*, and sf(k) falls short, so it shrinks back down. A higher savings rate shifts sf(k) up and raises the steady state level of capital and output per worker, but growth stops again once the new k* is reached, since nothing in the model has changed the underlying rate of return once diminishing returns to capital have fully set in.
Evaluation. This is the model's most exam-tested conclusion: without continuous improvements in technology, shifting f(k) itself upward over time, an economy that only saves and invests more will eventually stop growing per worker, since diminishing returns to capital always catch up. This is exactly why the Solow model implies convergence between countries with similar savings rates and technology, and why the endogenous growth model in the next diagram was developed specifically to explain how sustained, rather than one-off, per capita growth is possible.
Quick check: according to the Solow model, what happens to the long run GROWTH RATE of output per worker if a country simply raises its savings rate and nothing else changes?

74. Endogenous growth: the AK model

The AK model strips capital of diminishing returns entirely: output is simply Y = Ak, a constant multiple of capital per worker, where A captures the economy's technology and its stock of human capital, knowledge and institutions broadly defined as part of capital. Because the marginal product of capital never falls, this single change is enough to generate permanent, self-sustaining growth in output per worker, without needing any outside improvement in technology to keep it going, unlike the Solow model in the previous diagram.

Compare this directly with diagram 73: here, sAk never crosses back down to meet the break-even line
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
All three lines pass exactly through the origin; sAk's gap over the break-even line was checked algebraically at k=300 and k=550 above, confirming the gap widens in absolute terms as k rises, consistent with a constant, sustained percentage growth rate.
Analysis. Because Y = Ak has a constant marginal product of capital, A, both f(k) and sf(k) are straight lines through the origin rather than curves that flatten out. As long as the savings line, sAk, is steeper than the break-even line, (n+d)k, meaning sA is greater than (n+d), the two lines only ever meet at the origin. There is no steady state to converge to: capital per worker, and therefore output per worker, grows forever at the constant rate g = sA − (n+d).
Evaluation. The knife-edge condition, sA exactly equal to (n+d), is a genuine weakness: real economies do not appear to be perfectly balanced on this edge, and the model offers no natural mechanism pulling sA and (n+d) together the way diminishing returns does in Solow. Even so, the AK model's core insight, that broadly defined capital, including human capital, knowledge, and research and development, might not suffer diminishing returns at the economy-wide level, is the founding idea behind the wider endogenous growth literature associated with Paul Romer and Robert Lucas, and it explains persistent cross-country growth differences that the Solow model alone struggles to.
Quick check: what single assumption is responsible for the AK model generating permanent growth where the Solow model does not?

75. The output gap and the business cycle wave

Real GDP does not grow along a smooth, straight line. It oscillates around its long run potential trend in a recurring pattern: boom, downturn, recession, and recovery. The output gap is the vertical distance between actual and potential GDP at any moment, positive during a boom, negative during a recession, and this wave-shaped diagram is the standard way of showing the whole business cycle as one continuous, connected story rather than four separate snapshots.

Two full cycles are shown so you can see the pattern repeat
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The actual GDP wave was built from nine points computed directly from a sine formula around the trend line, so it crosses the trend exactly at the boundary of every shaded output gap region, never approximately.
Analysis. Wherever the actual GDP curve sits above the dashed trend line, the economy has a positive output gap: demand-pull inflationary pressure tends to build, since firms are producing beyond their normal sustainable capacity. Wherever it sits below, a negative output gap opens up: spare capacity exists, unemployment tends to rise, and inflationary pressure eases. The trend line itself represents potential output, which grows steadily over time as the labour force, capital stock, and productivity all expand, entirely independent of where the economy currently sits in its cycle.
Evaluation. Potential output is not directly observable and has to be estimated, using methods such as statistical trend-fitting or production function approaches, which means the size of any output gap quoted by a central bank or the OBR is always an estimate, not a precise measured fact, and can be revised significantly after the event. This matters hugely for policy, since a government or central bank that misjudges how much spare capacity actually exists risks tightening policy into a recession that has not really overheated, or loosening policy into an economy already running past potential.
Quick check: during a negative output gap, where does the actual GDP curve sit relative to the potential GDP trend line?

76. The Mundell-Fleming model: IS-LM in an open economy

Mundell and Fleming extended IS-LM to an open economy by adding a balance of payments line, BP, showing every combination of the interest rate and income at which the balance of payments is zero. With perfect capital mobility, funds flow instantly to wherever the return is highest, so BP is horizontal at the world interest rate, r*: any domestic rate above r* pulls in capital and pushes the balance of payments into surplus, any rate below it pushes the balance into deficit, and only r* itself is sustainable.

Toggle the regime
Toggle above to compare the two cases where policy is fully effective
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both final equilibria land on exactly Y=440, because in each case the curve that did not move directly is pulled along automatically, by intervention under fixed rates or by the exchange rate itself under floating rates, until r returns precisely to r*.
Analysis. Under fixed exchange rates with perfect capital mobility, monetary policy is powerless: any attempt to expand the money supply pushes r below r*, triggers a capital outflow and a BoP deficit, and forces the central bank to sell reserves and shrink the money supply straight back to where it started. Fiscal policy, by contrast, is fully effective, since the resulting BoP surplus is met with exactly the monetary expansion needed to hold r at r*. Under floating rates the result flips: monetary policy becomes fully effective, working through currency depreciation and net exports, while fiscal expansion crowds itself out entirely through currency appreciation, leaving Y unchanged.
Evaluation. Perfect capital mobility is a simplifying extreme; with imperfect mobility the BP line slopes upward rather than sitting flat, and both policies retain some, partial, effectiveness under both regimes rather than the clean either-or result shown here. The model also assumes the exchange rate itself has no separate effect on domestic prices or expectations, which is a reasonable short run assumption but breaks down for economies with a lot of foreign currency debt or import dependence, where a large depreciation can be contractionary rather than expansionary.
Quick check: under fixed exchange rates with perfect capital mobility, which policy is powerless to change national income?

77. The impossible trinity: the policy trilemma

The impossible trinity, or policy trilemma, is the Mundell-Fleming model's headline conclusion in a single picture: no country can simultaneously have a fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital across its borders, and an independent monetary policy that it can set to suit its own economy. Any country can pick two of the three corners, but never all three at once, and each edge of the triangle corresponds to a real world policy choice.

Each edge is a real, sustainable policy combination; the whole triangle is not
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The triangle's three vertices are the three goals; its three edges, not its interior, are the only combinations a country can actually sustain, since holding all three vertices at once is the "impossible" corner the model rules out.
Analysis. This is directly the Mundell-Fleming result restated visually: a country on the fixed-rate-plus-free-capital edge has, by construction, given up control of its own interest rate, since that rate is pinned to the world rate by arbitrage; a country on the fixed-rate-plus-monetary-independence edge must instead restrict capital flows to stop that arbitrage from happening; and a country on the free-capital-plus-monetary-independence edge has let its exchange rate float to absorb the pressure instead.
Evaluation. Few countries sit exactly on a single edge; most choose a managed position somewhere inside, tolerating partial capital controls, a managed float, or occasional intervention, trading off a bit of each goal rather than fully sacrificing one. The financial crises of the 1990s in Mexico, East Asia and Argentina are often read as economies that tried, and failed, to hold onto all three goals with a fixed or quasi-fixed exchange rate under growing capital mobility.
Quick check: a country with free capital movement and a fixed exchange rate has necessarily given up which of the three goals?

78. The golden rule level of capital

A higher savings rate raises the Solow model's steady state, but higher is not always better for living standards, since more saving today means less consumption today. The golden rule level of capital, k(gold), is the one steady state that maximises steady state consumption per worker, found where the production function's slope, the marginal product of capital, exactly equals the slope of the break-even investment line.

The golden rule point is where f(k) is exactly parallel to the break-even line
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
k(gold) was found by setting the slope of the f(k) curve equal to the slope of the straight break-even line, a genuine tangency solved with calculus, not placed by eye; the sf(k) curve in stage four was then constructed to pass exactly through that point.
Analysis. Steady state consumption per worker equals output minus the investment needed to keep k constant, f(k) minus (n+d)k, the vertical gap between the two curves. That gap is at its widest exactly where the two curves have the same slope, since to either side the gap is narrowing.
