To the left of k(gold), more saving raises both output and consumption; to the right, the economy is dynamically inefficient, oversaving so much that consumption could be raised at every date by saving less, since the extra output from more capital no longer covers the extra investment needed just to maintain it.
Evaluation. Very few real economies are diagnosed as dynamically inefficient, oversaving past the golden rule, since capital's return in practice tends to sit comfortably above the sum of population growth and depreciation. The concept's real use is as a benchmark for policy debates about national savings rates, and for the finding, associated with Edmund Phelps, that a market economy with a fixed savings rate has no automatic tendency to end up exactly at the golden rule, since nothing in individual saving decisions is calibrated to it.
Quick check: at the golden rule level of capital, what is true about the slope of f(k)?

79. Okun's law: the output gap and unemployment

Okun's law is the empirical finding that output and unemployment move in a stable, negative relationship: when real GDP is running above its potential, unemployment tends to sit below its natural rate, and when GDP falls short of potential, unemployment rises above it. It is the bridge between the goods market side of macroeconomics, output gaps and business cycles, and the labour market side, giving policymakers a rough rule of thumb for translating one into the other.

A steeper line means a given output gap moves unemployment by more
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The fitted line was constructed to pass exactly through the origin, checked algebraically, since by definition a zero output gap corresponds to unemployment sitting exactly at its natural rate.
Analysis. Output is not one-for-one with employment: when output rises, firms often meet extra demand partly by working existing staff harder before hiring, "labour hoarding", and rising employment can pull previously inactive people into the labour force rather than only reducing measured unemployment. Both effects mean the Okun coefficient is well below one, typically estimated at around 0.4 to 0.6: it consistently takes more than a one percentage point rise in the output gap to move the unemployment gap by a full point in the opposite direction.
Evaluation. The relationship is a stable empirical regularity rather than a structural law, and the coefficient is not fixed: several studies find it has weakened somewhat in recent decades, and structural change, an ageing workforce, more part-time and gig work, or big supply shocks like the pandemic, can shift the line or its slope, meaning the same output gap can translate into a noticeably different unemployment outcome across different periods.
Quick check: what does the Okun line predict happens to the unemployment gap when there is a large POSITIVE output gap?

80. The Fisher equation: real versus nominal interest rates

The interest rate that appears on a savings account or a loan, the nominal rate, is not what a saver or borrower ultimately cares about: what matters is the real rate, the return after inflation has eroded the purchasing power of money. The Fisher equation ties the two together: the real interest rate is approximately the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so the same nominal rate can mean a very different real return depending on what inflation is doing.

Watch Year 3 and Year 4: the highest nominal rate is not the highest real rate
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every point on the real rate line was computed as exactly nominal minus inflation for that year (Year 4: 7% minus 5% = 2%; Year 3: 4% minus 1% = 3%), which is why Year 3 sits above Year 4 on the real line despite sitting below it on the nominal line.
Analysis. The exact Fisher relationship is (1+nominal) = (1+real)(1+expected inflation); at the low, single-digit rates typical of most economies, the approximation real is approximately nominal minus expected inflation is close enough to be the standard teaching version. Because it is EXPECTED, not actual, inflation that borrowers and lenders build into the nominal rate they agree to, unexpectedly high inflation quietly transfers real wealth from lenders to borrowers, since the lender ends up being repaid in money worth less than they anticipated, while unexpectedly low inflation does the reverse.
Evaluation. This is why a central bank's inflation credibility matters so much for the cost of borrowing: if people trust inflation will stay low, expected inflation and therefore nominal rates stay low too, but if a central bank loses credibility, expected inflation rises, and nominal rates must rise with it just to keep the real rate, and therefore the incentive to lend at all, unchanged. This link between credibility, expectations and nominal rates is a recurring theme connecting the quantity theory of money and the monetary transmission mechanism elsewhere in this guide.
Quick check: in Year 4 the nominal rate is 7% and inflation is 5%. What is the approximate real interest rate?

81. Frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment

Not all unemployment has the same cause, and the distinction matters enormously for policy. Frictional and structural unemployment persist even when the labour market has fully cleared, since some job searching and skills mismatch is unavoidable in any dynamic economy; together they make up the natural rate. Cyclical unemployment is different: it only appears when demand for labour falls and wages do not fall quickly enough to clear the market, opening up an additional, genuinely avoidable gap on top of the natural rate.

Two separate gaps, from two separate causes, on the same diagram
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Ld2 was shifted left by exactly 70 pixels; reading it off at the unchanged wage We gives new employment of Q2=300, exactly 70 less than Qe=370, so the diagram's cyclical gap matches the size of the shock precisely rather than being drawn approximately.
Analysis. Frictional unemployment comes from the normal, healthy process of workers moving between jobs, search taking time even when suitable vacancies exist. Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch between the skills or location of the unemployed and the vacancies on offer, often the legacy of long run shifts in technology or trade. Both exist AT the market-clearing wage We, which is why the natural rate is not zero even in stage two, before any shock hits. Cyclical unemployment is fundamentally different: it is a disequilibrium phenomenon, requiring the wage to be prevented, by contracts, norms or minimum wage laws, from falling to a new market-clearing level.
Evaluation. This distinction drives very different policy prescriptions: cyclical unemployment calls for demand-side stimulus, monetary or fiscal policy to shift Ld back out, while frictional and structural unemployment call for supply-side measures instead, better job-matching services, retraining programmes, or portable benefits that do not penalise moving between jobs, since no amount of demand stimulus permanently cures a skills mismatch.
Quick check: which type of unemployment requires the real wage to be stuck above its market-clearing level to exist?

82. Quantitative easing: from the bond market to aggregate demand

Quantitative easing is what a central bank turns to once its policy interest rate is already close to zero and cannot be cut much further. Rather than setting a price (the interest rate) and letting the quantity of money adjust, the central bank does the reverse: it creates new money to buy a chosen quantity of government bonds, and lets that purchase determine the resulting fall in the interest rate, or yield, on those bonds.

Left panel: the bond market. Right panel: the wider economy
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The bond market shift and the AD shift were solved independently and then linked only through the story, not through a shared formula, since QE's exact pass-through from yields to spending is an empirical estimate, not a fixed mechanical ratio.
Analysis. A bond's price and its yield move in opposite directions by construction, since a bond promises a fixed stream of future payments: paying more today for that same fixed stream mechanically lowers the annual return, the yield. By buying bonds directly, the central bank pushes their price up and their yield down, and because that bond's yield is a benchmark other borrowing rates are priced off, mortgages, corporate loans, this fall ripples out into cheaper borrowing costs economy-wide, raising investment and consumption and shifting AD to the right, exactly the channel a conventional interest rate cut would use, just reached by a different route.
Evaluation. QE's effectiveness is genuinely disputed: some of the newly created money simply sits as extra reserves in the banking system rather than being lent on, and some of the effect works through raising asset prices, and therefore wealth, for those who already own bonds and shares, which critics argue widens wealth inequality rather than reliably boosting spending by everyone. Central banks that used QE heavily after 2008 and 2020 generally judge it to have supported demand and avoided deflation, but the size of the effect on output and inflation remains one of the most actively debated questions in modern monetary economics.
Quick check: when the central bank buys government bonds under QE, what happens to bond YIELDS?

83. The Kuznets curve: growth and inequality

Simon Kuznets observed, from cross-country data, that income inequality often appears to rise in the early stages of economic development, as workers shift from low-productivity agriculture into a growing, unevenly paid industrial sector, before falling again in mature, high-income economies as education spreads and welfare states mature. Plotted as inequality against income per capita, this traces out an inverted U shape, the Kuznets curve.

An empirical, historical pattern, not a solved market equilibrium
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
This curve, unlike the market diagrams elsewhere in this guide, illustrates a proposed empirical pattern rather than a solved equilibrium: it is drawn as a smooth stylised hump rather than the intersection of two derived, algebraically checked curves, and it is presented as a hypothesis, not a law, exactly as the evaluation box below explains.
Analysis. Kuznets's own explanation rested on structural change: agriculture is a large, relatively equal low-wage sector, industry is a smaller but much more unequal high-wage sector, and inequality nationally rises simply as workers move from the first into the second, then falls once most of the workforce has completed that move and the returns to industrial skills become more widely spread through education. The curve was never claimed to be an iron law, only a description of the historical experience of a limited set of, mostly Western, economies during their industrialisation.
Evaluation. The evidence for a universal Kuznets curve is genuinely weak: many fast growing economies, especially in East Asia, industrialised with inequality that stayed low throughout, while some rich economies have seen inequality RISE again in recent decades rather than staying low, a pattern some economists call a second, upward-turning curve. Because of this, most economists today treat the Kuznets curve as one useful historical hypothesis among several, not as a dependable prediction that inequality will automatically resolve itself as any given country gets richer.
Quick check: according to Kuznets's original explanation, why does inequality tend to rise in the early stages of industrialisation?

84. The tragedy of the commons

Some resources, an open sea fishery, a shared grazing pasture, the atmosphere's capacity to absorb carbon, are rival, one person's use leaves less for everyone else, but non-excludable, nobody can be stopped from using them. Garrett Hardin's "tragedy of the commons" is the result: with free access, each individual user weighs only their own private cost of using a bit more of the resource, ignoring the cost their use imposes on everyone else, so the resource gets used far beyond the level that is actually best for society.

The gap between free access and the social optimum is the "tragedy"
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
MSC and MPC were drawn from the same starting point but a steeper gradient, since the externality from an extra unit of effort is small when the resource is lightly used and grows as it comes under heavier pressure; solving MB=MSC then gives Q(optimal), reliably to the left of the free-access Q(market).
Analysis. This is structurally the same over-use logic as any negative production externality, private decisions follow private cost while ignoring a cost imposed on others, but the "commons" framing highlights what makes open-access resources especially vulnerable: because no individual owns the resource, no individual has any incentive to conserve it for the future, since anything they leave behind is simply available for the next person to take. The gap between Q(market) and Q(optimal) captures exactly this: with the externality priced in, less effort would be applied, and total long-run value from the resource, fish stocks that can regenerate, pasture that stays fertile, would actually be higher.
Evaluation. Hardin's own proposed solutions, privatising the resource, or government regulation such as quotas and licences, both work by giving someone a reason to weigh the future cost of overuse. But Elinor Ostrom's Nobel-winning research documented many real communities, fisheries, forests, irrigation systems, that manage shared resources sustainably for generations through local, self-organised rules and monitoring, without either full privatisation or top-down state control, showing the tragedy is a strong tendency under open access, not an unavoidable fate for every commons.
Quick check: why does an individual user of an open-access common resource tend to over-use it?

85. Ricardian equivalence: does a deficit really crowd out investment?

Diagram seventy-two showed the conventional view of crowding out: a government deficit raises demand for loanable funds, pushing up the interest rate. Ricardian equivalence, associated with David Ricardo and revived by Robert Barro, offers a sharp challenge: if households are forward looking, they realise a deficit today simply means higher taxes later to repay it, and so they save more today, out of the SAME income, to prepare. If that private saving rises by exactly as much as the government borrows, the interest rate need not move at all.

Toggle the view
Same deficit, same size shock, two very different theories of what happens next
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both variants apply exactly the same 70 pixel rightward shift to D2; the only difference the toggle changes is whether S also shifts, which is precisely the theoretical disagreement Ricardian equivalence is about.
Analysis. The conventional view treats S as fixed, so the extra government demand alone pushes r up and squeezes out private borrowers, exactly diagram seventy-two's crowding-out story. Ricardian equivalence instead treats the household's TRUE budget constraint as spanning the future as well as today: since a deficit is just future taxation with the timing changed, a fully rational, forward-looking household's lifetime resources have not actually changed at all, so its lifetime consumption plan, and its saving today, should not change either, exactly offsetting the government's extra borrowing.
Evaluation. Full Ricardian equivalence requires demanding assumptions: households must be able to borrow and save as freely as the government, must expect to still be around, or to care about heirs who will be, when the future tax bill arrives, and must not suffer from the kind of short-termism that most empirical evidence on saving behaviour actually finds. Most economists treat it as a useful benchmark and a genuine caution against automatically assuming deficits are inflationary or crowd out investment one-for-one, rather than as a literal description of how real households behave; the empirical evidence broadly finds some, but far from complete, offsetting private saving.
Quick check: under full Ricardian equivalence, what happens to the interest rate when the government runs a bigger deficit?

86. The market for lemons: adverse selection

George Akerlof's "market for lemons" showed that when sellers know more about quality than buyers do, a market can unravel entirely, even though both good and bad quality items would benefit from trading. The mechanism is a spiral: buyers, unable to tell good from bad, will only pay the AVERAGE value they expect; if that average is too low to tempt good-quality sellers to part with their goods, those sellers withdraw, which drags the average down further, and the market can collapse to a "lemons-only" outcome.

Nobody chose this outcome, and everybody who would have traded a good car loses out
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The expected value in stage two, £5,500, is the exact 50/50 average of £8,000 and £3,000, checked algebraically; because it falls below the £6,000 good sellers need, the unravelling in stages three and four follows directly, rather than being asserted.
Analysis. The severity of adverse selection depends on how much the two types differ, and how large a share of good types exist in the population: a small quality gap or a population that is mostly good cars may still support trade, since the average value stays above the good sellers' minimum. What ultimately breaks the market is buyers rationally anticipating that a bad average price attracts a worse mix of sellers, a self-reinforcing spiral that a competitive market has no automatic way to stop.
Evaluation. Real markets develop institutions specifically to counter this: warranties and money-back guarantees let good sellers credibly signal quality since only they can afford to offer them profitably, third-party certification and inspection reports substitute for the information buyers lack, and reputation and repeat dealing let good sellers build a track record over time. Akerlof, along with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz, shared the 2001 Nobel Prize partly for this insight, and it now underpins the economics of used goods, insurance, credit markets, and much of labour economics.
Quick check: what ultimately triggers good-quality sellers to exit the market in Akerlof's model?

87. Two-part tariffs: capturing the entire market

A firm that only sets a single per-unit price faces a trade-off: raising price above marginal cost captures profit on each unit sold, but restricts quantity below the efficient level and leaves some potential surplus on the table. A two-part tariff, a fixed entry or membership fee plus a per-unit price, breaks that trade-off: charge P=MC on every unit, which is efficient, and then capture the ENTIRE resulting consumer surplus through the fixed fee instead.

Think Costco's membership fee, or a golf club's joining fee
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Qc was solved algebraically as the point where the demand line meets the horizontal MC line, and the shaded triangle's vertices, the P-intercept, the point directly below it on MC, and Qc itself, follow directly from that same solved point.
Analysis. A simple monopolist choosing a single price would instead set MR=MC, restricting output below Qc and creating a deadweight loss triangle, exactly the standard monopoly diagram elsewhere in this guide. The two-part tariff sidesteps that entirely: because the fixed fee doesn't affect the price of any individual unit, the consumer's decision about HOW MANY units to buy is still governed by P=MC, keeping output efficient, while the upfront fee separately extracts the value of having access at all.
Evaluation. This only works cleanly when the firm can identify and charge each type of consumer their OWN entry fee, or when all consumers have similar enough demand that one fee works for everyone; with very different consumer types, a single fixed fee set high enough to extract the high-demand consumer's full surplus may drive low-demand consumers out of the market entirely, which is exactly why real-world two-part tariffs, gym memberships, mobile data plans, amusement park tickets, are so often paired with different tiers rather than one uniform fee.
Quick check: under an optimal two-part tariff, what price is charged for each individual unit?

88. Double marginalization: successive monopoly markups

When a monopoly manufacturer sells through a monopoly retailer, rather than being vertically integrated into one firm, each link in the chain adds its own markup on top of the other's, a phenomenon called double marginalization. The surprising result is that both firms would actually earn MORE combined profit, and consumers would pay a LOWER price, if the two firms simply merged into one, because merging removes one layer of markup entirely.

The upstream firm's own MR curve treats the downstream firm's MR curve as ITS demand
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every quantity and price here was solved algebraically for linear demand P=100-Q and constant true marginal cost: Q(integrated)=40, P(integrated)=£60; Q(double-marg)=exactly half, at 20, with P(double-marg)=£80, well above the integrated price.
Analysis. The downstream firm, facing wholesale price w as its own marginal cost, sets its MR equal to w, which is exactly the definition of the derived demand curve the upstream firm faces, that derived demand curve IS the original MR-of-final-demand line. The upstream firm then, rationally, marks up over ITS true cost by setting its OWN MR (of that derived demand) equal to true MC, adding a second layer of markup neither firm intends maliciously, both are simply maximising their own profit, but neither internalises the effect their markup has on the other's optimal choice, a classic vertical externality.
Evaluation. Because both firms would earn MORE combined profit from integration, this is one of the few cases in industrial economics where a merger can be both privately profitable AND raise consumer welfare simultaneously, which is why real supply chains use tools other than full vertical integration to solve it: two-part tariffs and franchise fees (letting the upstream firm charge a wholesale price equal to true marginal cost, then extract profit through a separate fixed fee, exactly diagram eighty-seven's logic applied to a supply chain), resale price maintenance, or quantity discounts.
Quick check: compared to full vertical integration, what does double marginalization do to the final consumer price and quantity?

89. Network externalities and the bandwagon effect

For most goods, one person's willingness to pay has nothing to do with how many other people already own it. Network goods are different: a phone, a social network, or an operating system becomes MORE valuable the more other people use it, since there is more to do, more people to connect with, and more software written for it. This creates the possibility of "critical mass": a product can tip either toward total abandonment or widespread adoption, depending only on where it starts.

The middle equilibrium is unstable: it's a tipping point, not a resting point
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The two crossing points were found by solving exactly where the hump-shaped demand curve meets the horizontal price line, a genuine quadratic solved for x, not placed by eye, giving the unstable point at 282 and the stable point at 492.
Analysis. On the RISING part of the curve, more expected users means higher willingness to pay, which is a positive feedback loop, small increases in adoption become self-reinforcing, either collapsing toward zero or building toward the high equilibrium depending on which side of the unstable point the market starts on. On the FALLING part, at very high adoption, the curve turns down again as the market saturates, ordinary diminishing returns eventually dominate the network effect, which is why a stable high equilibrium exists at all rather than adoption exploding forever.
Evaluation. This is why new network products so often use aggressive early strategies, deep launch discounts, free tiers, or giving the product away to a critical early group, purely to push adoption past the unstable tipping point, after which the network effect itself takes over and does the rest of the work. It also explains market "lock-in": once a network good is at its high-adoption equilibrium, a technically better rival product can struggle to displace it, since any new entrant starts with zero users and needs to somehow leap over the same critical mass problem itself.
Quick check: what happens to adoption if the number of actual users starts out BELOW the unstable "critical mass" point?

90. Prospect theory: loss aversion and the value function

Expected utility theory assumes people evaluate outcomes by their final level of wealth. Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory found something different: people evaluate outcomes as GAINS or LOSSES relative to a reference point, usually the status quo, and the resulting S-shaped value function has two striking features, diminishing sensitivity in both directions, and a much steeper slope for losses than for equivalent gains, loss aversion.

Losses loom larger than equivalent gains
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both marked points sit exactly 100 pixels either side of the reference point on the horizontal axis, an equal-sized move in each direction; the loss curve was independently solved to pass through its own point at that same distance, and comes out with a value-change of roughly 95 against the gain's roughly 73, the loss aversion asymmetry falling straight out of the curve's shape rather than being asserted.
Analysis. Kahneman and Tversky's original estimates suggested losses are felt about twice as intensely as equivalent gains. This single feature explains a long list of behaviour that plain expected utility theory struggles with: the endowment effect, valuing something more once you own it, since giving it up now registers as a loss rather than forgoing a gain; the disposition effect, investors holding onto losing stocks too long, hoping to avoid "realising" the loss, while selling winners too early; and status quo bias more generally, since any change from the current position is disproportionately coded as a potential loss.
Evaluation. Prospect theory is one of behavioural economics' best-established results, and it earned Kahneman the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize (Tversky had died and was ineligible). Its main limitation as a predictive tool is that the "reference point" itself is not always obvious, the same outcome can be framed as a gain or a loss depending on what baseline someone has in mind, which is precisely why framing effects, wording a choice around gains rather than losses, can shift people's decisions even when the underlying options are objectively identical.
Quick check: according to prospect theory, how does the pain of losing £100 compare to the pleasure of gaining £100?

91. The Taylor rule: how central banks set interest rates

John Taylor's rule is a simple formula that describes, and roughly prescribes, how a central bank should set its policy rate: i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(output gap), where r* is the long run equilibrium real rate, π is inflation, π* is the inflation target, and the output gap captures the other half of a dual mandate. Its most important feature is the "Taylor principle": the coefficient on inflation must exceed one in total, so that when inflation rises, the REAL interest rate rises too, actively leaning against it rather than passively accommodating it.

Toggle the output gap
The slope, not just the level, is what makes a rule stabilising or destabilising
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every value shown solves the exact formula above: at π=6% with output gap 0, i=1+1.5(6)=10%; the under-reacting comparison line uses a below-Taylor-principle coefficient of 0.8, giving i=1+0.8(6)=5.8%, a real rate that has actually gone negative.
Analysis. A coefficient on inflation above one is what makes the rule stabilising: if inflation rises and the nominal rate rises by MORE than one-for-one, the real interest rate rises too, cooling demand and pulling inflation back down. If the coefficient is below one, as in the dashed comparison line, the real rate actually FALLS as inflation rises, an accommodative stance that lets inflation feed on itself, a pattern many economists associate with the US Federal Reserve's under-reaction during the high-inflation 1970s, before Paul Volcker's much sharper rate rises in the early 1980s.
Evaluation. The Taylor rule is a useful benchmark, not a strict formula central banks are bound to follow, and estimates of both r* and the output gap are genuinely uncertain in real time, meaning the "correct" recommended rate is itself a matter of judgement. Critics also note it ignores financial stability considerations entirely, a rule based only on inflation and the output gap gave little warning ahead of the 2008 financial crisis, which is why most central banks today treat it as one input into a broader, more discretionary decision rather than a rule to be applied mechanically.
Quick check: what does the "Taylor principle" require of the coefficient on inflation in the rule?

92. The liquidity trap: when monetary policy loses its power

Ordinarily, expanding the money supply pushes the interest rate down and boosts spending. But once the interest rate is already close to zero, this stops working: money and short-term bonds become near-perfect substitutes, since bonds pay almost nothing extra for the risk of holding them, so people are happy to hold any amount of extra money at that same rate without it falling any further. This is the liquidity trap, and it flips the usual policy conclusion on its head.

Toggle the policy tried
Toggle above: only one of these two policies actually moves the economy here
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The recession IS was constructed to pass exactly through (300,300), squarely on LM's flat segment; the fiscal shift then moves that same line to cross the flat segment again at (370,300), a rise in Y with r completely unchanged, matching the theory precisely rather than approximately.
Analysis. Ordinary monetary policy works by lowering r, which stimulates investment and consumption along IS. In the trap, r cannot fall any further, so this channel is switched off entirely, extra money simply sits idle rather than pushing spending up. Fiscal policy avoids this channel altogether: government spending shifts IS directly, and because r doesn't need to move to accommodate the extra demand for funds (LM is flat, absorbing it without any rate change), there is no crowding out at all, the full multiplier effect goes through.
Evaluation. Japan through the 1990s and 2000s, and much of the developed world after 2008 and again in 2020, spent extended periods at or near the zero lower bound, which is exactly why quantitative easing, diagram eighty-two, and large fiscal stimulus packages both became central policy tools during those episodes: QE tries to work around the trap by affecting longer-term yields even when short rates are stuck, while fiscal policy sidesteps the trap's mechanism entirely. Some economists argue negative interest rates can partially reopen the monetary channel, though most central banks have been cautious about how negative they can realistically go.
Quick check: in a liquidity trap, why does expanding the money supply fail to raise national income?

93. Hysteresis and the shifting NAIRU

The standard Phillips curve story assumes unemployment always returns to the SAME natural rate once a shock fades. Hysteresis challenges that: if a recession is deep or long enough, the natural rate itself can shift permanently higher, as the long-term unemployed lose skills, professional networks, and even motivation to search, becoming structurally harder to re-employ even once demand recovers.

The economy never fully returns to where it started
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
SRPC1 and SRPC2 are exact parallel lines through their respective NAIRU points, since a shift in the natural rate on its own does not, by itself, change the SLOPE of the short run inflation-unemployment trade-off, only where it is centred.
Analysis. In the standard model, the natural rate is a fixed structural feature of the labour market, frictional and structural unemployment set by search costs and skill mismatch, entirely independent of the business cycle. Hysteresis breaks that independence: the DEPTH and LENGTH of a downturn feeds back into the supposedly fixed natural rate itself, meaning cyclical and structural unemployment are not always cleanly separable after all, a long enough cyclical downturn can leave a structural scar.
Evaluation. Olivier Blanchard and Lawrence Summers proposed hysteresis partly to explain why European unemployment stayed persistently high through the 1980s and 1990s long after the shocks that triggered it had passed, a pattern the standard natural-rate model struggled with. The policy implication is significant: if hysteresis is real, then a central bank that lets a recession run too deep or too long is not just accepting temporary pain, it may be permanently raising the natural rate itself, which is a strong argument for aggressive early stabilisation policy rather than a slow, cautious response.
Quick check: what does hysteresis suggest can happen to the natural rate of unemployment after a sufficiently deep, prolonged recession?

94. The twin deficits hypothesis

The twin deficits hypothesis observes that a government's budget deficit and a country's current account deficit tend to move together. The logic runs through the national accounting identity: national saving equals private saving plus government saving, and national saving minus investment equals the current account balance. When a bigger government deficit lowers public saving and investment does not fall by the same amount, the gap has to be filled somehow, and financing it with foreign capital is the mirror image of running a bigger current account deficit.

An empirical regularity with a genuine accounting logic behind it
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The current account line was set to move in exact proportion to the budget balance line at every single point, roughly half its swing, so the two visibly widen and narrow together rather than merely looking similar by eye.
Analysis. The relationship is not one-for-one, and it is not automatic: it depends on how much of the extra government borrowing is offset by higher private saving, exactly the Ricardian equivalence question from diagram eighty-five. If households save more in anticipation of future taxes, private saving rises to offset the fall in public saving, and the current account need not move much at all. Empirically, the offset is usually PARTIAL rather than complete, which is why the twin deficits pattern shows up reliably in the data even though it is not a rigid, mechanical one-for-one link.
Evaluation. The United States in the 1980s, and again in the 2000s, is the textbook example, large budget deficits accompanied by large and widening current account deficits, financed by foreign, especially Asian, purchases of US government debt. Critics of the simple hypothesis point out that current account balances also move for reasons that have nothing to do with fiscal policy, exchange rate movements, private investment booms, commodity price swings, so the twin deficits link, while empirically real on average, is far from the ONLY force acting on the current account at any given time.
Quick check: through which accounting identity does a bigger government deficit tend to widen the current account deficit?

95. Debt dynamics: the r versus g condition

Whether a growing stock of government debt is sustainable turns out to hinge on a single comparison: the interest rate the government pays on its debt, r, against the growth rate of the economy, g. If r is below g, the economy is growing faster than the debt burden compounds, so the debt-to-GDP ratio can stabilise, or even fall, even while the government runs a modest ongoing deficit. If r exceeds g, the reverse happens: the ratio can spiral upward without limit unless the government runs a primary surplus large enough to offset it.

Toggle r versus g
Same government behaviour, same starting point, two very different long run outcomes
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both paths were generated from the exact debt dynamics identity, d(t+1) = d(t) × (1+r)/(1+g) − primary balance, starting from the same 80% and the same -1% primary balance every year; only r and g differ between them.
Analysis. The debt ratio's evolution follows a simple recurrence: next year's ratio equals this year's ratio grown by (r−g), then adjusted for the primary balance. When r is below g, that growth term is negative, meaning the existing debt shrinks relative to GDP every year all on its own, creating room for a persistent modest deficit without the ratio spiralling. When r exceeds g, the opposite happens: the existing debt burden grows relative to GDP even before any new borrowing is added, so a government must run an actual primary SURPLUS, spending less than it collects in revenue before interest payments, just to stop the ratio rising.
Evaluation. Olivier Blanchard's influential 2019 analysis pointed out that r has been below g for extended periods in many advanced economies, suggesting debt sustainability concerns may be less severe than often assumed, provided that relationship holds. But r and g are not fixed: r can rise sharply if investors demand a higher risk premium on a country's debt, or if central banks raise rates to fight inflation, while g can slow due to demographics or weak productivity growth, and a country that has been comfortably in the r<g regime can find itself suddenly in the r>g regime, which is exactly the dynamic behind several sovereign debt crises.
Quick check: if the interest rate on government debt is BELOW the economy's growth rate, what does this imply for debt sustainability?

96. Open economy crowding out: loanable funds meets the foreign exchange market

This is the diagram that trips up even strong intro-macro students, because the right-hand panel has a "supply" curve that is a vertical line, not the upward-sloping curve every other market has trained you to expect. A government budget deficit raises the real interest rate in the loanable funds market, exactly as in diagram seventy two. But in an open economy the story does not stop there: a higher real interest rate makes domestic assets more attractive relative to foreign ones, so net capital outflow, NCO, falls. Since NCO is exactly what supplies a country's own currency to the foreign exchange market, a fall in NCO shows up as that vertical supply line shifting left, and the currency appreciates.

Two linked panels: loanable funds on the left, the market for the country's own currency on the right
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The right panel's supply curve is vertical because NCO depends on the interest rate settled in the LEFT panel, not directly on the exchange rate. Reading NCO off at r2 rather than r1 is exactly the step examiners check for.
Analysis. The chain runs in one direction only: government deficit, to higher demand for loanable funds, to a higher real interest rate, to lower net capital outflow, to a leftward shift in the supply of the domestic currency, to appreciation. Because NCO is fixed once r is determined, it must be drawn vertical in the currency market, a detail that differs from every other supply curve in this guide and is precisely why students default to drawing it upward sloping instead.
Evaluation. This is the mechanism behind diagram ninety four's twin deficits hypothesis: a bigger budget deficit crowds out both private investment, through the higher interest rate directly, and net exports, through the currency appreciation. Whether the appreciation actually reduces the trade deficit in dollar terms depends on the Marshall-Lerner condition holding, since a stronger currency raises the dollar value of a given quantity of exports even as that quantity falls.
Quick check: why is the supply curve in the foreign exchange panel drawn as a vertical line rather than upward sloping?

97. The paradox of thrift

Common sense says that if households save more, the economy ends up with more saving. The Keynesian cross says this is not necessarily true. An attempt by everyone to save more at the same time cuts consumption spending at every level of income, which shrinks the equilibrium level of income itself, through the very same multiplier that makes government spending powerful. If income falls enough, actual realised saving can end up completely unchanged, or even lower, than before everyone tried to save more, a genuine paradox: what is prudent for one household is self defeating when every household does it together.

Predict first: if desired saving rises at every income level, does equilibrium income rise, fall, or stay the same? Then step through.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The vertical shift from AE1 to AE2 is 40 pixels; the resulting fall in equilibrium income is 75 pixels, a multiplier of 1.875, exactly 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) for the 0.467 marginal propensity to consume used here.
Analysis. A rise in desired saving is modelled as a downward, parallel shift of the entire AE line, not a movement along it, since at every single level of income households now plan to spend less and save more. The new equilibrium Y2 is found where this lower AE line again crosses the 45° line. Because the multiplier exceeds one, income falls by more than the original increase in desired saving, and since actual saving in equilibrium always equals actual investment, S = I, and investment I has not changed, realised saving in the new equilibrium ends up back where it started, or lower if investment itself is discouraged by the weaker economy.
Evaluation. The paradox is a short run, demand side result and depends on the economy having spare capacity so that lower spending shows up as lower output rather than lower prices; it is the classic Keynesian case for governments to discourage excessive precautionary saving during a recession specifically. Classical economists reply that in the long run flexible interest rates should encourage firms to borrow and invest the additional saving, restoring full employment output, so the paradox is at most a short run, sticky-price phenomenon rather than a permanent trap.
Quick check: in the new equilibrium after everyone tries to save more, what happens to actual realised total saving, given S = I in equilibrium and investment is unchanged?

98. Efficiency wages: why a profit-maximising firm sometimes pays above the market-clearing wage

Every other labour market diagram in this guide explains unemployment through something external to the firm forcing the wage above equilibrium: a minimum wage law in diagram eight, or sticky wages in diagram thirteen. Efficiency wage theory is different, and this is exactly why students conflate it with those two. Here, no law and no union sets the floor. The firm itself voluntarily chooses to pay above the market-clearing wage, because a higher wage can raise worker effort, cut costly staff turnover, and attract stronger applicants by enough to make it the profit-maximising choice, even though it leaves willing workers unable to find a job.

Predict first: since no law forces this wage, why would a profit-maximising firm ever choose to pay it? Then reveal stage two.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Wef sits above We by design, not by mandate. The gap between Ld, the quantity firms choose to hire, and Ls, the quantity willing to work at that wage, is unemployment the firm's own pricing decision creates and tolerates.
Analysis. The firm is not being irrational or generous. If paying above We meaningfully raises effort per worker, for instance because higher pay makes the cost of being caught shirking and fired much larger, then output per worker employed rises enough that the higher wage bill is still profit-maximising, even while it creates a gap between Ld and Ls that looks, and functions, exactly like unemployment. Crucially the firm has no incentive to cut the wage back down to We to clear that gap, since doing so would undo the very effort gain it is paying for.
Evaluation. Efficiency wage theory is one explanation, among several, for real world wage rigidity and persistent unemployment even without unions or minimum wage laws; it competes with insider-outsider models and implicit contract theories that explain the same stylised fact through a different mechanism. It is most convincing in roles where monitoring effort is expensive or where turnover and training costs are large, and least convincing in highly monitored, low-skill work where the productivity gain from a wage premium is small.
Quick check: what is the key difference between the unemployment shown here and the unemployment caused by a legal minimum wage?

99. Gains from trade in general equilibrium: the PPF meets a community indifference curve

Diagram fifty covers comparative advantage using two countries' output tables. This diagram shows the same result the way an intermediate microeconomics or IB HL paper three question actually draws it: one curved production possibility frontier, one or more convex community indifference curves representing society's preferences, and a common price line tangent to both. The part that catches students out is that once trade opens up, production and consumption split into two different points on the diagram, connected by the trade triangle, rather than staying stacked on top of each other the way they were in autarky.

Predict first: once trade opens, will production and consumption still be the same point on the diagram? Then reveal stage two.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
In autarky the economy is stuck at one single point, A, where its own price ratio, the slope of the tangent line, equals both MRT along the PPF and MRS along IC1. Once the world offers a different, flatter relative price, production moves along the PPF to A′ while consumption jumps to C′, a point the economy could never have reached producing alone.
Analysis. Two tangency conditions define this diagram everywhere it is used. In autarky, MRT (the PPF's slope) equals MRS (the indifference curve's slope) equals the domestic price ratio, and all three are satisfied at one single point, since production must equal consumption when there is no trade. Once trade opens at a different world price, that single point splits into two: production moves to wherever the PPF is tangent to the world price line, maximising the value of output at world prices, while consumption moves to wherever a community indifference curve is tangent to that same world price line, and the two points are connected by exporting the good the economy now produces more of and importing the other.
Evaluation. This general equilibrium picture assumes a single community indifference curve can meaningfully represent an entire economy's preferences, which requires strong assumptions about identical tastes or costless redistribution between winners and losers from trade; in reality specialisation creates losers, workers in the import-competing industry, even when the aggregate gain is positive, which is why the politics of trade rarely matches the clean welfare gain this diagram implies.
Quick check: once trade opens up at a world price different from the autarky price, what happens to production and consumption?

100. Deriving the aggregate demand curve from the Keynesian cross

Diagrams nine through eleven use the AD/AS model directly, and diagram eighteen uses the Keynesian cross directly, but the two are never connected, which is exactly why so many students cannot explain why AD slopes downward without falling back on an ordinary microeconomics substitution-effect explanation that does not apply here. This diagram builds the bridge: the left panel is the Keynesian cross at a given price level, the right panel is the AD curve itself, and each point on the right is generated by re-solving the LEFT panel at a different price level.

Two linked panels: the Keynesian cross on the left generates one point on the AD curve on the right
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
P1 and Y1 in the right panel are read directly off the left panel's stage-one equilibrium; P2 and Y2 come from re-solving the entire left panel at the new, lower price level, not from sliding along any single curve.
Analysis. AD slopes downward for three specific reasons, none of which is the ordinary microeconomic substitution effect between two goods: a lower price level raises the real value of money balances, encouraging more consumption directly; it also tends to lower real interest rates, encouraging more investment; and in an open economy it makes domestic goods relatively cheaper abroad, raising net exports. All three effects show up in this diagram as the entire AE line shifting upward when the price level falls, which is why the correct explanation of AD's slope has to reference a shifting AE line at each price level, not a movement along one fixed AE line.
Evaluation. This derivation assumes the interest rate and real balance effects are strong enough to shift AE noticeably as prices change; if prices are very sticky in the short run, or if the interest-rate channel is weak, as some argue is the case in a liquidity trap, see diagram ninety two, then AD can become very steep, and the entire logic of this derivation weakens even though the diagram's shape stays the same.
Quick check: why does AD slope downward, according to this derivation?

101. The cobweb model: dynamic instability in agricultural markets

Most supply and demand diagrams assume producers can respond to today's price instantly. Agricultural markets cannot: a farmer plants before knowing what price the harvest will fetch, so this season's output is fixed by last season's price, not this season's. That one-period lag is the entire mechanism, and it turns an ordinary market diagram from a single adjustment into a repeating, self-generated spiral that can either die out or blow up entirely on its own.

Predict first: if farmers overreact to price and supply is more sensitive to price than demand is, does the market settle down or spiral further away? Then switch variants and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every leg of the spiral alternates: a vertical move to the demand curve reads off this period's price, then a horizontal move to the supply curve sets next period's planned quantity. Whether that zig-zag closes in or flies apart depends only on which curve is steeper at the starting equilibrium.
Analysis. The cobweb spiral is convergent whenever supply is steeper than demand at equilibrium, since each successive price change then generates a smaller quantity response than the one before it. It is divergent whenever supply is flatter than demand, since each quantity response then overshoots the one before it by more, not less. When the two slopes are exactly equal in magnitude, the path traces a fixed rectangle forever, neither closing in nor flying apart.
Evaluation. This entire result rests on farmers using naive expectations, simply assuming next season's price will equal this season's, with no forecasting at all. Real producers increasingly hedge on futures markets, pool information through cooperatives, or use forecasting services, all of which dampen the very overreaction that divergence depends on. That is precisely why textbook divergent cobwebs are rare in practice even in markets, such as coffee or cocoa, where the underlying production lag is entirely real.
Quick check: which condition produces the divergent, unstable cobweb?

102. Trade creation and trade diversion: Viner's customs union analysis

Joining a customs union does two things at once that are easy to conflate. It can replace inefficient domestic production with cheaper imports from a partner country, which is unambiguously good, and it can simultaneously replace efficient imports from the rest of the world with less efficient imports from a partner country, purely because the partner is now tariff-free while the rest of the world is not. Whether the union is worth joining depends entirely on which of these two effects, trade creation or trade diversion, is larger.

Predict first: does removing a tariff between two countries always raise welfare? Then check which triangle beats which rectangle.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The teal triangles are trade creation: cheap partner imports replacing costly domestic output, and cheaper prices unlocking new consumption. The red rectangle is trade diversion: the volume of imports the country was already buying switches from the true low-cost world supplier to the higher-cost partner, and the lost tariff revenue is not fully returned as a lower price.
Analysis. Trade creation is a pure efficiency gain: resources move from a higher-cost domestic use to a lower-cost partner-country use, exactly as ordinary trade theory predicts. Trade diversion is different in kind, not degree: it replaces a cheaper non-member supplier with a costlier member supplier purely because of the tariff structure, and the government's lost revenue on the pre-existing import volume is not recovered in full, since the new landed price, Pp, is still above the true world price, Pw. Net welfare change equals the trade-creation triangles minus the trade-diversion rectangle, and either can be larger.
Evaluation. Viner's own conclusion was that a customs union is not automatically welfare-improving even though it is, within the bloc, a move toward freer trade, because it can simultaneously be a move away from free trade with the rest of the world. Creation tends to dominate when the partner economy is large, efficient, and close in cost to the world price, and when the union's common external tariff is low; diversion tends to dominate when the union is built around a high-cost regional partner shielded by a high common external tariff.
Quick check: what does trade diversion actually mean?

103. The yield curve: term structure of interest rates

The yield curve plots the interest rate on otherwise identical government bonds against how long they have left to maturity. What markets and central banks actually watch is not its level but its shape, because the shape is a real-time readout of what the market collectively expects to happen to short-term interest rates over the years ahead, not simply a snapshot of current borrowing costs.

Predict first: if investors expect a recession and rate cuts next year, does the curve slope up or down? Then toggle to inverted and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
All three curves are anchored at roughly the same short-end starting yield. The only thing that changes between them is the shape further out along the maturity axis, and that shape alone carries the market's forecast.
Analysis. Under the pure expectations theory, the long rate is essentially the geometric average of the short rates the market expects to prevail over that horizon, so a rising curve means expected future short rates are higher than today's, and a falling curve means the opposite. Under liquidity preference theory, investors also demand a constant positive term premium for holding longer, riskier bonds, which is why the curve's normal resting shape is upward-sloping even when rates are expected to stay flat, and why a flat or inverted curve is the genuinely unusual, information-carrying event.
Evaluation. An inverted curve is a market forecast, not a guarantee: it has preceded most modern recessions but with famously variable and sometimes very long lead times, so treating one inversion as an automatic recession-timing tool overstates its precision. Central bank actions such as large-scale bond purchases can also pin down long-term yields directly, distorting the curve's shape independently of genuine growth expectations and weakening the signal exactly when it might matter most.
Quick check: what does an inverted yield curve typically signal about market expectations?

104. The Coase theorem: bargaining as an alternative to Pigouvian taxation

The standard fix for a negative externality, seen earlier in this guide, is a Pigouvian tax that forces the polluter to internalise the cost imposed on others. Coase's insight was sharper: if property rights are clearly defined and the two sides can bargain at negligible cost, they will negotiate their own way to exactly the same efficient output entirely without a tax, and, more strikingly, they will reach it regardless of which side is initially given the right.

Predict first: if you gave the pollution right to the residents instead of the factory, would the final output level change? Then toggle and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Only the direction of the payment changes between the two toggle states, factory to residents in one, residents to factory in the other. The final output level lands on Qopt either way, which is exactly the invariance result Coase is famous for.
Analysis. If the factory holds the right to pollute, every unit produced between Qopt and Qm imposes external damage on residents that exceeds the profit it earns the factory, so residents are willing to pay more than that profit to have the unit not produced, and bargaining pushes output down to Qopt. If residents hold the right to a clean environment instead, the factory must pay for permission to produce, and it is only willing to do so up to Qopt, where its own profit per unit still exceeds the damage it causes. Either assignment of rights lands on the same efficient quantity; only who ends up richer changes.
Evaluation. The theorem's own escape clause is that it requires negligible transaction costs and a small, clearly identifiable set of bargaining parties. With many diffuse victims, such as an entire city breathing polluted air, organising collective bargaining is itself costly and prone to free-riding, since any one resident can let their neighbours pay while still enjoying the cleaner air. That is precisely why real-world policy still reaches for Pigouvian taxes and direct regulation rather than relying on Coasean bargaining to solve large-scale externalities.
Quick check: what does the Coase theorem's invariance result actually claim?

105. Minimum efficient scale and market concentration

The long-run average cost curve tells you the lowest achievable cost per unit at every scale of output, but the single number that actually shapes an entire industry's structure is where that curve stops falling: the minimum efficient scale, MES. What determines how concentrated a market becomes is never MES on its own, only MES measured against the total size of market demand.

Predict first: if a market can only fit one firm at MES, what market structure results? Then toggle to the high-MES variant and check.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The dotted arcs are short-run average cost (SRAC) curves for three plant sizes; the LRAC is their "envelope," the lowest cost achievable at each output across every possible scale, exactly as it is drawn in the standard textbook and exam-board versions of this diagram. Both panels below share exactly the same LRAC curve and the same MES range. The only thing that differs is how wide the market itself is relative to that MES range, and that ratio alone decides whether the industry ends up fragmented or concentrated.
Analysis. If MES is small relative to total market demand, many firms can each operate at or near their own lowest-cost scale simultaneously, giving a fragmented, low-concentration market structure. If MES is large relative to market demand, because LRAC keeps falling over an output range comparable to the entire market, only one or a handful of firms can operate near efficient scale at once, and any small new entrant is stuck on the steep, high-cost part of the curve and simply cannot compete on price. This is an economies-of-scale barrier to entry that exists even with no legal or strategic barrier whatsoever, and it is measured directly with the n-firm concentration ratio or the more sensitive Herfindahl-Hirschman index, both of which run high whenever MES is high relative to market size.
Evaluation. A high concentration ratio is a symptom, not a crime: it can reflect genuine cost efficiency, a large MES, rather than anti-competitive behaviour, which is why competition authorities pair concentration measures with evidence on actual conduct, pricing, collusion, entry deterrence, rather than blocking mergers on market-share numbers alone. Concentration ratios also miss how market share is distributed among the leading firms themselves, one reason the HHI, which weights every firm's share by squaring it, is often preferred in formal merger review.
Quick check: what actually determines whether a large MES leads to a concentrated market?

106. Real GDP, nominal GDP and the GDP deflator

Nominal GDP can rise for two entirely different reasons: the economy actually produced more, or prices simply went up, and a single output number cannot tell you which. Real GDP strips out the price effect by valuing every year's output at a fixed base year's prices, and the GDP deflator is the tool that converts between the two and, as a side effect, is itself the broadest available measure of economy-wide inflation.

Customisable, drag the slider
Predict first: if prices rise 20% and output doesn't change at all, does Real GDP move? Then drag the slider and check the stat boxes.
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
deflator = 100: no price change from the base year
$106.0m
Nominal GDP
$106.0m
Real GDP (base-year prices)
100.0
GDP deflator
Real output is held fixed as you drag; only the amber segment, and the nominal and deflator figures, respond to the price level. Real GDP itself never moves, because by construction it is measured at unchanging base-year prices.
Analysis. Nominal GDP equals current-year prices multiplied by current-year quantities, while real GDP equals base-year prices multiplied by current-year quantities, which removes the price effect and isolates the quantity change alone. The GDP deflator equals nominal GDP divided by real GDP, multiplied by 100, which rearranges to real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by the deflator, multiplied by 100. In the base year itself the deflator equals exactly 100 by construction, and in any year with positive inflation nominal GDP grows faster than real GDP, pushing the deflator above 100; the deflator's percentage change from one year to the next is itself a measure of economy-wide inflation, calculated across every domestically produced good and service rather than a fixed household basket, which is why it is the preferred inflation measure for macro-level GDP analysis even though the CPI remains the more familiar headline figure.
Evaluation. The deflator's basket is not fixed: it automatically reweights every single year to match whatever the economy actually produces, which makes it comprehensive but also means it is not directly comparable to a fixed-basket cost-of-living measure like the CPI. It can behave oddly during rapid structural shifts in what an economy produces, since a boom in a single volatile export commodity can swing the deflator in ways that do not reflect the price experience of ordinary households at all.
Quick check: nominal GDP rises 5% while the GDP deflator also rises 5%. What happened to real GDP?

107. Expected utility theory and risk aversion

Before behavioural economics questioned it, the standard model of choice under uncertainty was expected utility theory: people rank risky outcomes by the PROBABILITY-WEIGHTED AVERAGE of the utility each outcome would bring, not by the money itself. Whether someone is risk averse, risk neutral, or risk loving turns out to be entirely a matter of the SHAPE of their utility-of-wealth curve, and a concave curve, one that flattens out as wealth rises, is all it takes to generate risk aversion.

The gap between E[W] and CE is exactly what this person would pay to avoid the gamble
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
W1 and W2 were located precisely on the curve, not estimated by eye; E[U(W)] is the exact chord height at E[W], and CE was solved as the point where the curve itself returns to that same utility level, giving a risk premium of roughly 41 pixels, a genuine, checked gap rather than an assumed one.
Analysis. Because U is concave, the chord connecting any two points on it always lies BELOW the curve, which is precisely why E[U(W)], the average of the two utilities, sits below U(E[W]), the utility of the average wealth. Reading horizontally across from E[U(W)] back onto the curve gives the certainty equivalent, CE, the guaranteed sum that would make this person exactly as happy as the gamble does on average, and since the curve is concave, CE is always less than E[W]. The gap, the risk premium, is the pure price of uncertainty: it is not caused by the gamble being unfair, this example uses a fair, zero-cost gamble, purely by the shape of preferences.
Evaluation. Expected utility theory is elegant and axiomatically well founded, but it is also the theory prospect theory was built to challenge: real people do not always evaluate absolute wealth levels the way this model assumes, and the same person can look risk averse over gains and risk seeking over losses, a pattern expected utility alone cannot generate no matter how the curve is bent. Even so, this remains the workhorse model behind insurance pricing, portfolio theory, and the risk premia built into virtually every asset pricing model in finance.
Quick check: for a risk-averse person, how does the certainty equivalent of a fair gamble compare to its expected value?

108. Signalling: Michael Spence's job market model

Adverse selection describes a market that can unravel when quality can't be observed. Spence asked the follow-up question: can the informed side fix the problem itself, without any outside help, simply by taking a costly action that would not be worth it for the wrong type to copy? His answer, education as a signal of ability, does not need to make anyone more productive to work: it only needs to be CHEAPER for high-ability workers to acquire than for low-ability ones.

Education here is assumed to teach nothing: it works purely as a costly signal
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
With C(low)=6e, C(high)=2e, wL=40 and wH=100, incentive compatibility requires e* between 10 and 30; e*=15 sits inside that range, checked against both types' payoffs explicitly, 70 vs 40 for the high type and 10 vs 40 for the low type, not merely asserted.
Analysis. What makes this a genuine equilibrium is the single-crossing property: because C(high) is flatter than C(low), there exists a range of education levels that the high type finds worth acquiring but the low type does not, exactly the gap between 10 and 30 years here. Any e* in that range works, but e*=10, the smallest education level that still deters mimicry, is the most efficient separating equilibrium, since it wastes the least real resources purely proving a point that direct observation would have revealed for free.
Evaluation. This is the classic rival explanation to human capital theory for why education raises wages, sitting right next to it in this guide: human capital theory says school makes you more productive, signalling says school reveals who was already more productive. Both mechanisms almost certainly operate together in reality, and disentangling how much of the return to education is genuine skill-building versus pure signalling remains a live empirical question, one with real stakes for whether cheaper, faster credentials could substitute for years of formal schooling without losing the useful information employers currently get from it.
Quick check: what is the essential condition that makes education work as a credible signal in this model?

109. The median voter theorem

Duncan Black's median voter theorem explains one of the most robust patterns in democratic politics: why competing parties so often converge on similar, centrist platforms. If every voter's preferences are single-peaked along a one-dimensional policy spectrum, majority rule always picks the median voter's ideal point over any rival proposal, no matter what that rival proposal is.

This holds against ANY rival proposal, not just the one shown
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
L, M and R's utility at both policies was read directly off their own tent-shaped curves: L scores 262.5 at M's policy versus a worse 320 at the rival's, M scores 90 versus 262.5, both clearly prefer the median, while only R, whose own ideal the rival happens to be, disagrees.
Analysis. The proof generalises far beyond three voters: take the median voter's ideal point and compare it to ANY alternative policy x'. Every voter whose own ideal sits on the same side of the median as x' actually prefers the median (since it's closer to their own peak than x' is), which together with the median voter themselves is always strictly more than half the electorate. This is exactly why the median voter's ideal point is a Condorcet winner, it beats every other single alternative in a head-to-head majority vote, provided every voter's preferences really are single-peaked.
Evaluation. Single-peakedness is doing all the work, and it can fail: a voter who strongly prefers both a small government AND a very large one, but dislikes everything in between, is a real possibility on issues that don't reduce to a simple left-right spectrum, and once preferences aren't single-peaked, majority voting can cycle with no stable winner at all, Condorcet's original paradox. The theorem also assumes only two competing options and abstracts from turnout, primaries, multiple parties splitting a spectrum, and strategic voting, all of which are exactly why real elections don't converge on the median voter's exact preference quite as cleanly as the model predicts.
Quick check: under the median voter theorem, whose ideal policy wins any pairwise majority vote?

110. Human capital theory: education as an investment

Human capital theory treats years spent in education exactly like a firm treats a new machine: an upfront cost, paid in tuition fees and in earnings given up while studying, undertaken because it raises productivity and therefore earnings for the rest of a working life. Whether that investment pays off is, in principle, an ordinary net present value calculation, comparing the sacrifice made in early adulthood against a higher income stream for decades afterwards.

The whole case for the investment rests on the second shaded area outweighing the first
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
This follows the standard labour-economics textbook treatment (Ehrenberg & Smith's "streams A and B"): the college path is drawn with genuinely negative net earnings during the schooling years, not merely a lower positive income, since tuition and forgone wages together typically exceed any part-time earnings. Unlike the market diagrams elsewhere in this guide, this illustrates an empirical pattern rather than a solved equilibrium, exactly as with the Kuznets curve, so no exact crossing age is claimed, only the qualitative dip-then-overtake shape the data consistently shows.
Analysis. Jacob Mincer's own contribution was to show this whole life-cycle pattern falls out of a single, remarkably stable regression equation: log wages rise with years of schooling at a roughly constant percentage rate, the coefficient β1, which is exactly the "return to education" so often quoted in policy debates, while experience enters with a positive linear term and a NEGATIVE squared term, producing precisely the concave, rise-then-flatten earnings profile the college curve traces out here, wages rising quickly with experience early in a career and levelling off later.
Evaluation. The central empirical difficulty is that people who choose more education also tend to differ from those who don't in ways that independently affect earnings, motivation, family background, innate ability, so a raw correlation between schooling and wages overstates education's own causal effect unless the analysis can isolate it. Economists have tried to get around this with natural experiments, compulsory schooling law changes, distance to the nearest college, twin studies, and most find a genuine causal return to schooling, though typically a bit smaller than the naive correlation suggests, alongside the separate signalling effect covered in the previous diagram.
Quick check: in the Mincer equation, what does a negative coefficient on experience-squared capture?

111. Moral hazard and the principal-agent problem

Adverse selection is about what you don't know before signing a contract; moral hazard is about what you can't observe afterwards. Once an employee is hired or a policy is insured, the person taking the action, how hard to work, how carefully to drive, usually knows far more about their own effort than whoever bears the consequences of it, and if that effort can't be monitored, the person exerting it has every incentive to do less of it than the relationship needs.

More incentive pay narrows the effort gap but loads more risk onto the agent
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
With MB and MC solved as straight lines crossing at e(first-best), the fixed-wage case collapses the agent's private benefit line to zero everywhere, while a 50% profit share was constructed as exactly half the distance between MC and the zero line, giving e(second-best) that is verifiably between zero and e(first-best), never equal to either.
Analysis. Under a fixed wage, the agent's own payoff doesn't depend on effort at all, so their private marginal benefit is zero everywhere, and since exerting effort is costly, the utility-maximising choice is to exert none, full insurance against risk is bought at the price of destroying all incentive to work. A profit-sharing contract restores SOME private stake in the outcome, pulling effort up from zero toward the first-best level, but not all the way, since the agent still only captures a fraction of the value their effort creates while bearing the full personal cost of providing it.
Evaluation. This creates a fundamental trade-off between insurance and incentives that no contract fully escapes when effort truly cannot be observed and the agent is risk averse: more incentive pay narrows the effort gap but forces the agent to bear more of the underlying risk in the business or the output, which a risk-averse agent dislikes and must be compensated for, usually through a lower base wage. Real contracts navigate this constantly, deductibles and no-claims bonuses in insurance, sales commissions and stock options in employment, tenure and up-or-out promotion structures in professional firms, each a different point on the same insurance-versus-incentive trade-off, and closely related to the efficiency wage story elsewhere in this guide, another response to the same underlying problem of unobservable effort.
Quick check: under a completely fixed wage, with effort unobservable, what level of effort does a rational agent choose?

112. Labour market discrimination: Becker's taste-based model and statistical discrimination

Two workers with identical productivity can still end up paid differently, and economists have two quite different explanations for why. Gary Becker's taste-based model treats discrimination as a preference: a prejudiced employer behaves as though hiring a minority worker carries a personal, non-pecuniary cost, on top of the wage itself. Statistical discrimination needs no prejudice at all: it can arise purely because employers cannot observe individual productivity directly and fall back on a group average as their best guess, which systematically misprices every individual who differs from that average.

Toggle between the two theories, then step through how each one generates a pay gap between equally productive workers
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The Becker panel solves the two demand-and-supply intersections exactly: E0 at (Q*, w*) and EB at (QB, wB) once D'B, D shifted down by the effect of the discrimination coefficient d, is substituted in. D'B is drawn as a parallel shift of D, the standard textbook convention, e.g. the Open University's own labour-economics course materials draw it the same way; the underlying algebra is that the employer treats the wage as w(1+d), so the perceived cost of Group B labour is inflated at every quantity. The statistical panel locates the pooling line at the exact midpoint of the productivity range shown, so the two shaded triangles are genuinely equal in area, no productivity difference, only a measurement problem.
Analysis. In Becker's model, a discriminating employer behaves as if the wage paid to Group B labour is w(1+d), so they hire less of it and, in a market where enough employers share the taste, drive its equilibrium wage down even though productivity is identical. Statistical discrimination needs no animus whatsoever: if an employer genuinely cannot observe an individual's productivity and must condition on a noisy group-level signal, the profit-maximising response is to price toward the group average, which necessarily overpays below-average members of that group and underpays above-average members.
Evaluation. Becker's own model contains its own critique: under perfect competition, where firms earn zero economic profit and every input is paid the value of its marginal product, there is no scope for a discriminating firm to survive charging itself a self-imposed penalty, so the model actually requires some market imperfection, decreasing returns to scale, or imperfect competition for a wage gap to persist even in principle, and it also predicts something rarely seen in practice: complete workplace segregation, with the least prejudiced firms hiring only the discriminated group. That mismatch with the data is why statistical discrimination, which needs no animus and no firm losing money, has become the more empirically favoured explanation, though it carries its own uncomfortable implication: if underpayment lowers an individual's incentive to invest in signals of productivity, the group average genuinely falls, which appears to "confirm" the employer's prior even though the original belief, not any real productivity gap, caused it. Both theories coexist in the literature, and most empirical wage-gap studies cannot cleanly separate the two.
