Quick check: under Becker's taste-based model, why should competition in the long run tend to erode a discrimination-driven wage gap?

113. Auction theory: first-price, second-price and revenue equivalence

How an item is sold changes how bidders behave, even when nothing about the item itself changes. In a first-price sealed-bid auction, the winner pays exactly what they bid, so bidding your true value guarantees zero profit if you win: rational bidders shade their bids below value. In a second-price, or Vickrey, auction, the winner pays the second-highest bid, which makes bidding your true value a weakly dominant strategy: it does at least as well as any other bid, whatever anyone else does. Remarkably, under a standard set of assumptions, both formats raise exactly the same expected revenue.

Toggle the number of bidders and watch the first-price bidding line move closer to the 45° line
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The first-price bidding lines use the standard symmetric equilibrium under independent private values drawn from a uniform distribution, b(v) = ((n−1)/n)v, evaluated exactly at n=2 and n=6. The two revenue bars in stage four are drawn to equal height on purpose: that equality is the theorem's actual content, not a simplification.
Analysis. Shading is a genuine trade-off for a first-price bidder: bid too close to your true value and you win only a razor-thin profit; bid too far below it and you lose to a rival who shaded less. The equilibrium bid function balances those two forces, and as the number of bidders rises, the risk of losing to someone else dominates, so equilibrium bids converge toward true value, exactly what moving the toggle from 2 to 6 bidders shows.
Evaluation. The Revenue Equivalence Theorem is elegant but fragile: it requires risk-neutral bidders, independent private values drawn from the same distribution, symmetry across bidders, and that the highest bidder always wins. Relax any one of these, risk-averse bidders tend to bid more aggressively in a first-price auction than a second-price one, correlated or common values invite the winner's curse, and revenue equivalence can break down, which is exactly why real auction design, from spectrum licences to online ad exchanges, is a far more delicate engineering problem than the baseline theorem alone would suggest.
Quick check: in a second-price sealed-bid auction, why is bidding your true value a weakly dominant strategy?

114. Present value, discounting and the net present value rule

A pound promised next year is worth less than a pound in your hand today, not because of inflation alone but because money today can be invested to earn a return. Discounting converts every future cash flow into today's equivalent, its present value, by dividing it by (1+r) once for every year it is delayed. Summing every discounted inflow, subtracting the upfront cost, gives the net present value, and the NPV rule is the single most widely used investment appraisal test in finance: accept a project only if NPV is positive at the firm's true cost of capital.

A four-year project: £100 invested today for four years of £35, discounted at 10%
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Every discounted bar height was computed exactly, CF/(1.1)^t for t=1..4, and the running total in stage three, 10.9, is the genuine sum, not a rounded placeholder. The lower NPV profile was solved at six discount rates using the actual annuity factor, so the curve crosses zero at the project's true internal rate of return, roughly 15%, rather than an assumed figure.
Analysis. Discounting is compounding run in reverse: if £100 today grows to £100(1+r) in a year, then £100(1+r) in a year must be worth exactly £100 today, so dividing by (1+r) is the only consistent way to compare money that arrives at different times. The NPV rule simply extends this to a whole stream of cash flows: sum every discounted inflow, net off the initial outflow, and the sign of the result tells you, in a single number, whether the project clears the return that money could otherwise have earned elsewhere, the opportunity cost of capital.
Evaluation. NPV is preferred by finance theory over simpler rules like payback period because it accounts for both the time value of money and every cash flow over the project's full life, not just how quickly the initial outlay is recovered. Its main practical weakness is that it is only as reliable as the forecast cash flows and the chosen discount rate feeding into it, small changes in either can flip a marginal project from accept to reject, which is why sensitivity analysis and a risk-adjusted discount rate typically accompany any real-world NPV calculation, and why the closely related internal rate of return, the rate at which NPV hits exactly zero, is reported alongside it.
Quick check: a project has an NPV of +£10.9 million when discounted at the firm's 10% cost of capital. What does the NPV rule say?

115. Returns to scale, the Cobb-Douglas function and the expansion path

Diagram 41 showed how a firm picks the cheapest labour-capital combination for one given output level. Returns to scale asks a different question: if a firm scales every input up by the same proportion, does output rise by more, by exactly the same proportion, or by less? For the Cobb-Douglas production function, Q = A L^a K^b, the entire answer is carried in one number, a + b, and the cost-minimising path traced out as output expands, the expansion path, is always a straight line through the origin.

Toggle the returns-to-scale case and watch how far apart the equal-proportion isoquants sit along the same expansion path
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The three tangency points in every toggle share the same first point, since all three cases start from the same baseline scale; only the spacing of the second and third points along the identical ray differs, exactly the comparison the returns-to-scale classification is meant to isolate.
Analysis. For Q = A L^a K^b, multiplying both inputs by a constant λ changes output to A(λL)^a(λK)^b = λ^(a+b) A L^a K^b = λ^(a+b) Q. Comparing λ^(a+b) with λ itself gives the whole classification: a+b > 1 is increasing returns to scale, a+b = 1 is constant returns, and a+b < 1 is decreasing returns. Because relative factor prices do not change as the firm scales up, the tangency condition, MRTS equal to the wage-rental ratio, is satisfied along a fixed ratio of K to L at every output level, which is exactly why the expansion path for a Cobb-Douglas firm is a straight ray from the origin rather than a curve.
Evaluation. Returns to scale is a long-run, whole-firm concept and must not be confused with diminishing marginal returns, a short-run concept about adding one variable input to a fixed one, the two frequently get mixed up in exam answers. Empirically, most industries appear to show roughly constant returns to scale over a wide range of output, with increasing returns concentrated in industries with very large fixed or infrastructure costs, utilities, telecoms, some manufacturing, and decreasing returns emerging mainly once coordination and monitoring costs start to outweigh any technical gains from scale.
Quick check: for Q = A L^0.3 K^0.5, what does this production function exhibit?

116. The Heckscher-Ohlin model: factor endowments and trade

Ricardian comparative advantage, back in diagram fifty, came from countries having different labour productivities, a technology story, and it drew each country's production possibility frontier as a straight line because a single factor, labour, moved between two industries at a constant rate of exchange. Heckscher and Ohlin asked a different question: what if both countries have access to exactly the same technology, but simply hold different relative amounts of capital and labour? With two factors that are imperfectly substitutable across industries, opportunity cost now rises as a country specialises further, so each frontier bows outward instead of running straight, and comparative advantage comes entirely from the country's endowment, not its technology.

Both frontiers bow outward, unlike diagram fifty's straight lines, because two imperfectly substitutable factors mean opportunity cost rises with specialisation
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both countries share identical technology throughout. Country H's frontier bulges toward the steel axis because it holds relatively more capital, the factor steel uses intensively; Country L's frontier bulges toward the cloth axis for the mirror image reason. That endowment gap alone, with no productivity difference at all, is enough to generate comparative advantage and gains from trade.
Analysis. The Heckscher-Ohlin theorem states that a country exports the good that uses its relatively abundant factor intensively, and imports the good that uses its relatively scarce factor intensively: here, capital-abundant H exports steel and imports cloth, while labour-abundant L exports cloth and imports steel. Notice the frontiers are drawn concave to the origin, bowed outward, rather than the straight lines used for Ricardo in diagram fifty. That curvature is the graphical signature of a model with two factors that cannot be perfectly reallocated between industries: pulling resources further into one good keeps costing more of the other, so opportunity cost rises rather than staying constant.
Evaluation. The clean result depends on assumptions almost as strong as Ricardo's: identical technology and tastes in both countries, no factor-intensity reversals between industries, and perfectly mobile factors within each country but immobile between countries. Two further results follow from the same model but are not shown above: the Stolper-Samuelson theorem, that opening trade raises the real return to a country's abundant factor and lowers the real return to its scarce factor, which is why capital owners in H and workers in L tend to favour free trade while the reverse groups resist it; and the factor price equalisation theorem, that free trade in goods can substitute for factor mobility and, under the model's strict assumptions, equalise wages and rental rates across countries entirely through the goods they trade. Empirically the theorem has fared unevenly: the Leontief paradox found the capital-abundant United States actually exporting relatively labour-intensive goods, a result usually explained by differences in labour quality, natural resources, and technology that the basic two-factor model assumes away.
Quick check: Country H holds relatively more capital per worker than Country L. What does the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem predict?

117. New trade theory: economies of scale and intra-industry trade

Comparative advantage explains trade between different countries in different goods. It cannot explain why Germany both exports and imports cars, trading with other rich, similarly capital-and-skill-abundant economies in what looks like the same industry. Paul Krugman's answer relies on internal economies of scale rather than comparative advantage at all: with a fixed cost per firm and a taste for variety, a bigger combined market supports more firms, each producing more and therefore more cheaply, at a lower price, even between two identical countries. Drag the slider to merge two national markets into one and watch the number of firms rise and the price fall together.

Customisable, drag the slider
PP never moves. Trade only shifts CC down, because a bigger combined market S lets any given number of firms sell more each, which is exactly what economies of scale need
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Home alone: 6 firms, price $10.00
PP is fixed: for a given number of firms, more competition always caps the price the same way regardless of market size. CC is what moves: at Home's market size alone the industry supports six firms at a $10.00 price; integrate Home with a similarly sized Foreign market through trade and the same industry supports around ten firms at roughly $9.20, more varieties for consumers in both countries and a lower price for each one.
Analysis. This is intra-industry trade: both countries end up both exporting and importing varieties of the same good, which the Ricardian and Heckscher-Ohlin models above cannot generate at all, since with identical countries neither has any comparative advantage in anything. The gain here is not reallocating production toward a cheaper opportunity cost, it is exploiting scale economies that neither country's market was, alone, large enough to fully capture, plus a straightforward gain in variety, since consumers value having more distinct products to choose between, not just a lower price for one.
Evaluation. The model predicts, correctly, that intra-industry trade should be largest between economies of similar size and factor endowments, which is exactly the pattern seen among rich, industrialised trading partners, and it explains why observed trade volumes between similar countries are far larger than a pure Heckscher-Ohlin world would predict. It says much less about which country ends up producing which particular variety, since that outcome is arbitrary in the model, historical accident or first-mover advantage as much as anything else, and it assumes free entry and symmetric firms, which understates how a handful of very large firms actually come to dominate many real scale-economy industries.
Quick check: two identical, equally capital-abundant countries open trade in a good produced under monopolistic competition. What does new trade theory predict?

118. The optimal tariff: a large country's terms-of-trade argument

Diagram fifty-one assumed the country was small: a price taker facing a perfectly elastic world supply curve, so any tariff could only shrink the market and create deadweight loss, with nothing to offset it. A large country is different. Because its own purchases are big enough to move the world price, restricting its imports forces foreign exporters to accept a lower price to keep selling at all, a genuine terms-of-trade gain for the home country. The government's optimal move is not zero tariff, but the specific tariff that sets marginal benefit equal to the true marginal national cost of importing, including that price effect. Drag the slider to set the tariff and watch the gain and loss areas trade off against each other.

Customisable, drag the slider
Because the export supply curve XS slopes upward, home is effectively a monopsony buyer of imports, exactly like diagram eight's labour market, only now the "employer" is an entire large importing nation
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
t = 40: imports 160 units, Pd $80.00, Pf $40.00, net national welfare +2400 (the optimal tariff)
The amber rectangle is the terms-of-trade gain, foreign exporters accepting a lower price, Pf, on every unit still traded. The grey triangle is the deadweight loss from importing less than the free trade quantity. At the optimal tariff the rectangle exceeds the triangle by the maximum possible margin; push the tariff higher and the triangle eventually grows faster than the rectangle, until a large enough tariff destroys all the gains and, taken far enough, all trade itself.
Analysis. Setting marginal benefit, MD, equal to the true marginal national cost of imports, MC of imports, is exactly the monopsony logic of diagram eight applied to a whole country's import purchases instead of one firm's hiring. Economists often express the same result algebraically as t* = 1 / (ε* − 1), the Bickerdike-Mill formula, where ε* is the foreign export supply elasticity: the more elastic that foreign supply, the closer to a small, price-taking country home behaves, and the smaller its optimal tariff. As that elasticity rises toward infinity, exactly the small-country case drawn in diagram fifty-one, the optimal tariff falls to zero, confirming that free trade is the small country's best policy and only a genuinely large importer has a terms-of-trade case for protection at all.
Evaluation. This is a purely national, not global, optimum: the foreign country's terms of trade worsen by exactly as much as home's improve, so world welfare falls even as home's own welfare rises, and a large enough foreign country will rationally retaliate with a tariff of its own, running the same logic in reverse. Once both sides retaliate, both typically end up worse off than under free trade, which is the standard case for the World Trade Organization's rules against unilateral tariff escalation: cooperative tariff reduction can reach outcomes neither large country can reach by acting alone, even though each has a unilateral incentive to protect.
Quick check: as the foreign export supply curve facing a large importing country becomes more and more elastic, what happens to that country's optimal tariff?

119. The Lewis dual-economy model: unlimited supplies of labour

Every trade model so far in this guide takes a country's stock of factors as fixed and asks how it should deploy them. Arthur Lewis, in "Economic Development with Unlimited Supplies of Labour" (1954), asked a development question instead: how does a poor, mostly agricultural economy industrialise at all? His answer split the economy into a traditional, subsistence sector with far more workers than it needs, and a modern, capitalist sector that can hire as many of those spare workers as it likes without ever having to raise the wage, at least until the surplus finally runs out.

Customisable, drag the slider
 The wage line WI cannot move on its own; only reinvested profit, pulling more workers out of the flat, surplus segment of agriculture's total product curve on the left, can push it further right
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Employment 10.0 units, 30.0 units of surplus labour remain in agriculture
Every worker gained in the modern sector on the right is a worker leaving the flat, near-zero-marginal-product segment of agriculture's total product curve on the left, so agricultural output barely changes while the surplus lasts. Drag the slider to its far end and the amber marker lands exactly on the kink at LA = 60: the point where the surplus is used up and the wage line WI can no longer stay flat.
Analysis. Two features make this a Lewis model rather than an ordinary competitive labour market. First, the wage in agriculture is set by the average product of labour, not the marginal product, since Lewis assumed family or communal farms share output roughly equally among members; that average-product wage is what pins down the subsistence floor that WI must sit above. Second, so long as LA stays inside the flat segment, agriculture's marginal product of an extra worker is roughly zero, so withdrawing that worker costs the economy nothing in lost farm output even though it gains the economy a full unit of industrial labour, a pure surplus that shows up entirely as capitalist profit. Lewis's central behavioural assumption, that workers save nothing and capitalists save and reinvest (close to) everything they earn, is what turns that one-off profit into a self-sustaining engine: reinvestment raises the capital stock, which shifts the MPL curve up and to the right, which raises equilibrium employment at the same fixed wage, which raises profit again, and so on, exactly the structural transformation from agrarian to industrial economy the model was built to explain.
Evaluation. The assumption doing the most work, and drawing the most criticism, is that agricultural marginal product is genuinely at or near zero for a meaningful pool of workers; Theodore Schultz and others argued that peasant farmers are usually already allocating labour efficiently, so removing a worker does reduce output more than Lewis assumed, weakening the "free" surplus story. The model also says nothing about what happens if urban jobs are created more slowly than workers arrive hoping for one, a gap the Harris-Todaro model later filled by showing that rational migration can continue even into open urban unemployment, so long as the expected wage, actual wages times the probability of actually landing a job, still beats staying on the farm. Empirically, several fast-growing economies, China prominent among them, are widely discussed as having passed through something resembling a Lewis turning point, with real wage growth accelerating once rural surplus labour thinned out.
Quick check: what exactly triggers the Lewis turning point?

120. Arrow's impossibility theorem: social choice theory

Diagram one hundred nine showed a median voter theorem that works cleanly because every voter's preference is single-peaked along one dimension. Take that restriction away, give voters three or more genuinely separate options to rank, and Kenneth Arrow proved something startling in 1951: no method of turning individual rankings into a single social ranking can simultaneously satisfy four conditions that each sound like the bare minimum any fair voting system should meet.

 Same fifteen voters, same three candidates, three different counting rules: toggle above and watch the declared winner change
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Arrow's conditionPlurality ruleBorda countPairwise majorityDictatorship
Unrestricted domain: always outputs a complete, transitive social rankingsatisfiedsatisfiedviolated, can cyclesatisfied
Pareto efficiency: if everyone ranks X above Y, so does societysatisfiedsatisfiedsatisfiedsatisfied
Independence of irrelevant alternatives: X vs Y ranking ignores how each voter ranks Zviolated, spoiler effectviolated, points shiftsatisfiedsatisfied
Non-dictatorship: no single voter always determines the outcomesatisfiedsatisfiedsatisfiedviolated, by definition
Every column fails at least one row. Plurality and Borda count both violate independence of irrelevant alternatives, since adding or removing a candidate who cannot win can still flip which of the front-runners is declared the winner, the spoiler effect stage two just demonstrated. Pairwise majority satisfies independence perfectly but cannot even guarantee a well-defined, transitive answer, exactly the cycle from stage one. Only a dictatorship escapes both problems, by giving up on non-dictatorship instead.
Analysis. Arrow's theorem, from "Social Choice and Individual Values" (1951), applies to any method for aggregating three or more individually-ranked alternatives into a single social ranking. It states that no such method can satisfy unrestricted domain, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and non-dictatorship all at once. The table above is not four separate anecdotes; it is the theorem's content made concrete, every realistic rule anyone has ever proposed trades one of these properties away, and the theorem proves no cleverer rule can avoid that trade.
Evaluation. The theorem's force comes entirely from its assumptions, so relaxing any one of them reopens the door. Restrict preferences to be single-peaked along a single dimension, exactly what diagram one hundred nine's median voter theorem does, and pairwise majority voting becomes transitive again, an unrestricted-domain escape route. Allow voters to express intensity of preference rather than only rank order, cardinal utility instead of ordinal, and other aggregation rules, including some forms of Borda-style scoring, regain more attractive properties, though at the cost of needing interpersonally comparable utility, itself a strong and contestable assumption. The theorem is also purely about aggregation mechanics: it says nothing about how often real-world preference profiles actually produce cycles in practice, which turns out to be fairly rare for many real electorates, only that no rule can guarantee avoiding one.
Quick check: which of Arrow's conditions does simple pairwise majority voting (the Condorcet method) fail?

121. CAPM and portfolio diversification: pricing only the risk that cannot be diversified away

Total risk on any single security splits cleanly into two pieces: unsystematic risk, the firm-specific noise from a factory fire, a product recall, a lawsuit, that is uncorrelated across companies, and systematic risk, the market-wide risk from interest rates, recessions and oil shocks that every company is exposed to in some degree. Holding a portfolio of imperfectly correlated securities cancels out unsystematic risk almost for free, since one firm's bad news is unrelated to another's; systematic risk cannot be cancelled this way because it moves every security in the same direction at once. The Capital Asset Pricing Model takes this one step further: since diversification makes unsystematic risk disappear at no cost to a rational investor, the market should not, and empirically does not, reward anyone for bearing it. Only systematic risk, measured by beta, earns a risk premium.

Toggle between the diversification curve and the CAPM security market line, then step through how each one isolates the risk that actually earns a reward
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The two panels are two views of the same idea: the systematic-risk floor that the diversification curve flattens onto on the left is exactly the risk that beta measures on the right, and it is the only risk priced along the SML. Securities A and B are plotted the same distance from the line in return terms, purely to illustrate mispricing symmetrically; nothing in CAPM says mispricing must be symmetric in practice.
Analysis. For a portfolio of n securities with average variance V and average covariance C between pairs, portfolio variance is V/n + C(n−1)/n. As n grows, the first term vanishes and the second converges to C, the average covariance, which is exactly the systematic risk that cannot be diversified away, confirming why the curve on the left flattens onto a floor rather than falling to zero. The CAPM formalises which risk is compensated: E(R) = Rf + β(Rm − Rf), where β = Cov(Ri,Rm)/Var(Rm) measures a security's sensitivity to market-wide, systematic movements, and Rm − Rf is the market risk premium per unit of that risk.
Evaluation. CAPM's central prediction, that a single factor, beta, should fully explain the cross-section of expected returns, has been persistently challenged empirically: small-capitalisation stocks and value stocks (high book-to-market) have historically earned higher average returns than their betas alone would justify, the anomalies that motivated Fama and French's three-factor model and its later five-factor extension. CAPM also rests on strong assumptions, that all investors hold the same, mean-variance-efficient market portfolio, can borrow and lend unlimited amounts at the risk-free rate, and face no taxes or transaction costs, none of which hold exactly in reality. Despite this, CAPM remains the standard benchmark taught and used in practice, both because of its clean intuition, that only non-diversifiable risk should be rewarded, and because more elaborate multi-factor models have not displaced it as the default cost-of-equity estimate in corporate finance.
Quick check: an investor holds a single stock and worries about the risk that its factory could burn down. According to CAPM, should the market compensate them for this risk?

122. The efficient markets hypothesis: how quickly should price reflect news?

The efficient markets hypothesis says a security's price already reflects all available information, so it should jump immediately and by the correct amount when genuinely new information arrives, and then simply drift as a random walk until the next surprise. Economists distinguish three forms by what information set is already priced in: weak-form efficiency, where price reflects all past price and volume data, so technical analysis cannot earn abnormal returns; semi-strong-form efficiency, where price also reflects all public information, so fundamental analysis of published accounts cannot earn abnormal returns either; and strong-form efficiency, where price reflects even private, inside information. The standard test of semi-strong efficiency is an event study: track the cumulative abnormal return, the return over and above what a normal market move would predict, around a public announcement, and see how quickly and cleanly it settles at its new level.

Three possible price reactions to the same piece of good news, only one of them is consistent with an efficient market
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
All three paths are drawn converging on the same fair value, +6% cumulative abnormal return, they differ only in the speed and shape of the adjustment, exactly what an event study around a real announcement, an earnings surprise, a merger bid, a regulatory ruling, is designed to measure. Overreaction implies negative return autocorrelation after the event (a reversal); underreaction implies positive autocorrelation (a drift), and both are the empirical signatures researchers actually search for in stock-return data.
Analysis. Weak-form efficiency says price reflects all past price and volume information, so chart patterns and moving averages cannot predict future returns. Semi-strong-form efficiency extends this to all public information, published accounts, analyst forecasts, macroeconomic data, so that fundamental analysis of publicly available information cannot systematically beat the market either. Strong-form efficiency goes further still and says price reflects even private, insider information, a form almost universally rejected empirically, since corporate insiders trading on undisclosed information do earn abnormal returns, which is precisely why insider trading is illegal. The event-study methodology in the diagram is the standard test of semi-strong efficiency: if the cumulative abnormal return keeps drifting predictably after public news breaks, that is direct evidence against semi-strong efficiency.
Evaluation. Real event studies have found evidence of both patterns shown here. Post-earnings-announcement drift, stock prices continuing to move in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks afterward, is one of the most robust anomalies in finance and looks exactly like the underreaction path, while short-term overreaction followed by reversal has also been documented, notably by De Bondt and Thaler's work on long-run contrarian returns. Two defences of EMH remain: first, many anomalies shrink or vanish once realistic transaction costs and trading constraints are applied, so predictability on paper is not always exploitable in practice; second, Eugene Fama's joint hypothesis problem means every test of market efficiency is simultaneously a test of some asset-pricing model, so an apparent anomaly might instead just mean the wrong model of required returns was used as the benchmark. Behavioural finance, built on ideas like those in prospect theory (diagram ninety), argues the anomalies are real and reflect systematic investor psychology, overconfidence, herding, anchoring, rather than data mining or mismeasured risk.
Quick check: post-earnings-announcement drift, where a stock keeps rising for weeks after a positive earnings surprise, most closely resembles which path in the diagram?

123. The Modigliani-Miller theorem: does capital structure affect firm value?

Modigliani and Miller's 1958 theorem is a deliberately startling result: in a world of no taxes, no bankruptcy costs and perfect capital markets, a firm's total value is completely independent of how it splits its financing between debt and equity, since investors can replicate or undo any leverage the firm chooses simply by borrowing or lending on their own account. Proposition II follows immediately: the cost of equity must rise linearly with leverage, exactly offsetting the extra weight put on cheaper debt, so the weighted average cost of capital never moves. The theorem is a benchmark, not a description of real firms, and its real value is diagnostic: it identifies precisely which real-world frictions, corporate tax, bankruptcy costs, must be doing the work whenever capital structure is observed to matter in practice.

Toggle between firm value and the cost of capital, then step from MM's idealised world to the real-world trade-off theory
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The two panels are consistent with each other: firm value is maximised, in the left panel, at almost exactly the leverage ratio where WACC is minimised in the right panel, since discounting the same expected cash flows at a lower WACC mechanically produces a higher present value. The distress-cost penalty used here is illustrative, a stylised cubic and quartic term added purely to bend an otherwise straight line, real trade-off models estimate the expected cost of distress from credit spreads and historical default and recovery rates.
Analysis. MM Proposition I states Vᴸ = Vᵟ (an unlevered firm and a levered firm with the same operating cash flows have the same total value), which follows from a no-arbitrage argument: if a levered firm were priced differently, an investor could borrow personally to replicate its leverage, or buy shares and lend to undo it, and pocket the difference, forcing the two values together. Proposition II follows algebraically: since WACC = (E/V)Re + (D/V)Rd must stay fixed at Ru (Proposition I in disguise), rearranging gives Re = Ru + (D/E)(Ru − Rd), cost of equity rising linearly in the debt-to-equity ratio. With corporate tax, interest payments are deductible, so the theorem's own arbitrage logic instead delivers Vᵟ = Vᴸ + TcD, the present value of the tax shield, an unambiguous case for more debt that only bankruptcy and distress costs can check.
Evaluation. Pure MM requires assumptions that never hold exactly, no taxes, no bankruptcy costs, symmetric information, and frictionless personal borrowing at the same rate as the firm, so the theorem's real use is as a diagnostic baseline: whatever makes capital structure matter empirically must be one of these frictions failing. The trade-off theory shown in stage three and four is the most direct extension, an optimal capital structure exists wherever the marginal tax shield equals the marginal expected cost of distress, but it is not the only account: pecking-order theory argues firms do not target a specific leverage ratio at all, financing new investment first with retained earnings, then debt, and only reluctantly with new equity, because of the information asymmetry between managers and outside investors, which better explains why the most profitable firms in an industry often carry the least debt, the opposite of what a strict trade-off optimum would predict.
Quick check: under Modigliani and Miller's original assumptions (no taxes, no bankruptcy costs, perfect capital markets), what happens to a firm's total value as it replaces equity with debt?

124. Scarcity and the basic economic problem

Every other diagram in this guide is a way of solving the same underlying problem: human wants are unlimited and constantly renewing, while the land, labour, capital and enterprise available to satisfy them at any moment are finite. That permanent gap is scarcity, and it is not a temporary condition that better policy could eliminate. It is the starting premise of the whole subject. Because resources are scarce, every individual, firm and government is forced to choose, and every choice has a cost, which is exactly what diagram 125 examines next.

The starting premise of the entire subject of economics
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Resources reach only as far as the lower bar. Wants, in principle, keep climbing off the top of the chart entirely — that is what "unlimited" means here.
Analysis. Scarcity is relative, not absolute: it exists for a billionaire choosing between a second yacht and a third holiday home just as much as for a subsistence farmer choosing between planting maize or beans, because in both cases wants still exceed what is available. Scarcity also applies to time itself, which is why "the opportunity cost of your time" is a meaningful phrase even for someone with unlimited money. This is the single premise that makes economics necessary as a subject: if resources could satisfy every want, there would be nothing left to study.
Evaluation. It is worth distinguishing scarcity from poverty. Poverty is a specific, and in principle solvable, shortage of resources relative to basic needs; scarcity is a permanent feature of any economy at any income level, because wants expand to meet, and then exceed, whatever becomes available. It is also worth distinguishing renewable resources, which regenerate if managed sustainably, from non-renewable ones such as oil, which cannot, since this distinction is exactly what underlies later debates in this guide about growth, sustainability, and the tragedy of the commons (diagram 92).
Quick check: which of these best describes the basic economic problem that gives rise to the entire subject of economics?

125. Opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative forgone

Scarcity forces choice, and opportunity cost is the price of every choice. It is defined precisely as the value of the single next best alternative given up, not the value of everything else you didn't pick. That precision matters: students very commonly answer exam questions as though opportunity cost were the sum of all forgone options, which overstates the true cost of a decision and is one of the most consistently penalised errors in introductory economics.

Watch which alternative actually counts as the cost, and which one doesn't
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Bar height stands for the value the decision maker places on each option, not a cash price, since opportunity cost applies just as much to unpriced alternatives.
Analysis. Opportunity cost is not confined to spending decisions. Studying for an extra hour has an opportunity cost measured in the leisure or sleep given up; a government building a new hospital has an opportunity cost measured in whatever else that budget could have built, such as schools or roads. Because it is defined only against the single next best alternative, ranking every option in order of preference, as this diagram does, is the necessary first step before opportunity cost can be identified at all.
Evaluation. Two confusions recur in exam answers. First, opportunity cost is not the same as sunk cost: money already spent and unrecoverable is gone regardless of what you choose next, and should play no role in a forward looking decision. Second, "free" is rarely free in an opportunity cost sense: a firm using a warehouse it already owns still incurs an opportunity cost equal to the rent it forgoes by not leasing that space out, even though no cash changes hands. In practice, the next best alternative is also not always easy to value, particularly for non-market activities such as unpaid caregiving, which is one reason opportunity cost, while conceptually precise, can be genuinely difficult to measure.
Quick check: you choose Option A. What is the opportunity cost of that choice?

126. The three economic questions and the spectrum of economic systems

Because scarcity forces choice, every economy, regardless of its politics, has to answer the same three questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. What differs between economies is not whether these questions get asked, but who answers them, and how. That difference is best pictured as a spectrum running from a pure market economy at one end to a pure command, or centrally planned, economy at the other, with almost every real economy sitting somewhere in the mixed middle.

Toggle the system above, then step through how it answers all three questions
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
No real economy sits at either pure endpoint. The marker shows roughly where each label on the toggle sits relative to the other two, not a precise scientific measurement.
Analysis. Positive and normative economics, discussed next in diagram 127, run right through this comparison: which system answers the three questions "better" is a normative judgement, but where a given real-world economy currently sits on the spectrum is, in principle, a positive, checkable question. Nearly every functioning economy today is mixed: even the most market-oriented economies provide some goods through the state (national defence being the clearest example), and even the most planned economies allow some private activity.
Evaluation. Markets are generally credited with efficiency, consumer choice and innovation, driven by the price mechanism explored in diagram 130, but left alone they under-provide public goods, generate externalities, and can produce sharp inequality. Command economies can in principle direct resources at scale toward a shared national goal and avoid market failure by decree, but they face what Friedrich Hayek called the knowledge problem: no central planner can gather and process the price information that millions of decentralised market transactions generate automatically, which historically has produced chronic shortages, surpluses and misallocation. This trade-off is exactly why almost every economy has settled somewhere in the mixed middle rather than at either extreme.
Quick check: which type of economic system answers what, how, and for whom to produce mainly through price signals in free markets, with little direct government involvement?

127. Positive versus normative economics

Positive economics deals in statements that are, in principle, testable against evidence, even if they later turn out to be false. Normative economics deals in value judgements, statements about what ought to happen, which cannot be proven right or wrong by data alone. Almost every real policy debate blends both, and separating the two, rather than letting a value judgement pass itself off as a fact, is one of the most practically useful skills economics teaches.

Notice the giveaway words in every normative statement
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Analysis. Being positive does not mean being true. "Inflation was 4.2% last year" is a positive statement whether or not it is actually correct, because it could, in principle, be checked against official statistics. What makes a statement normative is not whether it involves government policy, but whether it smuggles in a value judgement about what ought to happen, using words such as should, ought, fair, or better.
Evaluation. The line is not always as clean in practice as this diagram makes it look. Choosing which data to collect, which model to build, or which time period to study is never entirely value-free, so even careful positive economics carries some implicit judgement about what matters. That said, the positive/normative distinction remains one of the most useful tools for evaluating a policy argument: real debates almost always combine a positive claim (what will happen if we do this) with a normative one (whether that outcome is desirable), and untangling the two is usually where the actual disagreement lies.
Quick check: "The government's tax rise reduced household disposable income by around 3% last year." Is this statement positive or normative?

128. Factors of production and their factor payments

Every good or service, from a haircut to a smartphone, is produced by combining four types of resource. Land covers natural resources, labour covers human effort, capital covers man-made aids to further production, and enterprise covers the risk-bearing organisation of the other three. Each factor earns a distinct type of payment in return, and knowing which payment goes with which factor is a frequently tested piece of basic vocabulary that underpins later diagrams on labour markets and the circular flow of income.

Each factor has exactly one matching factor payment
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Capital here means physical, man-made capital, such as machinery and buildings, not money itself. Money is only a means of acquiring capital, not a factor of production in its own right.
Analysis. Land, labour and capital earn contractual payments, agreed in advance and paid regardless of whether the firm ultimately makes a profit. Profit is different: it is a residual, whatever is left over once every other cost, including rent, wages and interest, has been paid, which is precisely why it can be negative and why enterprise is described as the risk-bearing factor.
Evaluation. How the total income of an economy splits between these four factor payments, known as the functional distribution of income, is not fixed and is genuinely contested. Automation and AI-driven capital deepening are widely argued to be shifting a larger share of national income toward capital and enterprise and a smaller share toward labour, though the size and inevitability of that shift remains an active empirical debate rather than a settled fact, and the basic four-factor model here does not by itself resolve it.
Quick check: an entrepreneur borrows money to buy machinery and hires workers on rented land, bearing the risk that the product might not sell. What is the reward for the entrepreneur's own contribution, enterprise, called?

129. The demand and supply curves: movement along versus shift of the curve

Before the equilibrium diagram in diagram 26 puts demand and supply together, each curve deserves to be understood on its own. A demand curve shows quantity demanded at every possible price, and a supply curve shows quantity supplied at every possible price, both drawn holding every other influence constant. The single most examined distinction in this whole topic is between a movement along a curve, caused only by a change in the good's own price, and a shift of the entire curve, caused by a change in anything else.

Toggle demand or supply, then compare a movement along the curve with a shift of the whole curve
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
The same curve is used for stages one through three; only stage four adds a second, shifted curve, so the distinction between the two ideas stays visually obvious.

What shifts each curve (non-price determinants)

Demand shifts with: price of substitutes and complements · income · tastes and fashion · expectations of future prices · the number of buyers.

Supply shifts with: costs of production (input prices) · technology · the number of firms or producers · indirect taxes and subsidies · expectations · for primary goods, weather and natural shocks.

Analysis. A change in a good's own price can never shift its own curve, it only moves you along the curve that already exists, because the curve is itself defined as the relationship between that price and quantity. Every one of the determinants listed above works differently: change any of them and an entirely new curve has to be drawn, since the old relationship between price and quantity no longer holds at every point.
Evaluation. This distinction is not just semantic, it drives the direction of an argument. Confusing the two is one of the most common ways a student loses marks: describing a tastes-driven fall in demand as "a movement down the demand curve," for instance, implies the good's own price fell, when in fact the whole curve has shifted left at every price. Getting the direction of causation right here is also the necessary foundation for correctly analysing tax incidence, price controls, and welfare effects in every diagram in this guide that builds on demand and supply.
Quick check: a new health study reports that red meat raises long-term health risks, and buyers reduce the quantity they buy at every price level. Is this best described as a movement along the demand curve, or a shift of it?

130. The price mechanism's three functions: rationing, signalling, incentivising

In a market economy, no single person or committee decides what should happen when a good suddenly becomes scarcer. Price does that job on its own, through three functions operating simultaneously. This is Adam Smith's invisible hand: millions of decentralised decisions, each responding only to a single number, coordinate into an outcome that pushes resources toward their most valued use, without anyone directing the process from the centre.

One price change, three jobs done at once
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
All three functions come from the same single price movement, P0 to P1. They are separated across stage four only for teaching purposes; in a real market they happen at once.
Analysis. Rationing is the price mechanism excluding buyers who are unwilling or unable to pay the new higher price, closing the shortage without any queue, lottery, or official allocation. Signalling is the price change itself carrying information: a higher price tells everyone in the market, instantly and without any announcement, that this good has become more scarce relative to demand. Incentivising is the resulting movement along the supply curve, existing sellers expanding output and new sellers being drawn in, because the higher price now makes doing so worthwhile.
Evaluation. The price mechanism only allocates resources well when prices genuinely reflect scarcity: full information, reasonably competitive markets, and no significant externalities. When those conditions break down, for instance because of monopoly power, poor information, or a cost imposed on third parties, the three functions can misfire, since price then signals, rations and incentivises around the wrong number. That is exactly the market failure territory this guide returns to from diagrams 3, 4 and 5 onward.
Quick check: a sharp rise in the price of tickets for a suddenly popular event encourages existing sellers to release more tickets and draws new resellers into the market. Which function of the price mechanism does this illustrate?

131. Reading equilibrium from a demand and supply schedule: the gasoline market

Diagram 26 lets you slide demand and supply around freely. This diagram does the opposite and pins every point to a number, using the gasoline schedule that OpenStax uses to introduce the whole model (Tables 3.1 to 3.3 of Principles of Microeconomics 3e). The lesson is that a demand curve is nothing more than a demand schedule drawn out: each dot is a row of the table, and equilibrium is simply the row where the two quantity columns agree.

Every dot sits exactly on its row of the OpenStax gasoline schedule; hover the shaded bars to read the surplus and shortage arithmetic
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Plotted directly from Table 3.3 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e: seven prices from $1.00 to $2.20 in 20 cent steps, with the demand and supply quantities in millions of gallons. Equilibrium is the single row where the two quantity columns coincide.
Price per gallonQuantity demanded (millions of gallons)Quantity supplied (millions of gallons)Qd − Qs
$1.00800500+300
$1.20700550+150
$1.406006000
$1.60550640-90
$1.80500680-180
$2.00460700-240
$2.20420720-300

Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Table 3.3 (the schedules from Tables 3.1 and 3.2 combined). The final column is computed: positive means excess demand, negative means excess supply, zero is equilibrium.

Analysis. The curves in this diagram are straight segments joining the tabulated points rather than one smooth line, which is exactly how OpenStax draws Figures 3.2 to 3.4. Because the supply schedule adds 50, 50, 40, 40, 20 and 20 million gallons for successive 20 cent rises, the supply curve visibly steepens as price rises, whereas the demand schedule loses 100, 100, 50, 50, 40 and 40 million gallons, so the demand curve steepens as price rises too. The surplus and shortage bars are read straight from the final column of the table: 180 million at $1.80 and 150 million at $1.20.
Evaluation. A schedule with only seven rows cannot tell you what happens at $1.30 or $1.50; the straight segments between dots are an interpolation, an assumption that behaviour changes smoothly between the observed prices. Real markets do not usually publish their schedules, so economists estimate curves statistically from many observed price and quantity pairs, and the neat single equilibrium here is a model of the direction of pressure on price rather than a prediction that the price will settle at precisely $1.40 in any given week.
Quick check: using the schedule above, what happens at a price of $2.00?

132. The four-step process for a change in equilibrium: salmon and print news

OpenStax turns every "what happens to price and quantity if…" question into the same four-step routine: draw the market before the event, decide whether the event hits supply or demand, decide which way that curve shifts, then compare the new equilibrium with the old. This diagram runs the routine on both of the textbook's worked examples: the 2015 California salmon season, with the full numerical schedule from Table 3.6, and the decline of print news, which the book deliberately works without numbers.

Analysis. The two equilibria are read directly from the table: 250,000 fish at $3.25 is the only row where the 2014 supply column equals the demand column, and 550,000 at $2.50 is the only row where the 2015 column does. Quantity demanded rose from 250,000 to 550,000 without any change in demand, which is the single most tested distinction in this topic (diagram 129). The print-news case has a leftward demand shift along a fixed supply curve, so quantity supplied falls even though supply is unchanged.
Evaluation. The four-step method is powerful precisely because it forces you to commit to which curve moves before you look at the answer. Its weakness is that real events often shift both curves at once: the book itself notes that when demand and supply both move, one of price or quantity becomes ambiguous without knowing the relative sizes of the shifts. OpenStax also stresses that the salmon price here is the dockside price paid by commercial buyers, not the grocery price, a reminder that a diagram is only as good as the market definition behind it.
Quick check: in the salmon case, quantity demanded rose from 250,000 to 550,000 fish. Which statement is correct?

133. The budget constraint as an opportunity set: Alphonso's burgers and bus tickets

Diagram 38 treats the budget line as one half of the consumer choice model. OpenStax introduces it a chapter earlier, on its own, as the very first diagram of the course (Figure 2.2): Alphonso has $10 a week, burgers cost $2 and bus tickets cost 50 cents. The value of starting this simple is that every point on the line can be checked by arithmetic, and the slope turns out to be the price ratio, which is the origin of the idea of opportunity cost.

Every point can be verified as $2 × burgers + $0.50 × tickets; hover the shaded opportunity set
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Coordinates follow Figure 2.2 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e. Points A to F are the combinations the textbook labels; G and H are added to show an unaffordable point and a point that underspends the budget.
PointBus ticketsBurgersSpending on ticketsSpending on burgersTotal
A05$0.00$10.00$10.00
B44$2.00$8.00$10.00
C83$4.00$6.00$10.00
D122$6.00$4.00$10.00
E161$8.00$2.00$10.00
F200$10.00$0.00$10.00

Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Figure 2.2 and Section 2.1. Every row totals exactly $10, confirming each point lies on the constraint.

Analysis. The equation of the line is 2B + 0.5T = 10, so B = 5 − 0.25T: the vertical intercept 5 is income divided by the burger price, the horizontal intercept 20 is income divided by the ticket price, and the slope −0.25 is minus the price of a ticket divided by the price of a burger. Moving from D (12, 2) to C (8, 3) gains one burger and loses four tickets, exactly the slope. The point G (12 tickets, 3 burgers) costs $6 + $6 = $12 and lies above the line; H (4 tickets, 2 burgers) costs $2 + $4 = $6 and lies below it.
Evaluation. The budget constraint by itself says nothing about which point Alphonso will choose; that needs either indifference curves (diagram 38) or the marginal utility comparison the textbook develops in Chapter 6. It is also a model of a single week with no saving, no borrowing and only two goods. Its real purpose is to make opportunity cost concrete: the textbook's whole point is that the cost of a burger is best measured as four bus tickets, not as $2, because the tickets are what is actually forgone.
Quick check: Alphonso's income rises to $12 while both prices are unchanged. What happens to his budget line?

134. A labour market drawn from a schedule: nurses in Minneapolis-St Paul

Diagrams 8 and 54 build the labour market from theory: the marginal revenue product of labour and the wage-elastic supply of workers. OpenStax's first labour market (Figure 4.2, Table 4.1) is deliberately simpler. It applies the ordinary demand and supply toolkit to nurses in one metropolitan area, with employers on the demand side, qualified nurses on the supply side and the annual salary as the price. The numbers make the surplus and shortage at off-equilibrium salaries directly countable.

Plotted point by point from OpenStax Table 4.1; hover the bars to read the surplus and shortage arithmetic

Analysis. The diagram follows the table and the caption of Figure 4.2 exactly: equilibrium at $85,000 and 41,000 nurses, a surplus of 5,000 at $90,000 and a shortage of 13,000 at $75,000. Be aware that the body text of the same OpenStax section quotes slightly different figures, an equilibrium of $86,000 and a surplus of 43,000 against 39,000 at $90,000, which do not appear in Table 4.1; the table and the figure caption are internally consistent, so they are what is drawn here. The demand curve steepens at high salaries because each $5,000 rise removes progressively fewer nurses from demand (5, 3, 3, 1, 1 thousand), which is what a firm with few remaining substitution options looks like.
Evaluation. Treating labour as an ordinary market is a simplification with real bite. The textbook itself warns that the market for nurses is really many submarkets differentiated by experience and credentials, and that the true price of labour is total compensation including benefits, which can be up to 30 per cent of the package. It also assumes many competing employers; where one hospital system dominates a city the monopsony analysis of diagram 8 takes over and the salary is set below $85,000 even without any surplus. Finally, a shortage of 13,000 nurses does not disappear overnight, because training new nurses takes years, so supply is far less elastic in the short run than the schedule implies.
Quick check: a new medical school in the city increases the number of qualified nurses at every salary. What happens?

135. A financial market with a price ceiling: credit-card borrowing and usury laws

Diagram 28 shows price ceilings in a goods market. OpenStax makes the same point in a financial market (Figure 4.5 with Table 4.5, and Figure 4.8), where the "price" is the interest rate and the "quantity" is the volume of money borrowed and lent. A usury law is simply a legal maximum interest rate: a price ceiling. Whether it does anything at all depends entirely on whether it sits below or above the equilibrium rate.

Toggle between a binding ceiling at 13% and a nonbinding ceiling at 30%, then compare stage four
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Demand and supply plotted from Table 4.5 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e (interest rates 11% to 21%, quantities in billions of dollars). The 13% ceiling is a rate from the table; the 30% ceiling illustrates the textbook's remark that many state usury limits are set well above the market rate.
Interest rateQuantity demanded (borrowing, $bn)Quantity supplied (lending, $bn)Qd − Qs
11%$800$420+380
13%$700$510+190
15%$600$6000
17%$550$660-110
19%$500$720-220
21%$480$750-270

Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Table 4.5, Demand and Supply for Borrowing Money with Credit Cards. Final column computed from the table.

Analysis. The ceiling does not shift either curve; it stops the price from rising to where they cross. Reading the 13% row of the table gives the shortage directly: $700 billion demanded, $510 billion supplied, a gap of $190 billion. The quantity actually transacted is the smaller side, $510 billion, so the ceiling reduces lending by $90 billion compared with equilibrium even though it was intended to help borrowers. At 30% the ceiling is above the entire range of the schedule: the equilibrium row is still 15% and $600 billion, so the law is nonbinding and changes nothing.
Evaluation. Usury laws are a textbook case of a well-intentioned ceiling producing rationing. When the interest rate cannot rise, lenders ration by other means: tightening approval standards, cutting credit limits or adding fees, and the borrowers most likely to be excluded are the riskier, lower-income ones the law was meant to protect. The textbook's counterpoint is also worth stating: a ceiling that binds only in unusual conditions can act as a backstop against exploitative pricing without distorting the market most of the time, and the political case for usury limits rests on information problems and behavioural biases in credit decisions that the simple demand and supply model does not capture.
Quick check: a state caps credit-card interest at 17% in this market. What is the effect?

136. Elasticity is not slope: the midpoint method along a straight demand curve

Diagram 27 lets you feel elasticity with a slider. This one nails it down with the exact figures OpenStax uses in Figure 5.2 and Table 5.5: eight points on a straight demand curve where every $10 rise in price cuts quantity by 200 units. Because slope is constant but the base for percentage changes keeps moving, the same $10 and 200 units give an elasticity of 0.45 at the bottom of the curve and 1.47 at the top. The midpoint (arc) formula is used throughout, so the answer is the same whichever direction you move.

Every elasticity is computed with the midpoint formula from the table values; hover the shaded triangles for the arithmetic
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Points A to H are taken from Figure 5.2 and Table 5.5 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e. All elasticities use the midpoint method: percentage change measured against the average of the two endpoints, so the result is direction-independent.
Segment%ΔQ (midpoint)%ΔP (midpoint)|Elasticity|Classification
A→B-6.9%+15.4%0.45inelastic
B→C-7.4%+13.3%0.56inelastic
C→D-8.0%+11.8%0.68inelastic
D→E-8.7%+10.5%0.83inelastic
E→F-9.5%+9.5%1.00unit elastic
F→G-10.5%+8.7%1.21elastic
G→H-11.8%+8.0%1.47elastic

Source: point coordinates from OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Figure 5.2 and Table 5.5; every elasticity recomputed with the midpoint formula. OpenStax reports 0.45 for A→B and 1.47 for G→H, matching this table.

Analysis. The general formula on this line is |E| = (200 ÷ Q̄) ÷ (10 ÷ P̄) = 20 × P̄ ÷ Q̄, where the bars denote midpoints. Because P̄ rises and Q̄ falls as you move up the curve, elasticity must rise, reaching exactly 1 where 20P̄ = Q̄, that is at P̄ = 105, Q̄ = 2,100, the E to F segment. The line's equation is P = 210 − 0.05Q, so its full length runs from Q = 4,200 at P = 0 to P = 210 at Q = 0, and (2,100, 105) is precisely its midpoint, confirming the textbook rule that a linear demand curve is unit elastic at its centre.
Evaluation. Confusing slope with elasticity is the most common elasticity error in exam scripts, and this diagram is the cleanest refutation: identical slope, seven different elasticities. The midpoint method itself is a convention, chosen so that A to B and B to A give the same number; the simpler "percentage of the starting value" formula would give 6.7% ÷ 16.7% = 0.40 for A to B but 7.1% ÷ 14.3% = 0.50 for B to A. For very small changes both converge on point elasticity, (dQ/dP) × (P/Q), which is what applied work usually estimates.
Quick check: a seller in this market is currently at point B ($70, 2,800) and raises price to $80. What happens to total revenue?

137. Short-run production from a table: lumberjacks, total product and marginal product

Diagram 52 draws the law of diminishing returns as smooth curves. OpenStax's version (Table 7.2, Section 7.2) is a five-row table about lumberjacks sharing one two-person saw: capital is fixed, only labour varies, and each extra worker's marginal product is simply the change in total product. The smallness of the numbers is the point: you can see increasing returns (the second worker makes the saw usable), diminishing returns (from the third worker) and finally a zero marginal product, all from a table you can check in your head.

Every bar in panel (b) is the difference between two adjacent rows of panel (a); hover the bars to see the subtraction
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both panels are plotted from Table 7.2 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e. Total product is trees cut per hour; marginal product is the change in total product from adding one lumberjack to a fixed stock of capital (one saw).
LumberjacksTotal product (trees per hour)Marginal productAverage product
1444.00
21065.00
31224.00
41313.25
51302.60

Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Table 7.2, Short Run Production Function for Trees. Average product (TP ÷ L) is computed here as a check: it peaks with the second worker, where it equals marginal product's turning point.

Analysis. Marginal product is the discrete slope of the total product curve: MP for worker n equals TP(n) − TP(n − 1), which gives 4, 6, 2, 1, 0. Diminishing marginal product sets in as soon as MP falls, that is with the third worker, even though total product is still rising; TP only stops rising when MP reaches zero at the fifth worker. Average product, computed in the table, is 4.0, 5.0, 4.0, 3.25 and 2.6, and the relationship holds exactly as theory says: AP rises while MP is above it (worker 2, MP = 6 > AP = 5) and falls once MP is below it.
Evaluation. The lumberjack example is a caricature, but a useful one: increasing returns at low headcount are common wherever a fixed input needs a minimum crew (a saw, a kitchen, a lorry), and diminishing returns follow whenever more of the variable input is crammed onto the same fixed input. The law applies only in the short run, with capital fixed. Give the crew a second saw and the whole table changes, which is the long-run production story of diagrams 33, 41 and 115. It also says nothing about cost until a wage is attached: diagram 30 shows how these same marginal products generate a marginal cost curve that first falls and then rises.
Quick check: the marginal product of the third lumberjack is 2 trees, less than the second's 6. What is total product with three lumberjacks?

138. Profit maximisation from the numbers: the raspberry farm in perfect competition

Diagrams 7 and 32 draw the perfectly competitive firm with smooth curves. OpenStax builds it from a spreadsheet (Tables 8.1 and 8.3): a raspberry farm that sells every pack at the market price of $4, with total costs listed for every ten packs. Two routes lead to the same answer, comparing total revenue with total cost, or comparing marginal revenue with marginal cost, and this diagram lets you toggle between them and check that both put maximum profit at $90.

QuantityTotal costMarginal costAverage costTotal revenueProfit

Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Table 8.3 (extended with average cost = TC ÷ Q). Profit peaks at $90 for Q = 70 and Q = 80; MR = MC identifies Q = 80 as the last pack worth producing.

Analysis. The two methods agree by construction: profit is TR − TC, and its change from one row to the next is MR − MC, so profit stops rising precisely when MC reaches MR. Between 70 and 80 packs MC equals $4.00 exactly, which is why profit is $90 at both outputs; the eightieth pack adds $4 of revenue and $4 of cost, leaving profit unchanged, and the ninetieth would cost $6.60 and cut profit to $64. The profit rectangle in the marginal view, ($4.00 − $2.875) × 80 = $90, equals TR − TC = $320 − $230, so the two panels are one calculation drawn twice. One caution on the source: OpenStax Table 8.6 lists marginal cost at 120 packs as $31.50, but the total cost data ($550 to $715) give $16.50; the discrepancy lies outside the range plotted here.
Evaluation. The MR = MC rule is more useful in practice than the total approach because a real firm rarely knows its entire cost curve; it can experiment at the margin and observe whether profit rises. The example also shows why profit maximisation is not revenue maximisation: revenue keeps rising past 80 packs, but costs rise faster. Finally, $90 of profit on $320 of revenue is economic profit after all opportunity costs, and in a competitive industry it is a signal for entry, which diagram 7 shows would push the $4 price down toward the minimum of average cost, about $2.71 at 70 packs.
Quick check: the market price of raspberries falls to $2.50 per pack. Using the marginal cost column, what output should the farm choose?

Diagram 5 shows why monopoly output falls short of the competitive level. OpenStax's HealthPill example (Tables 9.3 and 9.4) makes every step of the monopolist's decision countable: a demand schedule for a patented drug, the total revenue it implies, marginal revenue that drops twice as fast as price, and a cost schedule. The firm chooses the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, then reads the price off the demand curve, not off the cost curve, and the resulting profit can be checked three different ways.

Analysis. Three checks converge on the same number. Rectangle: (P − AC) × Q = (800 − 330) × 5 = 2,350. Totals: TR − TC = 4,000 − 1,650 = 2,350. Margins: cumulative MR − MC = 700 + 725 + 575 + 350 + 0 = 2,350. The MR schedule is linear in Q with twice the slope of demand, MR = 1,400 − 200Q against P = 1,300 − 100Q, which is the general result for straight-line demand. Price exceeds marginal cost by $400 at the chosen output, which is the allocative inefficiency of diagram 5. Here, though, the deadweight loss is unusually small: buyers value a sixth unit at $700, already below its $850 marginal cost, so the efficient output where price equals marginal cost lies only fractionally above the monopoly's five units, because MC rises so steeply.
Evaluation. HealthPill is a patented drug, so the monopoly is deliberate: the patent is a temporary legal barrier granted to reward the fixed cost of research, the trade-off examined in the textbook's chapters on innovation and antitrust. The profit of $2,350 is what the patent is worth per period, and it is also what invites regulation, generic entry when the patent expires, or price discrimination between markets (diagram 6). The example assumes the firm knows its whole demand curve; a real monopolist estimates it, and the textbook stresses that even a monopolist cannot set both price and quantity, only pick one point on the demand curve.
Quick check: a regulator forces HealthPill to sell at a price equal to marginal cost. Reading the table, what is the closest outcome?

140. Internalising a negative externality with real numbers: the refrigerator market

Diagram 3 draws the negative production externality in the abstract, with MPC and MSC. OpenStax (Table 12.2, Figure 12.2) does the same thing with a schedule for refrigerators: each unit produced imposes $100 of pollution cost on third parties, and if firms are made to pay it, the supply curve shifts up by exactly $100. With numbers, you can see how much output falls, how much of the $100 buyers end up paying, and why the answer depends on the slopes of the two curves.

Plotted from OpenStax Table 12.2; hover the shaded strip for the change in output
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
All three schedules are plotted from Table 12.2 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e (quantities in thousands of refrigerators). S social is S private with $100 added to the price at every quantity, as the textbook constructs it.
PriceQuantity demandedQuantity supplied before pollution costQuantity supplied after pollution cost
$60050,00040,00030,000
$65045,00045,00035,000
$70040,00050,00040,000
$75035,00055,00045,000
$80030,00060,00050,000
$85025,00065,00055,000
$90020,00070,00060,000

Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Table 12.2, A Supply Shift Caused by Pollution Costs. E0 is the $650 row (Qd = Qs = 45,000); E1 is the $700 row (Qd = new Qs = 40,000).

Analysis. Both curves are linear in this table with slopes of equal size: demand loses 5,000 units per $50, supply gains 5,000 per $50. A vertical shift of $100 in supply therefore moves the equilibrium price by exactly half, $50, and quantity by 5,000. In general the share of an internalised cost that buyers pay is the supply slope divided by the sum of the two slopes, the tax incidence rule of diagram 1: with steeper demand buyers would pay more of the $100, with flatter demand producers would. The 5,000 units no longer produced are the ones whose social cost ($700 or more) exceeded the buyers' valuation, so E1 is the allocatively efficient outcome and the small triangle between D and S social over the 40,000 to 45,000 range is the deadweight loss the private market was generating.
Evaluation. The example assumes the $100 is known; measuring external costs is the hard part of environmental policy, and the textbook's later sections on the benefits and costs of environmental law are largely about that estimation problem. It also assumes the cost is constant per unit, whereas pollution damage often rises with concentration. And a pure supply-shift diagram says nothing about how the $100 is collected: a Pigouvian tax raises revenue for government, a tradable permit system lets the low-cost abaters do the cutting, and command-and-control regulation may achieve the same 40,000 output at higher cost. Diagrams 3, 84 and 104 take up those alternatives.
Quick check: if buyers' demand for refrigerators were much more inelastic than in the table, how would the $100 pollution cost be shared?

141. The poverty trap: how a 100 per cent benefit clawback flattens the return to work

Diagram 42 shows how a wage changes the choice between work and leisure. OpenStax's poverty-trap diagram (Figure 15.3, Table 15.3) applies that model to an anti-poverty program with a design flaw: a single parent earning $8 an hour is guaranteed $18,000 a year, but every dollar earned reduces the benefit by a dollar. The result is a budget line that is completely flat over the first 2,000 hours of work, so the financial reward for working is zero until the family is almost out of the program.

Every point on the flat segment is a row of OpenStax Table 15.3; the break-even hours are computed as $18,000 ÷ $8
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Drawn from Figure 15.3 and Table 15.3 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e: wage $8 per hour, maximum 2,500 hours, guaranteed income $18,000 reduced dollar for dollar against earnings. The textbook draws leisure increasing from left to right; here the axis shows hours of paid work directly, which reverses the horizontal direction but leaves every income value unchanged.
Hours workedEarnings ($8 × hours)Government supportTotal income
0$0$18,000$18,000
500$4,000$14,000$18,000
1,000$8,000$10,000$18,000
1,500$12,000$6,000$18,000
2,000$16,000$2,000$18,000
2,500$20,000$0$20,000

Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Table 15.3, Total Income at Various Combinations of Work and Support. Break-even (support falls to zero) occurs at 2,250 hours, between the last two rows.

Analysis. The budget line with the program is max($18,000, $8 × hours). Its slope, the marginal return to an hour of work, is $0 up to 2,250 hours and $8 beyond, so the effective marginal tax rate on earnings inside the program is 100 per cent. Whatever the family's preferences, the program cannot raise the number of hours it works: any point on the flat segment gives the same income with more leisure than point A, so a family that valued leisure at all would move left along it. The textbook's remark that income only rises above the guarantee at "say, 2,300 hours" is consistent with the exact break-even of 2,250.
Evaluation. The trap is a design problem, not an argument against support. The textbook's fix is to phase benefits out gradually, for example reducing support by 50 cents per dollar earned, which tilts the flat segment upward and restores a positive return to work at the cost of extending support to higher incomes; the earned income tax credit is the real-world version, paying a supplement that rises with earnings before phasing out. Every design faces the same three-way tension the book identifies: a generous guarantee, a low phase-out rate and a low total cost cannot all be had at once, because a generous benefit with a gentle phase-out reaches far up the income scale.
Quick check: the program is redesigned to reduce support by 50 cents for every dollar earned. What is the family's total income at 2,000 hours?

142. Free trade, no trade and an import quota with numbers: sugar in Brazil and the United States

Diagrams 51 and 102 analyse tariffs and quotas for a single small country. OpenStax's sugar example (Table 20.1, Figures 20.2 and 20.3) draws both trading partners side by side, so you can see that the world price with trade is determined where Brazil's export surplus exactly equals the United States' import gap, and that a quota pushes the two prices only part of the way back toward their no-trade levels. Every price and quantity is a row of one table.

Every price is a row of OpenStax Table 20.1; hover the shaded bars to see the export and import arithmetic
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Both panels are plotted from Table 20.1 of OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e. Free trade occurs at 16 cents because that is the unique row where Brazil's excess supply (15 tons) equals the United States' excess demand (15 tons); the 7-ton quota prices, 20 cents in the US and 14 cents in Brazil, are the rows where each country's gap is exactly 7 tons.
Price (cents per lb)Brazil: quantity suppliedBrazil: quantity demandedBrazil: excess supplyUS: quantity suppliedUS: quantity demandedUS: excess demand
