Source: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Table 20.1, The Sugar Trade between Brazil and the United States (tons). The two computed columns show why 16 cents (15 = 15) is the free-trade price and why a 7-ton quota gives 14 cents in Brazil and 20 cents in the United States.

Analysis. The free-trade price is found by equating Brazil's excess supply with the US excess demand, and the table makes this a single row: at 16 cents both equal 15 tons. At 14 cents Brazil would export only 7 while the US wants 11, and at 20 cents Brazil would export 24 while the US wants only 7, so 16 cents is the unique clearing price. The quota separates the two prices by 6 cents (20 minus 14); the difference between the US price and the Brazilian price on each of the 7 tons is quota rent, captured by whoever holds the import licences, unlike a tariff, where the same wedge would be government revenue. US consumer surplus falls and US producer surplus rises relative to free trade, but by less, so there is a net loss, the two deadweight triangles of diagram 51.
Evaluation. Drawing both countries reveals something a one-country diagram hides: the quota hurts Brazil too, lowering its price from 16 to 14 cents and its farm output from 40 to 35 tons, which is why trade barriers in rich countries are a recurring grievance for sugar-exporting countries. The example assumes zero transport costs and identical sugar; with shipping costs the two prices would differ even under free trade. The US sugar program in reality combines a price floor with strict quotas, which the textbook's public-economy chapter uses as a case study of concentrated producer gains defeating diffuse consumer losses.
Quick check: the United States raises its quota from 7 to 11 tons. Using the table, what happens to the US price?

143. The Keynesian consumption function: MPC, autonomous consumption and the 45° line

The consumption function is the microfoundation of the Keynesian cross (diagram 18) and the multiplier. It answers one question: how does planned consumer spending respond to income? Keynes's "fundamental psychological law" is that consumption rises with income, but by less than the full amount — which is exactly what gives the multiplier its finite size. Here it is drawn to scale from C = 100 + 0.6Y.

One law: consumption rises with income, but by less than one-for-one
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Intercept = autonomous consumption a; slope = MPC; break-even where the function meets the 45° line. Hover the shaded regions for the dissaving and saving arithmetic.
Analysis. The function plotted is C = 100 + 0.6Y, so the vertical intercept is exactly $100bn and the slope is exactly 0.6 (consumption rises $60bn for every $100bn of income). The break-even point solves C = Y: 100 + 0.6Y = Y, giving Y = 100 ÷ 0.4 = $250bn, which is where the teal line crosses the dashed 45° line. Saving is the vertical distance between the 45° line and the consumption function, S = Y − C = −100 + 0.4Y, so the saving line has intercept −100 and slope MPS = 0.4, confirming MPC + MPS = 1. The average propensity to consume, APC = C÷Y = 100÷Y + 0.6, falls as income rises and equals 1 exactly at break-even.
Evaluation. The linear consumption function is a deliberate simplification. Empirically the short-run MPC out of transitory income is high for credit-constrained households but much lower on average, and Friedman's permanent income hypothesis and Modigliani's life-cycle hypothesis argue that consumption depends on expected lifetime resources, not current income, which flattens the long-run relationship and helps resolve the Kuznets consumption puzzle. The function also holds wealth, interest rates, expectations and the distribution of income constant; a stock-market boom or a credit expansion shifts the whole line up (a change in autonomous consumption), which is distinct from a movement along it. Still, the positive, less-than-one MPC is one of the most robust regularities in macroeconomics and is all the multiplier logic requires.
Quick check: with C = 100 + 0.6Y, income rises from $250bn to $350bn. What happens to saving?

144. The money market: liquidity preference and the interest rate

Diagram 19 introduces the money market; this is its precise liquidity-preference form, the tool Keynes used to explain how the interest rate is determined and the foundation of the LM curve (diagram 71) and the monetary transmission mechanism (diagram 65). The interest rate sits on the vertical axis and the quantity of money on the horizontal — it behaves like an ordinary market, but the "price" is the interest rate and the supply curve is set by policy.

The interest rate is the price that clears the market for money
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Money demand slopes down (opportunity-cost logic); money supply is vertical because the central bank sets it. Equilibrium fixes r*; buying bonds shifts MS right and lowers r.
Analysis. The vertical money-supply curve is the defining feature: because the central bank sets the nominal quantity M and, in the short run, the price level P is given, the real money stock M/P does not respond to the interest rate. Equilibrium requires MD(r*, Y) = M/P, which uniquely determines r* = 6.5% for the drawn income level. An expansionary open-market purchase raises M/P, shifting MS to the right; since money demand is unchanged, the interest rate must fall (to 4.5%) to raise the quantity of money demanded back into balance — mechanically, the excess supply of money is spent on bonds, whose prices rise and yields fall. A rise in real income would instead shift MD rightward (more transactions demand L₁) and raise r*.
Evaluation. Liquidity preference is a short-run, fixed-price theory of a closed economy; it sits opposite the loanable-funds theory (diagram 20), where saving and investment determine a real interest rate. The two are reconciled in the IS-LM framework (diagram 71). The model assumes the central bank targets the money stock, whereas modern central banks typically set the interest rate directly and let the money supply adjust — which simply flips the diagram (a horizontal policy rate). It also treats "the" interest rate as single, ignoring the term structure (diagram 103) and risk premia, and in a liquidity trap (diagram 92) money and bonds become perfect substitutes, the MD curve goes flat, and open-market operations no longer move rates.
Quick check: real GDP rises while the central bank holds the money supply fixed. What happens to the equilibrium interest rate?

145. Stolper-Samuelson: winners and losers from a price change

Diagram 116 shows why factor endowments drive the pattern of trade; this diagram completes the story by showing the domestic distributional consequences. The Stolper-Samuelson theorem is one of the most politically important results in economics: it explains why free trade, though it raises total national income, creates losers as well as winners inside each country — and predicts exactly which group loses.

Trade raises national income but predictably reshuffles who gets it
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Higher relative price of the capital-intensive good → real return to capital rises, real wage falls. Trade raises that price in the capital-abundant country, so capital gains and labour loses.
Analysis. The two lines embody the Stolper-Samuelson theorem: for a small change in the relative price of a good, the real return to the factor used intensively in that good rises more than proportionately, while the real return to the other factor falls — the "magnification effect." In a capital-abundant country, Heckscher-Ohlin predicts exports of the capital-intensive good, so trade raises that good's domestic relative price (from the autarky line to the higher free-trade line). Reading up to the two curves, the real rental rate on capital rises and the real wage falls. Crucially both are REAL changes: capital owners can buy more of both goods, workers fewer, regardless of which good's price is used as the yardstick. The mirror result holds abroad: in the labour-abundant trading partner, trade raises the relative price of the labour-intensive good and so raises real wages there.
Evaluation. Stolper-Samuelson is a sharp, testable prediction and underlies much of the political economy of trade — for instance, why unskilled labour in rich, skill-abundant countries often resists liberalisation. But its assumptions are strong: two goods, two factors, perfect factor mobility between industries, both goods still produced after trade, and identical technologies across countries. Relaxing them softens the result. The specific-factors (Ricardo-Viner) model, where capital is stuck in its sector in the short run, predicts that the immobile factor in the export sector gains and in the import sector loses, with labour ambiguous — often a better description of the short run. Empirically, technology and the rise of global supply chains have muddied the link between trade and wages, and the theorem says nothing about the compensation that could, in principle, make trade Pareto-improving.
Quick check: a labour-abundant developing country opens to trade. Stolper-Samuelson predicts that its real wages will:

146. Covered interest parity: the no-arbitrage line in currency markets

The purchasing-power-parity diagram (64) pins down exchange rates through goods prices; covered interest parity (CIP) pins down the forward exchange rate through interest rates and is enforced by arbitrage almost perfectly. It is the backbone of foreign-exchange hedging and the carry trade, and its rare breakdowns — the "cross-currency basis" since 2008 — are watched closely as a gauge of stress in the global financial system.

No hedged free lunch: the forward rate absorbs the interest gap
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
CIP is a 45° line: the forward premium on a currency equals its interest-rate disadvantage. Points off the line are riskless arbitrage opportunities that trading quickly eliminates.
Analysis. Covered interest parity states F ÷ S = (1 + r) ÷ (1 + r*), which for small rates is approximately forward premium ≈ r − r*, the 45° line drawn here. The logic is pure no-arbitrage: an investor with home currency can either invest at home earning r, or convert at the spot rate S, invest abroad at r*, and sell the proceeds forward at the pre-agreed rate F. Because the forward contract removes all exchange-rate risk, the two strategies must yield the same certain return; if they did not, arbitrageurs would exploit the gap until F adjusted. A point below the line (forward premium too low relative to the interest gap) is exploited by borrowing the low-yield currency and investing the high-yield one fully hedged, which pushes F up and the point back to the line. Unlike uncovered parity, CIP involves no forecasting — every price in it is known today — which is why it holds so tightly.
Evaluation. CIP held almost exactly for decades, but since the 2008 crisis a persistent "cross-currency basis" has opened up: dealers' balance-sheet costs, regulatory capital charges and dollar-funding demand mean the arbitrage is no longer costless, so points can sit slightly off the line. Its cousin, uncovered interest parity — which replaces the forward rate with the expected future spot rate and so requires no hedging — fails routinely in the data (the "forward premium puzzle"), and the profitability of the carry trade is precisely a bet against it. So the diagram is best read as an exact statement about hedged, contractual returns and only a rough, often-violated guide to how spot exchange rates actually evolve.
Quick check: the home interest rate is 5% and the foreign rate is 2%. Covered interest parity implies the home currency trades in the forward market at:

147. The Malthusian trap: why living standards stagnated for millennia

Before the modern growth models (Solow, diagram 73; endogenous growth, diagram 74) can impress, students need to see the world those models escaped. Thomas Malthus's 1798 model explains the most striking fact in economic history: for thousands of years, average living standards barely rose despite countless inventions. It is also the intellectual ancestor of poverty-trap models (diagram 141) and of debates about population and resources.

For most of history, progress bought more people, not richer ones
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Income per head falls with population (diminishing returns on fixed land); population is stationary only at subsistence. Equilibrium pins income at subsistence — and a productivity gain is competed away by a larger population.
Analysis. Two relationships define the model. First, a downward-sloping income-per-head curve: on fixed land, the marginal and average product of labour fall as population rises. Second, a subsistence income at which the birth rate equals the death rate, so population is constant. Equilibrium is where the income curve crosses the subsistence line; it is stable because any income above subsistence raises population (a movement down the curve toward P*) and any income below it lowers population. The decisive comparative-static is a technology improvement, which shifts the whole income curve up: income per head jumps, population growth turns positive, and the economy slides along the new higher curve back to the same subsistence income — but at a larger population P. Living standards return to where they started; only the number of people is permanently higher.
Evaluation. The Malthusian model fits the pre-industrial data remarkably well — across two millennia, real wages oscillated around subsistence and population tracked technology, and shocks like the Black Death raised wages exactly as the model predicts (fewer people on the same land). Its famous failure is the modern era: since about 1800, sustained productivity growth has outpaced population growth, real incomes have risen more than tenfold in industrial economies, and — through the demographic transition — higher income now lowers birth rates rather than raising them, breaking the link Malthus assumed. So the model is not a law of nature but a description of a technological regime with slow innovation and income-driven fertility. It remains relevant for thinking about resource limits, and its logic recurs whenever gains are absorbed by a growing claimant population rather than rising per-capita welfare.
Quick check: in the Malthusian model, a new farming technique permanently raises land productivity. In the long run this leads to:

148. The Security Market Line: how CAPM prices systematic risk

Diagram 121 shows why diversification eliminates firm-specific risk, leaving only systematic risk to be priced. The Security Market Line is the payoff of that argument: the Capital Asset Pricing Model's single equation relating an asset's expected return to its beta. It is the workhorse of finance — used to set the cost of equity, judge fund managers, and value companies — and the sharpest statement of the idea that you are rewarded only for risk you cannot diversify away.

You are paid for market risk you can't escape, not for risk you can
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
SML runs from (β=0, r_f) through (β=1, r_m); slope = market risk premium. Assets above are underpriced, below overpriced. Only beta is rewarded.
Analysis. The Security Market Line is E(r) = r_f + β(r_m − r_f), plotted here as a straight line from the risk-free point (0, 3%) through the market portfolio (1, 9%) with slope equal to the market risk premium of 6%. Beta is the covariance of an asset's return with the market divided by the market's variance, so it measures the asset's contribution to the risk of a diversified portfolio, not its total volatility. That is why the horizontal axis is beta and not standard deviation: an asset with huge idiosyncratic volatility but zero beta plots at the risk-free return, because its stand-alone risk washes out in a portfolio. In equilibrium every asset lies exactly on the line; a positive "alpha" (a point above the SML) signals underpricing and is competed away as investors buy, raising the price and lowering the expected return back onto the line.
Evaluation. CAPM is elegant and still the most widely used cost-of-capital tool, but its empirical record is mixed. The line relating average returns to beta is flatter than CAPM predicts, and systematic patterns — the size, value and momentum effects — earn returns beta cannot explain, which motivated multifactor models (Fama-French) and the arbitrage pricing theory. The model rests on strong assumptions: a single period, homogeneous expectations, frictionless markets, and a truly market-wide portfolio that Roll's critique argues is unobservable. Even so, the core insight survives every extension: diversifiable risk is not priced, so only an asset's contribution to undiversifiable risk should determine its expected return. The SML is the clean visual statement of that principle.
Quick check: a stock is extremely volatile on its own but its returns are uncorrelated with the overall market (β = 0). CAPM says its expected return should be:

149. The bond price–yield relationship: inverse, and convex

The yield curve (diagram 103) plots yields across maturities; this diagram zooms into a single bond and the mechanical, inverse link between its price and its yield — the relationship that transmits central-bank rate changes into asset prices and drives gains and losses across the entire fixed-income world. Getting its shape exactly right (downward-sloping and convex) matters for everything from pension-fund hedging to the 2023 bank failures.

Fixed cashflows mean price must fall when the discount rate rises
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Price and yield move inversely; price = par when yield = coupon; premium below the coupon yield, discount above; the curve is convex, so a straight-line (duration) estimate understates the true price.
Analysis. A bond's price is the present value of its cashflows, P = Σ C÷(1+y)ᵗ + F÷(1+y)ⁿ, a strictly decreasing, convex function of the yield y. The curve crosses par (100) exactly where the yield equals the coupon rate (5%), because there the coupons discount to the face value; below that yield the bond is a premium bond and above it a discount bond. The slope of the curve at any point is (minus) the bond's dollar duration — its first-order sensitivity to yield changes — and the curvature is its convexity, the second-order term. Because the function is convex, the tangent line (a pure-duration estimate) always lies below the true price, so duration overstates the loss from a yield rise and understates the gain from a yield fall; the convexity term corrects this. Longer maturities and lower coupons make the curve both steeper and more convex.
Evaluation. The inverse price–yield relationship is exact, not a behavioural tendency, which is why it is so powerful: it turns interest-rate policy directly into capital gains and losses on trillions of dollars of bonds, and it explains why long-duration portfolios were devastated when yields rose sharply in 2022–23, contributing to bank failures where holdings were not hedged. The convexity refinement matters most for large yield moves and for portfolios of options-like bonds (callable and mortgage-backed bonds can even exhibit negative convexity, where the curve bends the wrong way). The diagram holds default risk and reinvestment risk in the background; in practice a bond's yield also embeds a credit spread, and the "yield" that clears the market reflects expectations, liquidity and risk premia layered on top of this mechanical relationship.
Quick check: you hold a 5% coupon bond and market yields rise to 8%. Your bond will now trade:

150. Hotelling's model: why competitors cluster and parties converge

The median voter theorem (diagram 109) shows political platforms converging on the centre; Hotelling's 1929 spatial model is its origin and its economic twin, explaining the same convergence for shops, products and parties with one simple line. It is the foundational model of product differentiation and location choice, and one of the most vivid demonstrations that individually rational moves can produce a socially wasteful outcome.

Individually rational moves toward the centre leave everyone clustered
Swipe to see the full diagram, or rotate your phone
Customers buy from the nearest seller. Each firm gains by edging toward the centre, so the unique Nash equilibrium has both at the median — minimum differentiation — even though spreading out would serve customers better.
Analysis. Model the market as the interval [0,1] with consumers distributed uniformly and each buying from the closer firm; a firm's demand is the length of line nearer to it. Given rival location, a firm's best response is to move just to the rival's inside, capturing the rival's near-side customers while keeping all of its own — so any pair of distinct locations is unstable. The unique Nash equilibrium in pure location choice is both firms at the median, 0.5, each serving half. Note the welfare comparison: the socially efficient configuration (minimising total travel distance) is the firms at 0.25 and 0.75, exactly where they do NOT end up. The private incentive to poach the marginal customer drives them together, raising average travel cost — a neat case of a Nash equilibrium that is Pareto-inferior. The same logic, with voters instead of consumers and platforms instead of locations, is the median voter theorem.
Evaluation. Minimum differentiation is a powerful intuition — it rationalises clustering of car dealerships, the near-identical menus of rival chains, and centrist convergence in two-party systems — but the sharp result depends on the setup. If firms also compete on price (not just location), d'Aspremont, Gabszewicz and Thisse showed the centre can unravel: standing too close triggers ruinous price competition, giving firms a reason to differentiate MAXIMALLY instead. With three or more firms, a uniform equilibrium at the centre may not exist. And in politics the model omits abstention, turnout, primaries, and multi-dimensional issues, all of which pull platforms away from the exact median. So Hotelling is best read as identifying one strong force — the pull toward the rival's position — whose real-world strength depends on whether price competition and consumer loyalty push back.
Quick check: two ice-cream sellers on a beach each want to maximise customers, who walk to the nearest cart. In equilibrium they will:

151. Discussion questions, glossary and further reading

Questions to work through, individually or in class

  1. Using diagram one, explain why governments raise more predictable revenue by taxing goods with inelastic demand, and give one UK example beyond cigarettes.
  2. Compare diagrams three and four. In both cases the free market gets the quantity wrong, but in opposite directions. Explain, using MPC, MSC, MPB and MSB notation, why the direction differs.
  3. Using diagram five, explain why price above marginal cost under monopoly is described as allocatively inefficient, and evaluate one argument for why monopoly might still benefit consumers over time.
  4. Using diagrams eight and thirteen together, explain why the same policy, a minimum wage, can raise employment in one labour market structure and reduce it in another.
  5. Using diagrams nine, ten and eleven together, explain the difference between a demand side shock and a supply side shock in terms of the direction that price level and output move.
  6. Using diagram twelve, explain why the long run Phillips curve is drawn as vertical, and evaluate whether this means governments have no tools available to reduce unemployment in the long run.
  7. Using diagram fourteen, explain the difference between actual growth and potential growth, and evaluate which is the more important goal for a government to prioritise, and why.

Glossary

Deadweight welfare loss
The reduction in total economic welfare, meaning consumer surplus plus producer surplus, caused by a market not operating at the allocatively efficient quantity.
MPC and MSC
Marginal private cost and marginal social cost. The cost to the producer alone, compared with the cost to society as a whole including any externality.
MPB and MSB
Marginal private benefit and marginal social benefit. The benefit to the individual consumer alone, compared with the benefit to society as a whole.
Pigouvian tax
A tax set exactly equal to the external cost per unit, designed to move MPC onto MSC and restore the socially optimal output.
Price discrimination
Charging different prices to different customer groups for an identical good, based on differing price elasticities of demand.
Monopsony
A market with a single or dominant buyer, most commonly analysed as a single major employer in a labour market.
MRP
Marginal revenue product. The extra revenue a firm earns from employing one more unit of a factor of production, such as labour.
LRAS
Long run aggregate supply. The total output an economy can produce once prices and wages have fully adjusted, determined by the quantity and quality of its resources.
SRAS
Short run aggregate supply. The output firms are willing to produce at each price level given their current wage and input costs, which shift when those costs change.
Output gap
The difference between actual real GDP and potential real GDP. Positive when the economy is producing above potential, negative when it is producing below.
Stagflation
A situation in which the price level rises while real output falls at the same time, typically caused by a supply side or cost push shock rather than a demand side one.
NAIRU
The non accelerating inflation rate of unemployment. The unemployment rate at which inflation stays stable rather than rising or falling, corresponding to the natural rate on the long run Phillips curve.
Marshall Lerner condition
The rule that a currency depreciation only improves the trade balance if the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds one.

Further reading

  • Your textbook's chapter notes on the same topic, since a second explanation in different wording, alongside worked diagrams, often clarifies a concept faster than rereading the same source twice.
  • Your exam board's own specification and past paper mark schemes, Edexcel, AQA, CIE 9708 or 9609, or IB, which remain the single best source for exactly which labels and shaded areas an examiner expects on each diagram.
  • A textbook with worked numerical examples, for instance calculating tax revenue or deadweight loss from given equations, to practise the mathematics behind these diagrams rather than only the shapes.
This guide presents standard, exam board aligned economic theory and diagrams built from first principles for teaching purposes. It does not reproduce text or images from any third party website. Coordinates in every diagram were checked algebraically, matching gradients and intersections, so that every shift shown is directionally and, where an exact number is stated, numerically consistent with standard microeconomic and macroeconomic theory. The six macroeconomics diagrams, numbers nine through fourteen, deliberately share the same starting equilibrium, so a student who works through them in order sees one consistent model economy respond to demand shocks, supply shocks, and growth, rather than six unrelated examples.
